We also bought little bags of spices at really low prices... a highly recommended experience!!!

clauses.clause_text: We also bought little bags of spices at really low prices...

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: Everything was great. We decided to visit this spice farm because it was the closest to our hotel and had good reviews. The visit is well worth it. They show you many fruits and spices they have on the plantation. Very friendly. At the end, a guy climbs a coconut tree at least 20 meters tall to give you a tasting of various fruits, and then he takes you to a shop where you can buy their products. The visit itself costs $5 per person. They really put a lot of care into it.

clauses.clause_text: The visit itself costs $5 per person.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content:
We spent 2 hours walking,exploring the garden, and in the end tasting delicious fruits.
Our young guides provided friendly, relaxed atmosphere.
Entrance fee 5$ or 10 000 shillings

clauses.clause_text: Entrance fee 5$ or 10 000 shillings

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content:
We booked with Mussa Abasi spice village during our recent holiday to Zanzibar.
Booking was super easy and we ended up booking for a same day visit.
Transfers were offered to us at a very reasonable rate and we were collected and returned to our hotel.
The visit was excellent and we learnt so much! Bilal was our tour guide and he was very knowledgeable. He took his time to show us all around the different spice and fruit trees/plants and sampling each one was great fun!
After the tour was finished, we enjoyed a fruit platter with Bilal and his colleagues and enjoyed wearing the hats and necklaces they made for us.
It was a fantastic afternoon spent in beautiful surroundings. It has also prompted us to try and become more self-sufficient at home!
The village children were also lovely to meet. There is an opportunity to purchase sweets for the children, along with spices to take home at the end of the tour.
Highly recommend a visit to this spice village. You will not be disappointed!
Thank you Bilal - Keep up the fabulous work!

clauses.clause_text: Transfers were offered to us at a very reasonable rate and we were collected and returned to our hotel.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content:
We spent 3 hours at the spice farm and Bilal was a really great guide to show us around. He explained us every plant and spice which is growing there: vanilla, pepper, ginger, orange, pineapple and many more. It was really interesting and we got the chance to try and smell every plant. In the end, we got a lot of fruits to eat - thank you again!
Entry fee was $5. you are also able to buy some spices for cheap prices.
Highly recommend this spice farm!

clauses.clause_text: Entry fee was $5.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content:
Everything was wonderful. Our guide, Balil, took the time to show us everything. Although the farm isn't very, very big, we saw and tasted many plants and trees. We were shown how to harvest coconuts from the palm tree, and of course, we got to taste them afterward. You can also buy various spices there, but you're not obligated to.
At the end, we received handmade gifts and ate fruit.
Thank you so much for this time, and I wish you all the best, Balil! 😇

clauses.clause_text: You can also buy various spices there, but you're not obligated to.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: This is our second visit to a spice farm in Zanzibar, and this one was decidedly less impressive. Almost all the trees were small or bare-bones. Three years ago, we visited a farm near Stone Town, and everything was more interesting.

clauses.clause_text: Almost all the trees were small or bare-bones.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: We visited this spice plantation today. It's not large. The staff is very friendly, smiling, knowledgeable, and helpful. The young guys are polite and accommodating. The refreshments were first-rate. We had a lot of fun... it's amazing how much we learned. We wish the plantation continued growth. The songs, the leaf decorations... a great atmosphere. The entrance fee of $5 per person is a good price. The parking lot is a bit tricky to get to and the sign is barely visible, which is a good sign for the company. We are very pleased and recommend it... that little guy climbing the palm tree really impressed us. Visit them and give them a chance... they're trying!!!

clauses.clause_text: they're trying!!!

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: I highly recommend it. You can take the dala dala (just get off at the intersection and walk about 800 meters). We were the only two people there, and the guide was very friendly and spoke very good English. We spent about three hours there, including a fruit snack. Entrance fee: 10,000 TSH.

clauses.clause_text: We spent about three hours there, including a fruit snack.
Entrance fee: 10,000 TSH.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content:
We have seen other Spice Villages, which were very touristic and a scam, but this one was very authentic and friendly. A little bit hidden from the main road, just follow the sign and the bumpy path to the back of the village. Our guide was not pushy and not tried to sell us anyhting. We would definitely recommend.
One recommendation to the owner: please clean up the garbage in your beautiful garden! There is a lot of waste around, please protect your land and soil.

clauses.clause_text: Our guide was not pushy and not tried to sell us anyhting.
One recommendation to the owner: please clean up the garbage in your beautiful garden!
There is a lot of waste around, please protect your land and soil.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: The tour lasted about two hours. The guide explained everything very well, and we discovered lots of new fruits. The tasting of different fruits was very enjoyable. We received lots of gifts, like bracelets made from plants. The people were very friendly and passionate. It was an incredible experience. The price of the tour was more than reasonable. I highly recommend it!

clauses.clause_text: The tour lasted about two hours.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content:
The visit itself was exceptional; we discovered about thirty different fruits, roots, and plants. The guide was very friendly.
Then, we arrived at the spices and tasting area, and that's when we saw a monkey on a leash... We couldn't possibly condone this. We paid for the excursion, not a penny more, and left immediately. Animal cruelty must stop!

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: We hunted for a non-commercial and very genuine experience. We were very happy to find this little spice farm with a host Muhammad that was very proud to tell you about the many spices and fruits that they grow! We were treated to a coconut climb, woven gifts, fresh tastings from what we had learned about, and had many laughs along the way! We recommend this sweet spice farm for an off-the-beaten-path experience! Don’t be afraid to turn your car down the dirt path as you come to the sign posted street-side! We would bring friends back!

clauses.clause_text: Don’t be afraid to turn your car down the dirt path as you come to the sign posted street-side!

content:
We had a great time at the village!
Mohd was a great guide. He is very funny and we had a lot of laughs with him. We learned a lot about various spices. Even my 8 year old brother had a lot of fun and he usually thinks this kind of stuff is boring.

place_name: Mussa Abasi village spice farm kisongoni
content: We had a great time at this small village owned farm and were amazed how many different types of spices and fruits can be found on this relatively small farm. Saka is a brillant tour guide that not only coordinated the pickup at our hotel (I just needed to contact him using the WhatsApp number on their homepage) but that professionally and with a great sense of humor explained all the different types of spices and fruits. We could taste plenty of fruits at the end of the tour and did purchase spices out of a huge variety and at very fair prices. A must do if on Zanzibar. At the end Saka joined us on traditional local dinner (Ugali) in the Mussa Abasi village center - truly unforgettable! THANKS Saka!

Definitely worth a visit!

At the end, we received crowns for our heads.
We wholeheartedly recommend it.
Adam and Karina.

Before leaving, he gave us palm leaf crowns! I highly recommend this visit, which is certainly much more authentic than the tours organized by agencies.

content:
Leaving this review only to counter the babies crying about the tide and sea urchins and lack of restaurants. It's a beach, in one of the few non-touristic parts of the island, and rich with life sustained by the rich, warm waters.
Only an absolute knob would not prepare for sea urchins (wear sea shoes..) - which Zanzibar is well known for. I swam and went snorkeling here pretty much every day for a week. Plenty to see, a clean beach and clear waters. The place to be if you're looking for a quiet time on an uncrowded beach - for all the high maintenance clowns, Paje is 20 minutes away.
P.S. Can't believe I have to say this but pretty much every tidal beach is only fit to swim in during high-tide.. Google the tide times.

place_name: TO THE HILL KIDICHI SPICE FARM
content:
Thank you to our guide, Adil, for his patient and professional explanations. He asked what kind of tour I wanted, and I said I wanted to learn more about spices without going into too much detail. I tasted and smelled spices throughout the tour, and he even showed me spice-based dyes and demonstrated their uses, which left a deep impression on me. This was a completely new experience for me, engaging all my senses—smell, taste, and touch. The guide was very knowledgeable; he even showed me the Chinese mimosa plant. The staff also wove straw hats for me and opened coconuts for me to drink. I thoroughly enjoyed it and was very happy.
The staff were also very helpful. Since I didn't have a ride back to Stone City, he called a friend of his who had a motorcycle to give me a ride. However, the friend didn't know where I was going and didn't speak English, so the owner decided to give me a ride. The owner was very talkative, asking about my impressions of the spice garden and Zanzibar, as well as how many languages ​​I spoke, which I enjoyed discussing. Thank you for the ride.
In short, I highly recommend this spice garden. I had a wonderful experience.

content: Very interesting tour with info/smelling/tasting approximately 15 different herbs and spices, plus fruit tasting (different fruits depending on season). There is a 10,000 entrance fee but the tour is entirely tip-based so up to you how much you pay (I gave 35,000 for the tour and they seemed happy). I went at midday so had the place to myself - apparently groups come in the morning and late afternoon to avoid the heat.

content:
A must visit when in Zanzibar.

content:
It's interesting to stroll around since there's a lot of choice.
Unfortunately, as a tourist, you pay many times more than usual. :)
For example, a bottle of sugarcane juice normally costs 1000 TSN.
Here, they charge between 5,000 and 10,000 TSN, or even 1000 TSN for snacks instead of 200.
No matter how interesting it is, I definitely wouldn't shop here, because people can see that you're white and a tourist.
As a result, you only get inferior or old spices, since locals don't buy this stuff; they only buy it in certain shops, and they pay much more.
It's better to sell outside the city and do something nice for people who aren't being ripped off and are happy to receive money or even a tip.
Alternatively, there are parking lots that cost 1000 TSN per hour or 3000 TSN per day.
You're often asked if you'd like to donate money – just like everywhere else in Zanzibar :) Unfortunately, with the children it starts with a friendly hello, followed immediately by "Money, money"... a real shame for what is otherwise a lovely little island.

content:
We heard about Zanzibar local (food and fish) market, now it was the time to see how it is, me and my friend, Colbet from South Africa decided to hv a look. We passed through narrow streets from stone town, and finally we reached to this place.
The Darajani market.
The Darajani Market is famous or known as Darajani Fish market or Darajani Food Market or even Darajani Local Market.
These are the names given by different people from different places according to their perspective and the way they categorize it as.
The Market is Open from around 07:30 Am to 10:30 pm and sometimes more depends on the customers.
The Darajani Market tour is one of things to do and you should never miss once you are in this Island, It became one of the most popular and most visited by tourist from around the world and local people, so its a tourist attraction.
Since it have More of the Variety of the Local food, and More Experience in Local trading and marketing experience, Small trade activities.
This is a cash only place, No Cards Services here.
This is One of the famous local food market in Zanzibar.
it's a place where you can find and have almost everything you need in the food section, (Fresh and at a very low / reasonable price.)
The market is very famous due to its unique style, arrangement (Specified Portions) and Running style.
The market has Beef Butches section, Fresh fish Section, Spice section , Fresh Fruits and mixed / different variety Section. so if you fail to find what you are looking for, just go to mixed / different variety Section, there you will get what you want.
so the Sellers have arranged them self in that way to make more life easy to their customers and quest visiting the market. Though the market is very populated especial during the afternoon since different people from part of Zanzibar going there for shopping but still you will find path ways to move around the market.
So if you need some fresh fruits, Vegetables, Fish and meat, Spices and further more even to experience Zanzibarian local life style this is the right place to visit.
I like the way people are so humble, everyone has his or her own internal motivation, Not only youth but even, Women and Older people they all seat together as a community with the aim of one goal to sell as the best they can,
once you are at the market it's a normal thing to see everyone is welcome you at his or her business. People from this area have high and good Customer care with pleasant language that will convince you to stop and buy from him or her and sometimes even just to have a look, this is what encourages them more.
The wonderful this you can come across a local guy Speaking your language, don't be surprised, or you hear someone speaks more than 3 Foreign language.
The market has the best products and cheap price ever,
For anyone you can go with your expensive camera to take pictures but with a request for a permission a person before taking the picture, Some they like to be in the picture some don't like to be in the pictures, so the better way is to ask the individual first.
Do you wanna have more fun, Say or talk to any local person a Swahili word there you go, you will love the moment of being there.
People are very friendly and its a Safe Market.
Thank you everyone these are some of my experiences of being there, i have much to say the beauty of this place but i leave for you to say more after passing to this place.

This is a cash only place, No Cards Services here.

content:
The market itself is definitely worth a visit; it remains very authentic, and the meat and fish section is a real step back in time.
However, beware of tourist scams; prices are significantly inflated. For example, a 250g bag of black pepper was quoted at 25,000 shillings in the market stalls. After some haggling, I got it down to 15,000. Then, looking in the back alleys, where locals seem to shop, the price was 8,000. I bought two or three things there, but the vendor didn't have all the spices I wanted. He took me to a better-stocked supplier, and in that stall, the same pepper was 4,000 shillings. That's a price divided by... six! So I stocked up on spices and came back with over 3 kilos.
It's the same with fabrics; once you're at the market, cross the main street and wander through the alleyways on the other side. Here you'll find the stalls where the locals do their shopping. The prices are much lower and there's practically no room for negotiation.

content:
Bilal's wasn't just a typical excursion to a spice plantation, but a true journey into a Zanzibar community that still lives almost entirely in traditional houses made of wood and mud. We visited the plantation and tasted all the spices picked from the trees, ate freshly picked fruit with Duly, a very friendly and expert guide who is learning Italian. We toured the village with Bilal, who told us about his community, meeting smiling and cheerful children (bring a bag of sweets; you'll make them all happy!). There's also the option, if you'd like, to make a small contribution by purchasing rice or other items at the village's small store. The entire visit took us
over three hours, spending about 20 euros each, half that if you just wanted to visit the spice plantation.
Thank you, Bilal and Duly, for this priceless experience!

content:
Visiting Bilal’s place for the spice and village tour was, without a doubt, one of the most meaningful, eye-opening, and unforgettable experiences I have ever had in Zanzibar.
As a European, being welcomed into the local community and having the opportunity to experience their culture, traditions, daily life, kindness, and incredible humility was something truly special. It gives you a completely different perspective and reminds you how much we can learn from people who live differently from us.
This is so much more than a tour. It is a genuine human experience, one that touches you deeply and stays with you long after you leave.
The village tour is an absolute MUST. Meeting the local people, seeing their everyday life, interacting with the children and families, and realizing how even a small donation can help provide food for the village makes the experience incredibly meaningful. What may feel like a small gesture to us can genuinely make a difference here.
You are not simply visiting Zanzibar. You are connecting with the real people who make this island so extraordinary.
I truly, truly recommend visiting Bilal and taking the time to discover this side of Zanzibar. And please, help spread the word. Tell your friends, recommend this experience to your hotel, and encourage other travelers to visit. The more people know about places like this, the more we can support local communities directly while experiencing something authentic and unforgettable in return.
Zanzibar is famous for its paradise beaches, but there is so much more behind them. If you come here, give yourself the chance to meet these wonderful people, listen to their stories, understand their way of life, and experience the true heart and soul of the island.
You may arrive thinking you are simply going on a spice and village tour, but you might leave with something much more valuable: a different perspective on life.
Please visit. Please support them. And most importantly, please speak about them.
Some experiences deserve more than five stars. ❤️
Highly, highly recommended.

clauses.clause_text: You are not simply visiting Zanzibar.
Zanzibar is famous for its paradise beaches, but there is so much more behind them.

Bilal told us 20 euros is not enough for a bag of rice and I didn't understand how much was enough (probably because I already felt stressed about people queuing up). To be honest it was the only dent in an otherwise authentic and good experience. Having this information upfront would make it much better.
Also, prepare to be assertive when being offered to buy soap or oils, but that applies all around.

I would probably opt in for going into one home and actually sitting down to get to know the family (even if only a little).

content:
This tour was an absolute highlight of my trip to Zanzibar. Doing this tour alone as a female traveler, I felt completely safe, comfortable, and welcomed at every single moment.
Bilal personally guided me through a traditional small village, offering a genuinely authentic glimpse into the daily lives of the locals. This was followed by a fascinating and highly educational spice tour in what felt like their own backyard. The young guide was incredibly knowledgeable, sharing insightful facts about every plant, and I got to taste and smell everything.
Later, we cooked a traditional meal together. The lady leading the kitchen was amazing and completely involved me in the cooking process, which was a fantastic experience. The food turned out absolutely delicious!
Logistics: The hotel transfer was perfectly organized. You can buy local items at the end, but there is absolutely no pressure to do so. A beautifully authentic tour that supports a great cause. Wishing the wonderful people there all the very best! 🙏🏼

clauses.clause_text: You can buy local items at the end, but there is absolutely no pressure to do so.

content:
Highly recommended!
We did the Spice Tour, the Village Tour, and the Cooking Class. Everyone involved was very friendly, knowledgeable, and always helpful.
The Spice Tour offers many new impressions and insights into everyday spices. It's incredibly interesting to see the plants and raw fruits in person.
The Village Tour is fascinating. Friendly hosts in a typical village for the region. Living conditions aren't easy. You get to see traditional and modern housing and building styles. Afterward, you can support the residents by shopping at the local store. They sell classic souvenirs, sweets, and household items. The latter two support the village and are available for the children on weekends.
The Cooking Class follows. It's worth coming hungry for this, as the food is delicious! The cook cooks over five or six coals at once and makes it look effortless. The farm's spices are used liberally in all the dishes, from fish and pilau to banana dessert.
All in all, I highly recommend it!
You'll find classic souvenirs as well as sweets and household items. P.S. for my fellow Germans: The tour will be conducted in English.

clauses.clause_text: The cook cooks over five or six coals at once and makes it look effortless.

The guide who conducted the tour (not Bilal) was knowledgeable but perhaps because it was the low season, the tour felt somewhat rushed, as if it was being completed out of obligation rather than enthusiasm.
It is a pity that we did not experience the full cultural and village activities that are often mentioned in other reviews, as those were a major reason we chose this tour.

content:
An incredibly impressive tour through a village and the flora of Zanzibar. Bilal, the company's founder, does amazing work in a very friendly way. The guided tour through the traditional village was deeply moving and incredibly grounding. The inhabitants live very simply and try to survive by selling their woven roofing materials, spices, and fruits. They also grow rice, but not enough. Unfortunately, it's not enough to get by, so they have two small shops selling basic foodstuffs (rice, beans, soap, diapers, and a few sweets—no, nothing from Ferrero). Anyone who wants to help can buy these items and donate them directly. Bilal raises awareness very sensitively and without pressure. And when you see the happy faces of the residents, especially the children with their lollipops, you know what €20 can do locally. I definitely had tears in my eyes. Such friendly and cheerful people, despite their very simple living conditions. After visiting the village, Ibrahim gave us a fantastic introduction to the world of spices and their uses, and I'm guessing he did it without ever having taken a sophisticated communication course. I learned some facts that I won't reveal here – I need them to show off! 😊 Of course, we also got to enjoy plenty of the local fruits (mangoes, melons, pineapples, coconuts, guavas, and bao bao, though they're not in season right now).
Booking the tour through the website is incredibly easy. Bilal responds to WhatsApp messages in no time. He also perfectly organized the transportation to and from Nungwi at a very good price. Everything was perfect – thank you, Bilal! 😍
It was an incredible day, and I'm so glad I stumbled across the website and chose this tour instead of a run-of-the-mill tourist trip.

content:
I walked into the Peace Memorial Museum in Stone Town without much expectation. From the street, the building looks as if it's been around for generations.
A white, round rotunda, old walls, shaded by palm trees. It was built in the early twentieth century, when Zanzibar was still a British protectorate.
The architect was John Sinclair, the same one who designed the Zanzibar House of Wonders. The architecture is a mixture of many elements: Arabic lines, a touch of colonial style, local plaster, and a feeling of the hot east coast.
Inside, the museum is simple, a bit chaotic, but there's a certain honesty to it. Old photographs of sultans, weapons, nautical charts, trade documents, and items from local homes are on display.
The exhibits look tired in places, but the objects themselves are powerful. The island's history is difficult, especially considering that Zanzibar was long a major center for the slave trade and maritime trade between Arabia, India, and East Africa.
I spent about an hour there. I walked slowly, reading the signs, listening to footsteps in the empty halls. I felt like I'd entered a place that remembers more than it tells. It's as if the museum stands at the junction of eras, where the colonial world, Arab culture, and African life have mingled and still remain connected.
If you love history and want to see Zanzibar not just from the beaches but through its roots, it's worth a visit. It's a quiet place, a little worn, but vibrant.

content:
Disappointing and Disturbing Experience at Jozani Forest
I visited Jozani Forest hoping to witness the rare and critically endangered red colobus monkeys in their natural habitat. Unfortunately, what I saw was far from respectful or responsible wildlife tourism.
Despite clear rules to keep a 3-meter distance from the monkeys, many tourists completely ignored them—getting far too close, even standing on or over the animals to get their photos. The monkeys appeared visibly stressed, and it was heartbreaking to watch.
Even more concerning was the behavior of the guides. Rather than ensuring the safety and well-being of the animals, they seemed more focused on collecting tips and pleasing the tourists. I saw no efforts made to correct or guide inappropriate behavior. It felt chaotic and disrespectful.
We left early, unable to continue watching such blatant disregard for the welfare of these beautiful, vulnerable animals. I hope real conservation efforts are implemented soon—before it's too late for the red colobus monkeys.

content:
*House of Wonders (Beit-al-Ajaib)*
History
- Built in 1883 by Sultan Bargash bin Said
- Served as a palace and a repository for Zanzibar's treasures
- Damaged by British warship HMS Philomel in 1896
- Restored in 2010-2012
Attractions for Tourists
1. *Exhibition halls*: Showcasing Zanzibar's history, culture, and natural environment
2. *Historic artifacts*: Including furniture, jewelry, and other relics from the palace
3. *Zanzibar's oldest elevator*: Built in 1883, it's one of the oldest in Africa
4. *Panoramic views*: Of Stone Town and the harbor from the top floor
Food and Beverages
1. *Traditional Zanzibari cuisine*: Including dishes like urojo (a spicy soup), mandazi (fried doughnuts), and chapati (flatbread)
2. *Seafood*: Fresh catches from the Indian Ocean, often served grilled or in curries
3. *Local fruits*: Like mangoes, coconuts, and pineapples
4. *Coffee and tea*: Served in traditional cafes and restaurants
Tips for Visitors
1. *Dress modestly*: Respect local customs and traditions
2. *Remove shoes*: When entering the palace or mosques
3. *Respect local rules*: No photography in certain areas, and no touching of artifacts
4. *Haggle politely*: When shopping in local markets
The House of Wonders is a must-visit attraction in Stone Town, Zanzibar. Its rich history, cultural significance, and stunning architecture make it an unforgettable experience.

content: Wonderful landmark building in Stone Town, Zanzibar. Largest tallest building in Stone Town, facing the Forodhani Gardens on the old town's seafront, in Mizingani Road. Lies between the Old Fort and the Palace Museum. It is one among the six palaces built by Barghash bin Said, second Sultan of Zanzibar and was built in 1883. First building to have electricity in Zanzibar and an elevator in East Africa. Light house which stood in front the building got destroyed in the Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 causing minor damage to Beit Al Ajaib. Renovation in1897 brought in Clock Tower into the façade of the building. It was a government office, a school and later a museum. After renovation it will shine fully with bygone glory. It is and will be one of Stone Town's major tourist attractions. Good luck.

content:
Nungwi Beach is truly beautiful. The white sand, the color of the water, and the scenery are spectacular.
Unfortunately, our experience was significantly marred by the sheer number of vendors and people constantly offering services.
While walking along the beach, you're approached repeatedly with offers of excursions, souvenirs, massages, and all sorts of other services. I wouldn't mind someone approaching you once to offer something; I completely understand they're trying to make a living. The problem is the frequency and, above all, the persistence. Often, politely saying "no, thank you" isn't enough.
Some people continue walking beside you, asking questions or trying to maintain a conversation even after you've made it clear you're not interested. When this happens every few minutes, something as simple as a peaceful walk on the beach becomes exhausting instead of relaxing.
My partner also felt particularly uncomfortable with the amount of attention she received, which made it even harder for us to enjoy the beach.
Hopefully, in the future they can manage this situation better so that visitors can enjoy such a spectacular place without feeling constantly harassed.

content:
Nungwi Beach is a beach in Tanzania, located in northern Zanzibar. It's a shame that such a beautiful beach loses all its charm due to the beach boys; they don't leave you alone, day or night. It's impossible to relax on these beaches.
What makes it special is its white sand, turquoise waters, and ideal sea for swimming for most of the day, even at low tide. Unlike other beaches on the island, the water here is usually more accessible. The beach contrasts sharply with the poverty inland, with high-end beach bars and beach boys right on the sand, and just 30 meters away... absolute poverty.
The sunsets are especially beautiful, with the traditional dhow boats creating a spectacular scene. In short, Nungwi Beach is a skippable stop in Zanzibar. A comfortable and different beach to enjoy the sea and the tropical atmosphere. If you can, look for other, more authentic options.

content:
We spent the day at Nungwi beach (northern part of the island) to jet ski and take a sunset cruise. It is a very busy and touristy part of the island (we stayed on the south east coast). The water is absolutely amazing and good vibes all round but the roads and parts of the beach are very busy.
Sunset Cruise on a Dhow: the entire experience lasted from about 4pm to 7pm. There is music on board, traditional songs and instruments. They also served fresh tropical fruit and drinks (drinks cost extra). At one point they stopped and allowed to jump off into the water, which my husband enjoyed! All in all a lovely experience!
Jet skis: we took a shorter ride option and it was safe and lots of fun! We negotiated the price down.
Be prepared with umbrella/chairs, else you pay to have shade and a lounger.
You will be approached by lots of locals trying to sell their services for jet skis and cruises, be prepared. We had our own guide with us so it was easy enough to avoid long talks etc. Understand that this is their way of earning a living, and they must make the most of the busy season as the island basically shuts down in the rainy months.

content:
Nungwi is exactly the type of beach where you realize why you travel thousands of kilometers for “ordinary” sand and sea. Fine white sand, turquoise water and palm trees like from a catalog, but without the sterile feeling of an artificial paradise. This is where it lives.
A big plus: minimal low tide. Unlike other parts of Zanzibar, you can swim practically all day, which sounds banal until you experience it elsewhere. The sea is calm, warm and ideal for swimming or just “standing in the water and staring into space”.
The atmosphere is a mix of local life and relaxed tourism. Fishing boats, Masai, beach boys, restaurants right on the sand, sunsets that really don’t deserve a filter. Nungwi is not a quiet haven for hermits – it’s a lively beach, but not annoying.
Food? Fresh fish, shrimp, octopus, simple beach bars and better restaurants. Prices are fair, if you know when to smile and when to say no politely.
Cons? More people, especially in high season, and sometimes overly active vendors. But honestly – that’s the price of a place that works.
Verdict:
Nungwi Beach is one of the best beaches in Zanzibar. Not only pretty for photos, but really great to stay. If you want a beach where you can live, swim, eat, drink and watch the sunset in the evening without thinking about the time – Nungwi is the right choice.

content: So, the beach and the water are absolutely wonderful. What's less nice are these fake Maasai who constantly try to sell you something. Sex tourism is a big issue, and you can see it clearly. There aren't any real Maasai on these beaches, but rather, as I said, fake Maasai; you find them on several beaches. The beach is very expansive, very wide, clean, the sand is white, and it would actually be quite wonderful. We were there on November 27, 2025, and there were very few people since it was the off-season. Nevertheless, there were an incredible number of vendors on the beach, and without a local guide, you'd probably be overwhelmed. The north of Zanzibar is the party area. Music is playing everywhere, and there are also many boats on the water with loud music. If you want peace and quiet, you shouldn't book a hotel there but head further east. content: Nungwi Beach is located on the shores of the village of the same name, in the north of Unguja Island. This island is the largest in the Zanzibar metropolitan area, and therefore is often referred to as "Zanzibar." Nungwi is one of the most densely populated villages on the island, not counting the capital, of course. It is primarily a fishing village, with its corresponding attributes. The Indian Ocean at this beach is warm and clear, mostly shallow in the coastal zone. As this is a fishing harbor, hundreds of traditional sailing fishing boats can be seen in the ocean. There are numerous starfish here, visible when walking in the shallow water at low tide. Sea urchins are almost absent, though they are abundant closer to the lighthouse. Low tides here reach a maximum of 500 meters, which is quite a bit. Therefore, low tide here is a fun way to walk along the ocean floor behind the receding water. The sand line is up to 50 meters wide, even at high tide. The beach is much wider in the section closer to the village of Kendwa. However, in Nungwi, the beach is also wide enough, even for playing soccer. The sand is white and fine as flour. The beach is very well-developed in terms of infrastructure. There are numerous restaurants, decent shops, souvenir stalls, and wonderful locals, who are a unique experience.

content: You arrive – and suddenly time stands still. The sand lies before you like sifted powdered sugar, dazzling white, soft as sleep, interspersed with tiny, pale blue stones that look like polished drops of the sky. They say they only exist here – noni stones, half myth, half memory. The sea? White. Clear. Immaculate. So pure it would seem like sparkling water – if it weren't so salty. 26 to 28 degrees Celsius, liquid light on your skin. No water. A temptation. Red and blue starfish glow between the waves, so clear it's as if someone forgot to turn them off. The sun? Non-existent. A magnifying glass. Anyone who walks along the beach for fifteen minutes without sunscreen or shade – even though the thermometer only reads 30°C – will burn their skin like in a microwave. Level three. Free. The ozone layer seems to exist here only as a memory. Shade is only found under the palm trees, and even they look stern. Sunscreen? SPF 50 is the polite start. Forgetting it makes you part of the geology – red like coral, silent like rocks. And yet: you stay. Because this beach – Nungwi, in the far north of Zanzibar – doesn't just dazzle, it transforms. There are guesthouses that seem like lost poems, two shops with everything and nothing, and they serve you the best fish barefoot, right at the grill, while the sea doesn't recede. There's low tide here too – but it comes quietly. No great retreat, just a whisper, a brief unveiling of the underworld before the sea reclaims it. Like a breath, not a withdrawal. And then: a tuna, yellow and blue like a painting, caught by fishermen, later served on the grill right on the beach. Smoke mingles with the salt air and the music of a guitar that no one is really playing – it emerges through the whisper of the wind, in the rustling of the palm trees swaying in the breeze. And they listen. Just like you. The place doesn't speak. It answers. Anyone heading south from here to Stone Town – about two hours – should budget between 40 and 70 euros for a taxi, or even 80 depending on their bargaining skills. I myself paid 70 euros from the airport to the Hilton in Nungwi – a fair deal. And it's worth it. In Stone Town, the narrow streets are fragrant with rosemary and fennel – a small Italian pizzeria, run by a woman from Abruzzo, bakes pizzas just like Mamma used to. They say she has the flour delivered directly from Italy – and you believe it when, in the hot streets, you suddenly think you can smell Naples. Anyone who's seen the film will also love visiting Freddie Mercury's birthplace – a small museum, a guided tour, a few minutes in which you feel like you're taking a step closer to him. And then there's Turtle Island – accessible by small boat. Some of the oldest animals in the world, they say. A hundred years old, some even older. And strong – so strong you'd think they could carry you. You can feed them, you can pet them – it's like a retirement home on the other side of the water, where time moves more slowly. And if you look closely: the old doors in Stone Town – massive, clad in iron – were built to keep elephants out. They used to roam these alleys. Now they're just stories. And somewhere among the shadows of these houses sit men making leather shoes, measured by foot, sewn by hand. A different pace, a different world. And then you're back. There, where the sky touches the sea, where the horizon seduces the dolphins with colors, consciousness hits you like a slap in the face – you recognize yourself… and forget your poem. The tuna isn't simply fried there, no – first charmingly advised by the waves, it leaps onto the grill with a hint of lemon – that was a meal. January 14-28

content:
Disappointed is the word. My visit to Zanzibar has been a profound disappointment, far removed from the idyllic image it usually projects. The experience has been marked by a series of negative points that have left me with a constant feeling of frustration and, at times, of being ripped off.
First of all, the initial costs are surprisingly high. Not only is transportation to the island expensive, but they also require payment for entry insurance, despite already having travel insurance purchased in my home country. This duplication of expenses is, to say the least, unjustifiable and makes you feel like you're being taken advantage of from the very beginning.
Hygiene is another of the most critical and disheartening aspects. The island is extremely dirty, with plastic and trash everywhere. The beaches, which should be the main attraction, are sadly polluted, marring the landscape and making the experience of enjoying them unpleasant. It's truly shocking to see such a level of environmental neglect in a place that depends on tourism.
Furthermore, the feeling of being constantly ripped off is palpable. Prices for tourists are blatantly higher than for locals, making you feel exploited in every transaction, from buying a simple souvenir to haggling over a service or taking the bus. To get from Stone Town to Nungwi, I was charged 10,000 tzh one way, while it costs locals 2,500, and then 5,000 tzh the return trip. It makes no sense. While food in restaurants can be affordable, eating on the street is a gamble and often results in being financially ripped off.
The only redeeming quality of my stay was the friendliness of the people. However, even this is overshadowed by their constant push to sell you something, which, while understandable in a tourist context, can become exhausting. Compared to my experience on the Tanzanian mainland, where I felt much more comfortable and at ease, Zanzibar didn't give me that sense of home or authenticity. I definitely feel let down and I, for one, will not be returning.

content:
Zanzibar is actually really disappointing for me, online you see a paradise with beautiful beaches, people snorkelling and swimming with turtles but in reality it’s not at all glamorous, there is rubbish all over the ground everywhere you go, people are living in super run down houses right next to massive fancy hotels, low tide is during the middle of the day so all of the beaches you want to swim at are just sand and reef until high tide at night time and it’s EXPENSIVE. There are much nicer places with lovely beaches that you can travel to for much cheaper and are easier to get around! (Thailand and the Philippines especially)
As a young person travelling Africa with a currency that’s not USD, Euro or Pound (we’re travelling on the Australian dollar -Aud) it’s been pretty reasonable with the conversion but in Zanzibar specifically it’s been crazy expensive, they try to charge everything in USD so trying to hire a moped or scooter for three days they wanted not only $60 USD for the hire ($97 Aud) but also $15 USD ($25 Aud) for a “government driving permit” even when we both have an international license or an IDP (international driving permit) that’s the second “government” fee we’ve come across because you now have to get mandatory Zanzibar insurance when entering at the airport which was $45 USD ($73 Aud) aswell as the Visa I needed for entrance to Tanzania which was $50 USD ($80 Aud) what is the government doing with all this money they’re extorting from tourists if it’s not to try clean up atleast some of the rubbish that’s everywhere, making nice roads or helping with peoples housing.
All of the restaurant menus are in USD and obviously not what the local price is because what local is paying $7 USD ($12 Aud) for a stew, no one. It’s just frustrating because they do obviously make their livings off of tourists (especially the middle age demographic of Americans) which is what you would expect from a popular destination like this but it’s pushing the price of everything up for everyone else. It’s disappointing as someone who loves to travel because of course things cost money but this has got to a point of actually just being ridiculous.
We’re staying where we heard most people stay in Jambiani which was an hour from the airport (it cost us 90,000 TZS/ $35 USD which is $56 Aud) because they only do taxi there’s no ride share app in Zanzibar so trying to get to and from the airport is crazy expensive.
So because we’re staying in Jambiani if we wanted to go and do a snorkelling tour, the turtle sanctuary cave or anything like that it’s all up on the top of the island (roughly a 2 hour drive) in Matemwe which would already be hard on a rented scooter but because the scooter hire is expensive we’d have to try get either a tuk tuk, taxi or on the back of a motorbike all the way there and back for the day it would be not only hard to find someone who would do it but also costly as well, so if you’re planning on doing those things while in Zanzibar (snorkelling tour, swimming with dolphins, turtle sanctuary cave, anything like that) it’s most likely up near Matemwe so definitely spend the extra money on accommodation up there to save the hassle of trying to get there.
Zanzibar is a tourist scam. End of story.

The constant harassment by beach boys and fake Maasai trying to sell items or scam tourists is overwhelming, which explains why the beach is nearly empty—most tourists stay in their resorts to avoid the hassle. content:
The road to Nungwi immediately gives you a sense of what a trip to this corner of Africa is like. Palm trees everywhere, people between cars, local shops that I have no idea what they were selling, lights nowhere, potholes that forced car owners to change their tires every 2 months, scattered houses with tin roofs, honking good mornings and smiles. The hotels are lined up on the beach, which is closed to locals and who can only access it from the village side. We visited 1 of the 3 schools in the village and after talking for a while with the teachers we gave stationery and toys to the children and took pictures with them after asking first of course. In Nungwi there is the phenomenon of tides and beach boys (whom we deal with with patience and kindness because they can be a little persistent but are generally polite and relaxed. If we say a polite and decisive no they will walk away saying hakuna matata, answer the same..)
All hotels have restaurants with traditional food pizzas fries pasta soups burgers seafood and alcohol. In the village there are bars and restaurants which we did not visit, but we did shop for local products and souvenirs (necklaces bracelets, fabrics, landscapes on banana leaves, paintings, wood carvings, drums and more). Support the locals!!. Except for those who sell shells and starfish (it is illegal). Among all of us are the young Maasai, a tribe that lives in the Serengeti desert from northern Tanzania, who have their own style and different way of approaching things (I should say that a little Maasai who followed us every day on our walk on the beach at low tide gave us a necklace as a gift..he was a very sweet and shy child). From Nungwi you can go to Mnemba for snorkeling, walk in Stone Town, to Nakupenda, visit Prison Island for its history and to see the huge turtles and take a sunset cruise.. we did all of that and it was all perfect ✨(all via beach boy Ricky). In Nungwi almost everyone speaks English because it is the second official language of the country. I think the important thing is to give these people a chance to talk to you, to get to know a little about their culture and their way of life, and they are all willing to tell you everything, about their family and the bond they feel, the political indifference and corruption, about the schools and the tuition they are forced to pay, while those who don't have them simply don't get an education, about their difficult living but everyone in the end smiles at you and says hakuna matata..no problem..!!!!!
I love you guys ❤️❤️❤️
ps: they don't care about the starfish that stay behind the low tide...a few seconds are enough for a single photo... out of water they die!!! We saw other tourists having these unfortunate beautiful animals out of the water for 3-4 and 5 minutes to take photos and selfies in all possible poses. Stop this..
Also be aware that at the airport, starfish shells raise an alarm and are confiscated..this does not offer anything to the animal, but it is a way to prevent theft from the sea or illegal trade..

content:
Superb beaches, divided into three distinct sections: the eastern section towards Kwenda, with its hotels and restaurants on stilts, diving clubs, and the tourist boat port—an area that isn't always very affordable.
Then there's the cape with its fish market and fishing port, and a fabulous beach restaurant between the Koranic school and the fish market.
Finally, the western section, past the Nungwi lighthouse, boasts a long, continuous beach accessible at low tide and during spring tides, and a string of hotels of varying quality. There are many touts offering excursions and Maasai people ready to take advantage of tourists with smiles and friendliness, but not always at the best prices. Avoid going to the beach alone at night to avoid ending up without even underwear (a misadventure experienced by an Englishman staying at the hotel)...
However, be aware that uncontrolled overexploitation of the beach (fishing for octopus, fish, crustaceans and shrimp, and harvesting of shellfish) and the reefs is sterilizing the area...

content: Nungwi Beach is magnificent, although quite small compared to neighboring Kendwa. The sand is so white it's practically impossible to walk around without sunglasses. The sea is azure, especially beautiful on sunny days. The water has both high and low tides. At sunset, around 6:00 PM, the ocean begins to recede by 100-150 meters, and around 1:00 PM, it begins to rise, and by 4:00 PM, you can swim. During the day, Kendwa Beach is a 15-minute walk away; the low tide there is virtually nonexistent, or no more than 25-50 meters. The olive grove has its advantages – you can admire starfish and other ocean inhabitants while walking along the ocean floor. Bring coral slippers for walking. There are several restaurants and bars on the beach, as well as two liquor stores. Prices are quite reasonable. Between the Coco Cabana and Gelato Italiano restaurants, the small stretch of beach is filled with annoying beach boys, offering excursions and other things every five minutes. If you don't be friendly and start a conversation, they'll leave. But by sunset, this can get pretty annoying, which is a big minus. Between these restaurants, there's an excellent bar right on the shore with cold drinks. You can sit under an umbrella and watch the sunset. Five minutes from the beach, there's a minimarket, a pharmacy, and inexpensive fruit and souvenirs in the village. Bargain, bargain, and bargain some more.

content:
A fascinating and well managed addition to Zanzibar's tourist attractions.
It's a welcome short break from the beach, and shows you a completely different side to the island.
Good for couples, groups and families, and easily accessible with a short drive from any hotels on the north-east coast.
This cave system is in a vast & beautiful protected forest.
There's a professional reception area with good washrooms.
You take a guided walk through the forest and descend down some steps into the caves. You get to walk quite a distance comfortably, past wonderful natural rock sculpures, stalegmites & stalegtites, and tiny bats clinging to the roof of the cave. Look out for the beautiful sparkling crystal rock, and then you get to the 'Kiwengwa Challenge' area, where the cave tightens and gets very low, and you have to crawl a few metres on the ground till you emerge into a bright little grotto, open to the sky and surrounded by forest creepers. You don't have to do this, but it's good fun & worth it for the end view. Be prepared to get very dirty! You need good walking shoes - and don't wear your best clothes..
The attention to safety & conservation is impressive. You are guided to stay on the forest tracks to avoid the sink holes into the cave below, given safety helmets & torches, and advised not to touch the rock formations or shine light onto the bats.
The management is committed to protesting the forest flora & fauna.
There are several lovely forest trails you can also take.
The temperature is cooler, the birdlife is interesting, there are butterflies, and there are red colobus and blue monkeys.
You can spend just an hour, or more there, and it's definitely worth the trip!

content:
The Kiwengwa Caves are located in the Kiwengwa-Pongwe Forest Reserve. These limestone caves extend over more than 150 meters and offer a fascinating underground ecosystem.
The caves are rich in stalactites and stalagmites, formed by the dissolution of calcium carbonate from coral rock. Various bat species, insects, and birds live inside the caves. Visitors can also see impressive tree roots and bark growing through the caves. Historically, local residents visited the caves to venerate their ancestors and made offerings at sacred stones.
Very nice caves for a reasonable price. Kassim was a nice guide who told us all sorts of things. I won't give everything away. In short, highly recommended.

content:
Totally worth the visit if you're in the area. Not super well developed or maintained but doesn't take away from the experience in the slightest. You'll be in the caves for 1 hour, with a guide and torches but no other lights apart from the occasional break in the ceiling and some breathtaking sights. Our guide also gave us a musical performance on stalagmites (of course you tip him later)!
Beware, you will have bats around you at one point and you'll have to crawl for 30 secs at another point, but it's a cave, that's what you want!
A little frustrating there's no fixed price advertised but hey. We paid $4 USD each. Still reasonable and very happy to contribute to keeping this place open.
So in summary, totally worth the money and genuinely fun.

content: The caves are beautiful. It is a nice way to spend a day out. Unfortunately, there doesn't seem to be much being done in terms of advertising or making this place more of an attraction. There's a small parks office, where you'll meet a guide and they'll provide with a flashlight and helmet. Inside the cave, there are no signs you'd probably get lost of you went in alone. The guide seemed very knowledgeable about the caves. There are bats, it gets hot and humid in some of the deeper parts of the cave and you may have to crawl to get into some of the other Chambers. It's a beautiful local attraction that I think would benefit from a little more business. If you're in the area, drop in. Spend a few hours. Put some money in the hands of the local guides and support a local attraction.

content:
Great company, great owner. We were staying near this beach, and from our accommodation, we were offered a dolphin-watching excursion for $100 USD for two people. So we decided to compare prices. The owner gave us the best offer directly, without any haggling, which saved us time. We also tried the excursion to Nungwi, which was cheaper (around $50 USD for two), but it was a shared tour with eight other people, and we didn't want to drive 50 minutes for that. So we contacted the owner the day before. He had prepared a large quantity of fruit for us, much more than we needed for two. His customer service was excellent: he asked for our feedback and made sure the skippers didn't pressure us to come back. We saw dolphins and were able to swim with them three out of four times. We then went snorkeling in one or two spots before relaxing on the sandbar. The sandbar was magnificent, one of the most beautiful beaches I've ever seen. We could have gone snorkeling again, but the water was starting to get a bit cold, so we decided against it. Some people have found starfish here.
The service was very professional. We had a local guide named Cappuccino, and the captain's name was Mobi. Cappuccino guided us in the water and also had a buoy with him for our safety throughout our snorkeling trip.
The journey from this beach to the dolphin watching site took longer than expected. Due to the low tide and shallow draft, the boat moved very slowly the whole way. It took almost an hour round trip. Factor this into your total time. We chose to leave at 7:30 a.m. (we left around 7:40 a.m.) and returned just after 12:10 p.m.
To avoid the crowds, I suggested leaving at 6:30 am as the owner had suggested, but that was too early, so we asked for 7:30 am. There were already a lot of boats. If you want to take pictures of the dolphins, be sure to do so before you go snorkeling, because you won't be able to turn back to see them again once they've left.

content:
A wonderful place to pass the time while waiting for food at the attached Bashasha Restaurant.
The tour begins with an introduction to the life stages of a butterfly, complete with plenty of visual aids. Before continuing, we were asked if we wanted to see a domesticated bushbaby. Of course, the children did. The guide then took it out of its sleeping box and held it. We were able to take photos, and the children could gently pet it. Contrary to other reviews, he never let go of it; in fact, he pointed out that this wasn't allowed. After the photo session, he let it run back into its sleeping box on its own.
Then we went to a small chameleon garden. At the time, there were only two animals. The guide told us a bit about the animals' habitat and the threats they face from the local population.
Finally, we went to the butterfly enclosure. They fluttered merrily about and could be attracted with flowers that the guide gave to the children.
We were able to stay in the enclosures as long as we liked. The guide found grasshoppers to feed the chameleons and flowers to feed the butterflies. He was always very careful to ensure we saw a lot while handling the animals gently.
All in all, a lovely little park.

content:
🇬🇧 Terrible experience, a place to absolutely avoid out of respect for the animals that are mistreated inside.
I visited the facility this morning with friends to see the butterflies and, between a chrysalis and a caterpillar, the guide brought out some galagos (bush babies) for us to take pictures with. The animals appeared stressed and terrified—one of them was even forcibly placed on my friend's hand and ended up biting him!
The guide didn't know what to do, so instead suggested we continue the cruel tour by holding other animals (chameleons).
We had to rush to the hospital to start rabies treatment, while the staff at the butterfly center made jokes about what happened, downplaying our reaction and repeatedly saying “hakuna matata, mzungu” (literally “white people, don't worry” in a dismissive tone), without offering a single apology.
It was disrespectful and dangerous toward tourists, but most of all, it was cruel to the poor animals kept in captivity.
We regret not having read the reviews beforehand, as this was a last-minute activity.
Please don’t support facilities that exploit animals in this way.

content:
If you think animal welfare is important, DO NOT VISIT THIS PLACE. IT IS NOT THE ZANZIBAR BUTTERFLY CENTRE. There was a bushbaby kept in a tiny cage without any enrichment! Awful to see. The guide also touched the animal, which was understandably very afraid and stressed out. He wanted to take it out to let us hold it, but we were not okay with that. It’s never okay to directly interact with wild animals to ‘please’ visitors. Also, bushbaby’s are nocturnal animals, so putting them on display in a tiny cage during the day, touching them, holding them,… is just pure animal cruelty. Keep them in their natural habitat, not in cages. We really didn’t expect to witness something like that and it made us very upset. There were also elephant shrews in an enclosure. The guide ‘chased’ them so they would move and we could take a ‘good picture’. We told him many times to stop, cause it scared them and we only wanted to see them in peace. He also grabbed a chameleon and put it on my partner’s hand. We put it immediatly back on the leaves, for the same reason as mentioned above. Don’t touch them, don’t stress them out, don’t keep them in cages. Let the animals be in peace. We visited because we thought it was the Zanzibar butterfly centre where they help them reproduce and then set them free in the wild, but it is not.
If we knew there were other animals there locked up and being handeld by humans, we would’ve never been there. I hope from the bottom of my heart that they release the shrews, squirrels, bushbaby’s, chameleons, lizzards, … back into the wild. And if that’s not possible because they wouldn’t survive cause they have been locked up too long, PLEASE make them a gigantic enclosure that resembles their natural habitat and don’t ever let visitors into their enclosure or touch them. Please leave them in peace…

Don’t touch them, don’t stress them out, don’t keep them in cages.

content:
A lovely little facility where a guide shares fascinating information about native butterflies. The entrance fee also supports the local village community, which gave up managing the forest in favor of the national park and now relies primarily on tourism for its livelihood. Besides a small butterfly aviary, you can also experience chameleons up close and see bush babies and tortoises in a rescue/rehabilitation station. It was a wonderful experience for our children to be able to observe the animals so closely.
It's worth emphasizing that during our visit, the guide handled every single animal, egg, pupa, cocoon, etc., with the utmost care, respect, and consideration, and the animals' welfare was clearly the top priority. In my opinion, this principle should be binding for every visitor. At no point did I feel that the animals were being presented superficially to satisfy the sensationalism of paying tourists. Therefore, I highly recommend a visit, if only to support the local village community and thus the continued existence of the national park.

content: Shangani Public Beach is where Stone Town breathes—its pulse steady, its rhythm timeless. Here, the Indian Ocean whispers against the shore, carrying with it the voices of Zanzibar’s past. Dhow sails catch the breeze, their silhouettes sharp against the horizon, as if drawn from a canvas. The beach is not grandiose; it is humble, but its energy is magnetic. Locals gather to exchange stories, the scent of cloves mingling with the salty air. Children dart along the shoreline, their laughter a melody that merges with the waves. It is here, at twilight, that Omar, a quiet observer of life, finds his muse. Sitting at the edge of the sand, he watches the ocean meet the dusk, his thoughts weaving between tradition and ambition. This is more than a beach; it is the soul of Zanzibar—a meeting point of history, community, and dreams yet to unfold.

content:
Hello everyone. We are a family of two adults and two children, and we're currently in Zanzibar.
Yesterday we took this excursion, and I want to tell you about our experience. It was one of the most beautiful experiences we've had in Zanzibar so far. Our guide, Marcello, speaks excellent Italian and knows everything about the plants that grow on the island and are used in cooking and medicine around the world.
On this tour, you'll taste the spices and fruits they grow. I should point out that you're not obligated to buy the spices.
Aside from spices, the staff also sell natural soaps, massage oils, and scented essences.
For those who complain about the price, I'd like to point out that in Italy, a vanilla pod costs around €5, while the bags they sell cost 6-8. For two bags of vanilla, we spent €8.
As for Stone Town, it's an almost mandatory stop, not only to see how these people live, but also to admire the architecture, a legacy of different cultures.
Best regards

The same applies to the spice sales at the end of the tour. They try to fleece tourists with astronomical prices. While I understand the situation and cultural differences, this goes too far; they risk alienating their customers. It's a shame, because the tour itself was very interesting.

content:
Review of Tour_Guide _Momba_zanzibar
During our holiday in Zanzibar, we decided to avoid the typical hotel-recommended guides from the beach. Instead, we found Momba – a certified guide recognized by the Tanzanian authorities with an education from a university in Kenya.
All of our initial skepticism was quickly put to rest. Momba showed us Zanzibar from a whole new perspective with his calm, knowledgeable spirit and a humor that made the entire experience both educational and unforgettable. His deep knowledge of the island’s culture, history, and nature was truly impressive, and it was clear that his education and passion for the area went hand in hand.
Momba took us to both well-known and hidden gems across Zanzibar, and his way of sharing stories and facts was engaging and captivating. It was also an important lesson for us to discover how many hotels attempt to recommend their own guides for financial gain instead of supporting the local community. Momba proved how much richer and more authentic an experience becomes when you choose a local guide who truly loves his work.
We can only give Momba the highest recommendations. Thanks to him for making our stay in Zanzibar absolutely fantastic and unforgettable!
Otto Lieber

We paid around $50 for the round-trip boat (just a 10-minute crossing), plus $22 per person for entry. In total, nearly $90 for two people, for a visit that lasted only 30 minutes.
You see a few turtles and walk around a poorly maintained sanctuary. The boat captain suggests staying 1h30, but in reality, you’ve seen everything there is to see in half an hour. The island looks large from afar, but almost all areas are closed off, forcing tourists to stay in a tiny, restricted zone. Save your money and skip this one.

content:
I took a boat from Stone Town to Changuu Island, and even the crossing felt like stepping into another world: turquoise water, warm light, palm trees on the horizon. The island is small, but it carries history and nature with an intensity that deeply moved me.
Our guide not only showed us the turtles on the tour—which was incredible in itself—but also gave us a concrete and well-informed introduction to the island's history: In the 19th century, Changuu was first used by Arab slave traders as a place to hold restless or unruly enslaved people before they were sold on to Stone Town and beyond. Later, the British planned a prison there, but it never functioned as such and instead served as a quarantine station for yellow fever and other diseases. Today, only the ruins of these facilities remain, standing as a silent but powerful witness to what happened here.
What impressed me most was how respectfully our guide conveyed this history – not embellishing it, not sensationalizing it, but clearly, factually, and with empathy. We walked through the ruins, listened, asked questions, and understood that this place is far more than just a photo spot.
But Changuu is also a wonderful place of nature. The Aldabra giant tortoises there make you stop and think: These ancient animals, some over a hundred years old, move serenely through the shade of the palm trees, take food from your hand, and appear so peaceful and dignified that you really want to remember that moment.
The tour is well-planned: Information panels explain both the ecological significance and the historical context. The guides answer every question – not just superficially, but with in-depth knowledge, authenticity, and respect for the people and nature that have shaped this island.
What also impressed me: The island isn't just a "zoo destination," but a place where conservation, education, and visitor experience work together seamlessly. You can sense that it's not just about attractive presentation, but genuine protection and explanation – and that makes the visit a truly profound experience.
The boat trip, the ruins, the ancient stories, the encounter with the tortoises – everything comes together to create a picture that has changed my perception of Zanzibar. Anyone who truly wants to understand how islands, wildlife, and history intertwine should start here.
My conclusion: Changuu Island isn't just a worthwhile day trip from Stone Town. It's a place of encounter – with nature, with history, with truth. A recommendation that will stay with me for a long time.

You have to pay for a boat across from Stone Town (included with our pre-booked guided trip).
Before getting on said boat, you must pay 3usd tax to a government desk on the beach, per person. No idea why. This will increase to 10usd from 1st September 2025.
To board your boat, it's feet in the filthy water. A choppy 25 minute crossing and you do the same the other end, although at least the water is clean here. There are taps upstairs to wash your feet off before refitting shoes etc.
At this point, you then find out that it's actually a zoo. The remains of the 'prison' (actually a quarantine facility) have been converted into a zoo, which they rarely refer to as a tortoise sanctuary but they're captive, you can't get away from it. From what I understand as soon as a tortoise appears near the path everyone flocks to it for photos which I imagine would be very stressful for them. The young are taken away from them and put in cages until they're older.
It costs an additional 12usd per person to enter the zoo when you arrive. After realising what it was we decided not to pay and returned to stone town on our dhow.
All information we found out previously suggested 'Prison Island' was the site of a long since ruined prison where giant tortoises are free to roam, unhindered. This is absolutely not the case, our guide told us that it used to be like that, but the government realised there was money to be made as a tourist attraction.
Waste of time and money.

place_name: Gos tour in #zanzibar. Get your guide for slave market & Stone town city
content:
Our visit to Slave Market was one of the most powerful and emotionally heavy experiences of our trip. This is not just a place you visit — it’s a place that makes you pause, reflect, and truly understand a difficult part of history.
Walking through the site, especially the underground chambers where enslaved people were once held, gives you a stark sense of the extreme conditions they endured. The spaces are small, dark, and suffocating even today — it’s hard to imagine how many people were confined there under such inhumane circumstances. It’s an experience that stays with you long after you leave.
The memorials and exhibits around the site help provide context and tell the stories of those who suffered here. The displays are informative and thoughtfully put together, helping visitors understand the scale and impact of the slave trade in this region.
The area also includes the Anglican Cathedral, which stands as a symbol of hope and transformation, built on the very grounds of the former market. The contrast between the painful history and the present-day setting is quite striking.
We would definitely recommend taking a guide here, as it helps you better understand the historical significance and the stories behind what you’re seeing. It adds depth and meaning to the visit.
Overall, the Slave Market is not an easy place to visit, but it is an important one. It offers a sobering reminder of the past and leaves you with a deeper appreciation of history and humanity.

clauses.clause_text: The spaces are small, dark, and suffocating even today — it’s hard to imagine how many people were confined there under such inhumane circumstances.

place_name: Gos tour in #zanzibar. Get your guide for slave market & Stone town city
content: Informative museum on the East African slave trade. Dark times for humanity. The shame of many prosperous countries in the world. It really gives you a lump in your throat here, looking at the depictions of villages being burned and families split up and shipped away. The East Africans were sent as slaves to mainly Arabia, after being imprisoned and bought here in Stonetown, Zanzibar. I knew a lot about the slave trade to the Caribbean, but not so much here, so it was very educational. Lots of history, pictures and illustrations in the museum, and stories on individuals. I got a good background on how Dr. Livingstone was on the side of the slaves and tried to promote trade of resources to phase out slavery. There are also some stories on the individual slave traders, if you can stomach their greed and heartlessness. There is also a basement under the church where the slaves were imprisoned, that you can explore. A guide is allocated to you with the price of admission. Our guide was really good.

content:
No val la p na la visita, l'únic que veuràs es una exposició que de plafons amb informació que pots trobar en internet, una església simple i una obra d'art morbosa que es el reclam turístic a 5$ l'entrada i uns guies que t'assalten a l'entrada i que expliquen coses no certes i venen un passat vergonyos com una atracció.
Història de la catedral:
Es va construir en set anys, posant la primera pedra el dia de Nadal de 1873 fins a l'obertura el Nadal de 1879, basant-se en una visió d' Edward Steere , tercer bisbe anglicà de Zanzíbar, que va contribuir activament al disseny. Com la majoria dels edificis de Stone Town, està fet principalment de pedra corall . Té un sostre de formigó únic amb forma d'una inusual volta de canó (això va ser la idea de Steere) i l'estructura general barreja detalls gòtics perpendiculars i islàmics . La catedral va ser consagrada el 1903 i va rebre el nom de la catedral de Canterbury .
L'església es troba a Mkunazini Road, al centre del nucli antic, i ocupa una gran àrea on antigament hi havia el mercat d'esclaus més gran de Zanzíbar; de fet, la construcció de la catedral estava destinada a celebrar la fi de l'esclavitud. Es diu que l'altar es troba al lloc exacte on abans hi havia el 'post de fuet'" principal del mercat. A la plaça hi ha un conegut monument als esclaus (unes quantes figures humanes encadenats que surten d'una fossa) així com un museu sobre l'esclavitud.

The cave itself is nice and cool to swim in, with some tiny fish and but also a lot of small stinging creatures. The advertised changing space and lockers didn't appear to exist. There were 2 toilets, one with a door that didn't close, no electricity, and a shower that didn't work. It was a very hot day, and we had planned to have lunch in the advertised restaurant, but it was closed (long-term) and there was nowhere even to get a bottle of water. The gardens are pretty, but the sitting areas were out of action and cushions wet or moldy. We read that there was a second beach, but found no sign of this, nor of the advertised yoga space. The cave is about 20 minutes' walk along a narrow bumpy track from the main road. We asked politely if we could have a reduction in the price once we realised the advertised facilities weren't available, but were told this was impossible.

content: The photos are of Kuza Cave, the name Kuumbi Cave is incorrectly described. It's located within the cultural center (formerly part of the village) and also associated with the local sacred area. Today, it features bathrooms, a changing room, a small restaurant, souvenirs, several buildings, music (a local sang two Polish songs), and a semi-open cave with very clear water, similar to a cenote in Mexico... up to several meters deep, about 30 meters long, with approximately 30 steps carved into the rock, plus a few meters along the rock in front of them and down them to the water itself. The water temperature is around 25 degrees Celsius.

content:
We are a family of 3 people and were very happy to experiment a 3days safari with our wonderful guide Bidan
Everything was perfectly planned and organised. We stayed in comfortable lodgings and had great food. Everything was included in the package (entry-fees of the national parks, accommodation, food and water).
The communication with Bidan was simple and fluent before and during our stay in Tanzania.
As soon as we met we felt like family members and Bidan our guide did all he could to make us feel great,
to please us and show us the most beautiful things (animals, landscapes, waterfalls etc.)
Even though it was the rainy season in April, we managed to see lions, girafs, impalas, elephants and many more.
Concerning the payment of the safari the good thing was that we could pay on arrival, so absolutely safe and without surprises.
In conclusion, these 3 days with Bidan were rell the trip. We start from Dar Es Salam to go to Mikumi National Park. We traveled in a confortable 4×4, the perfect way to enjoy the road and to see all te were very lucky to see a lot of animals (lions, éléphants, buffalo, hippopotamus, girafes, baboons, impalas, etc). We also visited an authentic Masaï Village near Mikumi. The last day we went to Udzungwa to see the highest waterfall in National parks. After the trip our guide (Bidan) brings us back to the harbor to go to Zanzibar but you can choose where you want to go after the safari.
The guide (Bidan) was always very kind and professional, we ate together every day and we spend good time with him. He did his best to see animals we wanted to see like lions. And he also help us to speak with the local people and to book our boat trip to Zanzibar.
Conclusion: we recommend you BLACKWILLOW SAFARIS if you want to have a great safari tour in Tanzania and meet nice people.

clauses.clause_text: The last day we went to Udzungwa to see the highest waterfall in National parks.

I strongly advise you against this agency that does not keep its word, that lies and steals. It is not a serious agency.

content: This was a brilliant tour! Arsheen met us very hospitably. First of all, the host made a brief about the stand up paddle. Then we went through the open ocean to the mangroves. The mangroves were amazing. It was like swimming at the top of a tropical forest. We even went through the mangrove thickets. Arsheen is a professional in the stand up paddling, so she even made some photos of us without waterproof cases. This is so much better than photos than I made with a waterproof case. After the tour, we were offered homemade snacks in the backyard. It was very romantic to watch the sunset near the ocean. I definitely recommend that tour to everyone who is visiting Zanzibar. Mangroves were even better than in the Jozani forest. Also, the host helped us with the transfer from the Nungwi. The taxi had a fixed price and driver was very friendly.

content: A great place. Zanzibar should focus on places like this, not some turtle-feeding pools. It's a natural tropical forest teeming with various animals. The monkeys, tricolored colobus monkeys, and black-and-gray monkeys, are accustomed to people, often walking half a meter past them, yet they don't bother us or steal phones, sunglasses, hats, etc. A great guide. He showed us around the park and explained everything. We bought the short tour, supposedly an hour for $12, but in total, it lasted over two hours. I highly recommend it.

Seeing the red colobus and blue monkeys was quite special but I'd probably recommend the shorter one hour tour.
