place_name: Jozani Forest VIP Tour | Middle and Long Tour I Birds and Night Tour
content:
Our nature walk with Kesi in Jozani National Park was nothing short of spectacular. We started our adventure walking through the mangroves spotting small crabs in the mud and learning about the mangrove tree species. Kesi found some mangrove seed pods and we were able to drop them in the mud to plant a new mangrove tree. Then we found ourselves amongst a troop of blue monkeys. These monkeys are difficult to capture on camera due to their quick movements and inability to sit still. Kesi gave us plenty of time to observe their habits, munching on fruit and leaves, swinging through the trees, grooming each other and even engaging in creating the next generation. We continued our hike, Kasi pointed out birds, giant snails, lizards and skinks along the way. Eventually we made our way to a red colobus monkey troop. Picturesque in nature, these monkeys were playful and exhibited the same behaviors as the blue monkeys. This red colobus subspecies endemic to Zanzibar was giving us a show. We saw up to 5 young red colobus playing together, rolling around and nipping and chasing each other around the trees. We saw plenty of baby red colobus breastfeeding from their mothers and eventually settling into the trees for an early afternoon nap. We eventually found another troop of red colobus a little deeper in the forest, these ones seemed a little less keen on humans observing their behaviors and stayed high up in the trees. Kesi spotted a snake and an elephant shrew. It was a great tour but bring something to eat and plenty of water.
Also, Abdul, our driver serenaded to and from the destination with his soulful voice.

content:
The transfer and the guide were excellent and greatly contributed to the success of the excursion. The snorkeling, the sandbar, and the natural pool were also very enjoyable.
However, lunch definitely needs improvement. I informed them the day before the activity that my mother suffers from severe food allergies, particularly to lemon, which can be life-threatening. The organizer confirmed that this information had been passed on to the team. As a precaution, we also checked with the guide on the day itself, who assured us that everything had been taken care of.
Imagine our surprise when my mother tasted the fries and discovered they had been drizzled with lemon juice. As for the seafood, not only were pieces of lemon arranged on the platter, but the entire dish contained lemon. As a result, my mother had an allergic reaction and was unable to eat almost any of the planned dishes.
Luckily, she had her medication and reacted quickly. Such negligence regarding a repeatedly reported allergy is unacceptable. Despite our messages, we received only apologies and no response to our request for compensation, even though this meal was included in the price of the excursion. Being a small, local business cannot justify such a lack of diligence on such a serious matter.

content:
Simply magnificent.
We contacted them via WhatsApp for a quote for a private boat trip for two.
There are several options available, including group bookings and private boat rentals.
The next day, a driver picked us up at the hotel at the precise departure time (8:00 am) (private transfer for two).
Then began a magnificent boat trip towards a sandbar.
Along the way, we saw dolphins. We turned off the engine to observe them without disturbing them (some companies actively seek out dolphins to satisfy their customers).
A dolphin encounter is not guaranteed, as they are still wild animals.
Then we arrived at a sandbar to take photos.
We returned to the boat and headed towards our first snorkeling spot.
The captain and his assistant remained on board. Your guide dives with you. He always has a buoy if you get tired and life jackets if you can't swim. Masks and snorkels are provided. The guide dives with you and explains the names of the fish and starfish. The corals are magnificent.
Then we head to another snorkeling spot. And that's when hunger strikes! We arrive at an island where a private table on the sand awaits us with barbecued lobster, tuna, and crayfish. The white wine is chilled—what more could you ask for?
After this wonderful break, we take a boat to the mangroves to swim in a natural pool.
Then it's back to the base, but here's another pleasant surprise: since we're on a private boat and the wind is good, we sail back (1 hour).
In short, it's magical, the crew is friendly and professional. You should definitely do this trip, either in a group or privately like we did.
Note: it's best to wear plastic shoes because at low tide, getting to the boat early in the morning is tricky; there are some sharp, slippery pebbles.

content:
Forget it!
An hour on an uncomfortable minibus (depending on where you're departing from) and two hours on a battered boat to see nothing.
Want a beautiful, spectacular beach with real, pure white sand? Go to Nungwi. Avoid this tourist trap.
25, 25 boats on a strip of light brown, NOT WHITE, sand. Hundreds of people crowded together and boats everywhere.
Let's not even talk about snorkeling! There's no coral, and you'll only see sangria fish attracted by the food thrown to them. Now, if you've never seen sangria fish all together, yes, it's cute, but don't expect anything else. Finally, the pool in the mangroves is a swamp. If you decide to take part in this madness and give away your money, at least bring water shoes. Lunch was a quick one, and everything was fried. Octopus, calamari, potatoes, shrimp, and half a lobster each. Want a cold beer? You'll pay over €3 (Zanzibar nightclub price, not beach trip price). Of course, there will be plenty of sales opportunities promoted by the guide. Photos with various animals held in captivity, mistreated, and exploited for profit (various monkeys and coconut crabs) are also a must.
Finally, if you decide to go and get fleeced, try to bargain! They charged us $150 between the two of us. We ended up paying $80. I've heard of people paying $110-$130 without batting an eyelid. Again, avoid.

I understand that people need to make a living, but by destroying this habitat, they will ultimately have nothing left to live from. I would never recommend it unless major changes are made to how these activities are planned and managed.

content:
We were lied to several times. The man(Captain Juma) we arranged the tour with, who promised that he would be our guide (as he spoke english) first passed us off to a driver (who he claimed spoke better english than him) that he now said would be our guide. He turned out to speak zero english and just as quickly passed us off to yet another man who didn’t speak english. There was zero organization, throughout the day we had to wait without any cover from the burning hot sun twice… for over an hour. The boat was rusty, small and uncomfortable. No one could tell us anything about anything since they didn’t speak english. They chased the dolphins aggressively with no respect, even when we clearly told them not to (and they also touched the starfish, which is not allowed as it can harm the animals). The snorkeling equipment was all broken, leaking goggles= no snorkling. We were not offered any drinks between 06 am when the tour started till lunch around 14 pm. Neither were we offered fresh fruits and sodas, as promised. Nor offered any life vests, which was also promised. Furthermore, we were assured there would be restrooms at at least one point, which was true. However, the only one nearby lacked a door and roof, so passerby’s could easily look in, and of course there was no toilet paper or seat.
We were also lied to about the price we would have to pay to enter the cave with the turtles and the guide kept nagging us about paying, even though we had agreed to pay at end of day.
The only good thing was the lunch.
All in all, not trustworthy, not organized and not worth paying for.

content: We were supposed to go to Mafia Island to swim with the whale sharks, traveling from Unguja. However, due to the unrest from the Tanzanian presidential election, our trip was cancelled last minute. While this was disappointing, the team a Safari Blue offered a full refund and a complimentary day trip including snorkeling, lunch, and a trip to a picturesque sandbar. While it wasn't how we hoped to spend our day, it was making the best of a situation that none of us could control. I thought that it was a very classy solution. I hope to make it back to east Africa in the future to see those whale sharks. If and when I do, I will make my arrangements via wetravel and the Safari Blue.

All in all, an okay tour but it could be executed better with some clearer communication and limit of boats going out. For a snorkel tour we also expected more time actually snorkelling

content: We spent the next day on a Blue Safari – a traditional dhow cruise through the Menai Bay protected area. Dhows were historically used to transport spices, but also slaves from mainland Africa. We started in Fumba, where we boarded the boat. The cruise was quite long, and we relaxed on Sandbank, a sand island that disappears at high tide, where we also ate delicious fruit. After setting out into the ocean, we could snorkel. Then we sailed to Kwale Island, where the ocean has carved incredible rock formations. On the island, we had a seafood lunch, and finally, we went to see the oldest baobab tree on the island. The tree fell 500 years ago, but part of it still lives; it is truly enormous. Finally, we snorkeled in the Blue Lagoon.

content:
I would say it was a complete SCAM from Cedok who sold it to us. They have stops at beautiful sandy beaches, snorkeling, starfish, the blue lagoon and lunch on an island where the biggest baobab tree is.
As a result, from the hotel at 1:30 by bus, then a terrible dirt road through the forest full of garbage before you get to the beach. Another almost hour of waiting to board and wading in the shallows (where there are sea urchins) to the boat, because there was little water for the boat.
Swimming on the boat was pleasant, there is probably nothing to spoil there. The first stop was snorkeling, where the boat parked with 10 others and the guide said Jump and that's it, because he wasn't standing, he didn't show. There were a few fish to see, the remains of coral and if another boat wasn't splashing water, you could dive. Who knows the Red Sea, there is a fraction of it here. But pleasant, swimming.
Stop 2: a sandy blob that looks nice at high tide, but it was low tide, so a kilometer of dead coral and a pile of sand. On it, dozens of temporary shelters where tour companies offer fruit. And over 300+ tourists who don't understand what they are supposed to be looking at there. The hotel has better sand (white), here yellow. And of course garbage, so a floating piece of pineapple or watermelon, a common thing. We quickly sat down as the crew of the boat and wanted to board and leave, except for the crowd there is nothing there.
Stop 3: a place to dive for starfish. I guess they confuse the terms starfish and jellyfish. Because the guide found one small starfish, but the jellyfish was not swimmable. Personally, I didn't find any starfish on the bottom. But yes, a piece of coral with an anemone and a clownfish (nemo) was nice. When we explained to the guide that there are dozens of starfish of different sizes near the hotel, he didn't find more than one. When they take them out of the sea, I'm not surprised that they've already died.
Stop 4: island with a baobab tree and lunch. Spoiler alert: a 500-year-old tree fell and a new one originally grows on its roots. Understandably, there are dozens of people near the tree, so you can barely see it. There are a lot of stalls on the island and they try to force something on you.
Lunch is the only thing that was nice, if you eat seafood. There was no other option. But the woman praised the lobster.
Stop 5: blue lagoon. See separate review. Interesting natural spectacle, lagoon ground in corals, mango trees with roots in the water. We didn't see it, it was already high tide. Otherwise a lagoon where 30+ boats stop and tourists rush into the water. Into the water where when the tide is high, it brings all the mess and you can smell gasoline from the boat. None of our crew dared to jump in there and we went home instead.
To sum it up: you can find starfish a short distance from The Rock restaurant to the north, on the beach you can find someone who will gladly take you there, or go swimming there. The sand is better on the east side of the coast. For diving, the Red Sea is better.
Of all the hotels we've ever had on all our vacations, this is the first one where I give 1 star, because 0 is not possible. Waste of money 75$/person.

content:
I selected this company after reading a lot of bad reviews of other 'blue safaris'. So we paid more hoping for a better trip. The organisation and service were good, not too crowded on the boat, drinks and fruits served during the trip. The attractions, not so much. We didn't go to see the dolphins, the first stop was on a sand bank which was nice but full of people at that time (20 or so other boats). It would be better to stop there on the way back when it was almost empty. The first snorkeling point was disappointing, unclear water, damaged coral and very little fish. The second spot was better but not spectacular. At least the water was clearer and we saw several kinds of fish. Unfortunately it started raining so we moved to the next location. The lagoon was nice at high tide. The boat goes inside and you can swim in calm water. We stayed there for a short time, I would prefer more. Then there is lunch which was served on the other side of the island. There was sea food and chicken and some vegetables. Not a fancy fish but I believe all was fresh. Again there were drinks, including beer, and then some fruits, and a small coffee with amarula liqueur. The visit to the baobab tree was a 2 minute walk, a chance to take a photo (it is really a large tree) and go back. There are some stalls with souvenirs and clothes but you can just pass them by. I think we spent maybe 2h there including lunch. I'm not sure if there is anything more to explore on the island, if you eat quickly and skip 'baobab attraction' you can probably walk around - the guide did not mention such a possibility. The way back was smooth. The wind was too weak to set the sail unfortunately.
To summarise, you can spend the whole day on the water, see some attractions and swim. Do not count on snorkeling as the best in the world (maybe when the company started their business in 1996 the reef was in better shape). It is enjoyable but quite expensive. Remember that due to the tides and weather your experience may be different.

content:
This experience was truly exceptional, and I highly recommend it.
First, the logistics were seamless; I was conveniently picked up from and dropped off back in Nungwi. The team was incredibly well-organized. Upon arrival at the main meeting point, don’t be concerned by the number of people you see. The team efficiently divides everyone into smaller groups (ours had 16 people, and it never felt crowded), each assigned to separate boats.
The sandbank was breathtaking—unlike anything I’ve ever seen. We were fortunate to visit during a very low tide around the full moon. We were also incredibly lucky to spot dolphins and even swim with them, which was undoubtedly the highlight of the trip. The snorkeling experience was fantastic—long enough to savor and truly immerse yourself in the beauty of the underwater world.
Lunch exceeded expectations. It was served buffet-style on a charming island, and I enjoyed fresh grilled fish, beans, lentils, and rice. There was also chicken and meat for those interested. The local fruits were abundant, and the crew thoughtfully explained each one in detail. The lunch area seemed to be privately managed by the company, and it featured sunbeds, perfect for relaxing after the meal. If you're interested in souvenirs, there are plenty of small local shops nearby.
One lovely surprise was when the crew sailed the boat after lunch instead of using the engine—a peaceful and delightful touch. Drinks were provided onboard (soda, water, and beer), along with fresh fruit and a local sweet treat.
As for concerns about crowding, I personally didn’t feel it was an issue. Perhaps we were lucky with the timing, but if it was the case, we’re all tourists contributing to the scene being crowded, and I think that’s just part of the experience.

content:

content: A great day out spent with extremely friendly and professional staff that look after you from start to finish. Communication was fantastic throughout, with multiple WhatsApp messages throughout the booking process and we were collected on time from our hotel at the exact meeting time. Don’t be put off when you arrive, as the beach is covered with hundreds of people from different resorts and it gets a little bit chaotic with not much organisation. However once you get on your boat it is smooth sailing. The boats are comfortable and spacious, with alcohol, soft drinks and water provided. Throughout the day snacks are also given, including fruits, homemade peanut butter chocolate bites and other treats. Initially you visit a small sand raised island for photos before beginning the snorkelling. You are taken to two snorkelling areas. Both were sadly a little disappointing. The first was too murky to see anything, and where the waters were clear there was nothing to see but dead coral. The second site you could see a reef but little marine life. Perhaps it is luck of the draw, and on other days will be better, but for a snorkelling excursion it was a little poor on this occasion. The blue lagoon you are taken to after is beautiful. On the main island, lunch makes up for the snorkelling, and really made our day. You are seated on long 20 seater tables by your boat name and called up table by table for lunch to be served to you. The bbq included lobster, chicken, fish, calamari and prawns. With rice, bread, cornflour cakes and sauces to accompany. Beer is included and there is also a bar where you can purchase additional alcohol. You get two hours on the island. Enough time to enjoy lunch and explore, with lots of shops nearby. This is the cheapest place for souvenirs and paintings. With items like fridge magnets just $2 and paintings in the range of $30. You will not find cheaper anywhere else in Zanzibar. The final treat came when you return to the mainland, and instead of using the motor, the staff put up the sail and you sail back. It is a really incredible experience. Overall a great day out and we would book again, it just needs to find a few better sites for the snorkelling!

content:
Safari Blue Zanzibar
Unfortunately, our experience with this trip was far from what the vendors had promised us beforehand.
The value for money was downright disappointing. For two people, we paid a total of 90 dollars, which turned out to be much too high in hindsight. After a one-hour bus ride, we arrived at a location where we boarded a boat with about 20 people for another hour-long boat trip. Once we arrived at a sandbank, we were served a fruit breakfast, but we were not the only ones: there were about 25 boats, meaning the sandbank was overcrowded with tourists. Furthermore, there was nothing to do on or around the sandbank.
After a 45-minute break, we continued to the snorkeling spot, a 20-minute journey. There were about 20 boats here, and everyone was dropped into the water at the same time. The skippers fed the fish, but it was far from a real snorkeling tour. It was much too crowded, and we constantly bumped into other tourists. In the end, we only snorkeled for 10 minutes and then went back onto the boat.
Next, we took a short boat trip to a lunch spot, where we had an hour break. The lunch was well catered for, and there was plenty of food for everyone.
After lunch, we went to a mangrove forest, where we were only able to swim for 10 minutes. Due to the tide, the mangrove forest was barely visible, so this also made little impression.
This was followed by a 1.5-hour boat trip and another hour-long bus ride back to the hotel.
In short, although the trip was beautifully described beforehand and the photos were promising, in reality, it turned out to be a very commercial affair. You pay far too much for an experience that offers very little.
NOT RECOMMENDED!

I went on a half-day trip that included visiting a beautiful mangrove lagoon, a sandbank that disappears and reappears with the tide, snorkeling, and barbecue lunch, and fruit sampling at Kwale Island. The crew was so helpful throughout the trip, helping me with my snorkel and life jacket when I was having trouble swimming. The assistant captain was very kind to guide me through snorkeling, as well as help my mom on the uneven beach when walking back to the dhow.
Snacks and drinks were available throughout the trip. One of the snacks was aged coconut and cinnamon-y chocolate - I wish I had remembered to ask for the name and recipe!
Unfortunately we didn't get to go swimming at the mangrove lagoon because the tide was going out - apparently, if we had stayed much longer, the dhow may have gotten stuck. We did not get to see any dolphins, but that is based on luck and did not diminish the experience.
Tip: bring a towel, as it can get chilly when you've just come out of the water and the dhow is moving.

Safari Blue turned out to be in my personal top things to do in Zanzibar. Actually, I’m not the person who would enjoy boat trip, but believe me I did!
So, there was a group of people, we got into the boat and off we went in the search of adventures.
We came to the first snorkeling place over some reef and spent time there. After the snorkeling the boat crew gave us some fruit, and we went to the second reef and snorkeled there for a while. After that we were proposed coconuts. And we went to the lagoon with an amazing crystal clear water and mangrove trees around, and snorkeled and swam there for a while.
After that we were taken to the island where we had lunch. We ate lobsters, shrimps, fish, rice and sauces. Also the fruit was proposed as desert.
After lunch we wandered around the island, saw a huge baobab tree, and an even huger another baobab tree. Took some pictures, walked a bit. Also there is a small market for those who would like to buy some souvenirs. After the lunch and walk we got back to the boat and went to the sandy island. That’s the small island which is covered in water in high tide. But while there’s low tide, the soft sand is looking out of the water and invites you to step on it. The island is just a few meters wide and maybe around twenty meters long. At least, that was the size when we were there. By the way, the boat crew took us there when there were no other people, so we could take some nice pictures looking like we are in a total solitude.
After that we got back into the boat and opened the sail and sailed back. And that was amazing! Even for such a naughty non-lover of the boats as me. I did enjoy and for sure I’ll keep this trip in my memory.

content: I would describe this as a glorified snokling event. First thing was the loading onto the dhow boat was nothing short of ridiculous. We had to wade through muddy waters where a smaller boat would pick you up to bring you to the dhow boat which was about 20 meters away. I understand that the low tides make it hard for the boats to enter the shallow waters. But if you have been doing this business since 1996 you should seriously consider constructing a small jetty that will overcome all these problems. Next, in the dhow boat we had 15 guests and 3 crew. We were sitting packed like sardines for the entire boat ride. The sand bank: not sure why we stopped here as there is nothing to do especially if you stay at a beachfront hotel. Snokling: this was the only fun thing except that I got bitten by some invisible jelly fish and was stinging all over my body, but the boatmen didn't seem to care or explain how I got the sting. Nice thig was that the other guests were offering medication and creams to alleviate my distress. Mangrove lagoon swim: a little enclave that is nice for some picture taking. Lunch: food was good, buffet style n free flow of beers. Overall, I felt sorry for most of the guests in my boat as they didn't seem too comfortable snokling and mostly stayed on the boat throughout. Next, the guide claimed that there was a 85% chance that we would see dolphines, but alas we didn't see any. I suspect the dolphins only come to that area at certain times of the year, so do you research before taking this trip. So overall my take was that I would have engaged a local operater to take me snokling near my hotel instead of spending the entire day with blue safari. One star is given for the snokling experience and the 2nd star is given for lunch.

content:
This trip is a very interesting, beautiful, adventurous full-day trip.
It includes three locations, a beautiful sandbank, where the group arrives from the Fumba pier. Here you can snorkel, then they serve local fruits, pineapple, coconut, red and yellow (lady fingers) bananas, mango.
Then we sailed to another island, where a large fish awaited us, with rice, fried potatoes and we got a very tasty sauce on the rice.
Lunch included grilled squid, crabs, tuna and lobster. The seafood was delicious.
After lunch, we went to a lagoon, where we walked in waist-deep water among the wonderful rocks, and then we visited a giant baobab tree.
It was an experience of a lifetime.
One thing to watch out for is that on the way back everyone will be soaked from the waves, so you need a towel, and what is not extra, you have to frequently apply body lotion with a sun protection factor of 50, which is not really enough, because we forgot about it anyway.
This excursion should be done towards the end of the trip. (Not in the first few days at least!)

content:
Safari Blue Beach Tour
Zanzibar’s most talked about sea adventure Sail away to sandbanks around the magnificent island of Unguja, Zanzibar. sailing, snorkeling, sunbathing on a Traditional Zanzibar DhowExplore the mangrove lagoon

The 200-year baobab tree is another attraction you just come and climb it and get a great view from the top! If you are lucky you can find massive coconut crabs living inside its hollow trunk.
Menai bay conservation society has several naturally occurring sandbanks with safe swimming and from there you can enjoy great snorkeling, relax under the shade and enjoy fresh coconuts and local snacks in paradise while you are surrounded by turquoise waters.

We had an amazing time with this trip (but we also had luck and were the first group at every spot).
In the morning you get your equipment and go on one of the traditional dhows. We were around 20 people which made the boat really full. But we were catered for with drinks and fruits. First you go to a Sandbank and can take nice pictures. It is a Sandbank so don't expect too much.
Then it goes to the first snorkeling spot which was amazing. So many corals and colored fish. We had one hour of snorkeling which was plenty enough. Then we went to one of the islands and had full lunch with chicken, lobster, kingprawns and delicious condiments. Highlight here was the fruit tasting, because the guide gave us like 10 different fruit to taste.
After that you can climb the Baobab tree or go shopping in the beachfront. The Baobab is really crowded when a lot of people come at the same time. Still impressive, though.
Second time snorkeling was at a spot where the coral reefs were almost dead. Sad to see the destruction but still we could look at some fish and anemones.
In the end we drove to a little bay with coral rocks.
Piece of advice: definitely bring reef shoes!
All in all a nice trip worth the money. However there are so many boats out there, sometimes snorkeling all in the same spot so you have to be prepared for that. Also you start snorkeling right of the boat and although the crew seemed knowledgeable we were not confident that they had every person in eyesight, e.g. would notice if someone was going under.

content:
We booked this tour directly in our hotel via Flash Tours, 85USD per person. This included also transport from Kiwengwa to Fumba and back.
We got onto the dhow, with totally different group of people (about 20) who were there with Johari tours (so it was organized by Johari).
We were lucky that the weather was beautiful and the locations were all looking the nicest they could. We were lucky that even if there were also other ships, it did not feel overcrowded. HOWEVER - it felt really rushed - Komonda island 20mins, snorkeling 20mins, sandbank 20mins and then Kwale island with the lunch. We did not even finish our beer and they were already telling us to go. Baobab 20mins, shops 20mins and then back to the ship. On Kwale we spent maybe 90mins including everything. We did not even go to the promised Blue Lagoon/mangroves (!!!) and sailed straight back to Fumba - we were the first ship to return! It was a letdown and although it really had a potential because the locations were so beautiful, we did not enjoy them to the fullest - we just needed to go somewhere else all the time.
Looking back, it feels like a rip-off.
Next time I'd definitely make much deeper research and go with someone else and/or go to Mnemba to enjoy the snorkeling.

content: Don't waste your time or money. We turned up to the boat station to find about 20 boats moored up, all doing the same tour. It was raining and the conditions were frankly dangerous. Low visibility and choppy water. They still decided to run the tour. We were stuffed onto a boat with 15 other people, all put under some tarp whilst waiting for the rain to pass. Once the rain did clear, we were taken to a mangrove forest only to be told that portion of the trip isn't possible as the tide was low, something the boat captain would've known before doing the tour. We were then taken to a sandbank where we ate fruit with about 100 other tourists who had been dropped off there. There is nothing to do there so you spend most of the time just sitting in the sand waiting for the tour operators to put everyone back on the boat. It also isn't a good swimming spot as there are sharp pieces of debris under the water. We were then taken on a 40 minute snorkelling trip which was 50 yards away from the sandbank. They also decided to feed the fish from the boat which upsets their natural habitat. We then had lunch which, to be fair, was quite nice. We saw no dolphins on the trip either. This is something they tell you that you will see. When speaking to a local, he said dolphins don't live in this area due to the amount of boat activity. In total, we paid $65 each to have an alright lunch as none of the other activities really lived up to expectations. We feel like we were mislead over the trip. They promise you the earth so if you do decide to go, go with no expectations at all.

Honestly, I don't recommend it; it's a waste of time.
You get on the boat and they take you to an area with about 20 other boats, where you can barely move around the boat for fear of being run over.
There's practically nothing to see while snorkeling, and they even threw food to the fish to attract them, disrupting their habitat and food supply. It's a disgrace.
Then they take you to a kind of lagoon where you can swim, but there are no fish. It's a complete waste of time.
They also take you to a sandbar where the 20 boats that were snorkeling are moored. There were easily 300 people crammed into about 700 square meters. It's a disgrace.
Then they take you to an island where they serve you food. The only noteworthy thing was the lobster, but it was quite small and nothing like what we're used to (at least in Spain). It's a disgrace.
The so-called island is full of shops selling souvenirs, etc.
On the way back, they lowered the sail in a rather dangerous way, hitting one of the passengers. REGRETTABLE AND DANGEROUS
Before reaching the shore, the sail was furled, also in a rather dangerous manner. REGRETTABLE AND DANGEROUS
Finally, to reach the shore, we had to pass a small boat that came right up alongside us and was being pulled closer with a single rope held by hand. The movement and the waves could easily catch an arm or a leg. REGRETTABLE AND VERY DANGEROUS
IN SHORT, DON'T WASTE YOUR TIME
Although I suppose it's similar with other companies, beware those who write reviews here. These ones are specifically called "The Safari Blue" and they all wear yellow shirts.

content: Tourist trap!! It was the rainy season, sure, but the crew made us leave just before a major storm, so we were soaked to the bone the whole crossing! A flimsy tarp held by hand... We were tossed around like crazy, everyone was vomiting, my terrified 12-year-old daughter begged us to go back, but it was no use!! The captain's cold stare at this spectacle said it all... the so-called captain's argument: we have to keep going because there's no visibility and he doesn't know where we're going!??! That's reassuring!! After I got angry, he said okay, we'll turn around, but keep going straight ahead... once we arrived, we disembarked on the island at low tide, so we had to walk through mud for quite a while... if you only have flip-flops, tough luck! Snorkeling in the pouring rain, three fish in the water, the meal was more than mediocre, so if you're sensitive to hygiene, steer clear. Then a stop in a mangrove... after the rain and high tide the water is dirty, no desire to swim in it... in short, the worst day in Zanzibar, the crew were liars, mocking and asked for tips at the end...

content:
It's a pretty fun activity, but my opinion of the excursion is mixed because the weather wasn't on our side. I think the weather plays a big role, both in terms of mood and the beauty of nature. (The crystal-clear sea under a blue sky is definitely less idyllic in the rain).
You leave in the morning aboard a dow (a local sailboat in Zanzibar), heading to a white sand island to swim and eat fresh fruit (a taxi picks you up from your accommodation). A snorkeling stop is planned before reaching the main island where you'll enjoy a huge fish barbecue with rice (the food was delicious!). After eating, you can browse a souvenir market and discover the Baobab, one of the oldest trees in the world (and also one of the largest!). You can also relax on the beach if the market doesn't interest you.

If you come to Zanzibar this is a must do!

content:
Don't do it!
* We were dropped off in deep water, 7-9 meters
* I couldn't see any fish because of the murky water
* The waves were very strong and it wasn't easy to get back to the boat
* The boat has a rickety ladder, causing people to keep falling back into the water while the staff laughed at them instead of helping them
* You get lured into a tourist trap again and a huge number of people rip you off with ridiculous prices or beggars who pull at you everywhere
* I even got food poisoning during lunch due to poor hygiene
The worst part was when we went to the mangrove! There is no supervision or rules and I could have cried when I saw how the ignorance of tourists was destroying the coral. They were allowed to walk on everything and everything was going under... a tragedy to see the creatures' habitat being trampled!

The starting point can vary depending on the part of the island you're on, but you always end up in the same places. The excursion consists of:
1. A small boat packed with tourists and their guides heads to a sandbank.
2. If you arrive early, the sandbank is great; otherwise, it's a crowded place. They give you delicious fruit.

content:
TL;DR - Bad experience.
It was unfortunate that we requested not to swim in coral reefs as that damages them however we still ended up going to a coral reef and told we could swim here. We also visited the giant tortoises... it says in the entrance “do not feed the tortoises” yet they give us food to feed them. The babies are locked in a 6x8 cage. The entire area is full of poop and the tortoises do not get to roam free at all. They’re captive and do not have the ability to escape the hands of tourism except probably at night time. It was extremely sad to see that people not only cage them but some people will pay a ton of money just for an instagram pic. One girl I saw was trying to hold the tortoise back to get a “good pic” and nobody stopped her although the tortoise was clearly trying to avoid her. We decided to skip out on the dolphins as some others we met along the trip mentioned how they cornered the dolphins and left their propellers on to herd them in a circle. Just hearing that made me cringe and I couldn’t do it. While snorkeling I was having trouble with my goggles and the captain nor the other workers even offered assistance. I didnt even get to swim. The snorkeling also only lasted about 15 minutes... we spent most of our day on the beach catching rays. If I wanted to spend time on the beach I’d go to Cancun. I wanted to experience something different but Sadly most of my experience was seeing greed. The beaches are beautiful, the water is great, the animals are lovely. The food was awesome as well. However my rating isn’t on just this, it’s also on Safari Blue & the greed surrounding tourism. My group and I were very discouraged and we decided to skip out on the last day. I hope whoever reads this, please do some research! Many groups pose as conservationists only to take advantage of you and the animal.

content: A classic, touristy excursion to do in Zanzibar. Departure by boat, stopping at the sandbar (about an hour) along with dozens of other boats and hundreds of people. Then snorkelling on a small nearby reef (few fish, though colorful, nothing like the Red Sea) for about half an hour. Then a boat ride in a natural pool surrounded by mangroves. Then a stop on the island for lunch: there's a covered area with tables and benches where each group eats. Then a half hour of free time (either on the beach, or on the beach itself, where there are about twenty stalls for shopping). Return at 3-4 PM. Ultimately, I definitely wouldn't do it again.

content: Blue Safari was the highlight of our trip to Zanzibar! We headed out on a boat fully stocked with drinks and fresh coconut and did guided snorkeling. This was my first time snorkeling and I was in awe! There were so many types of fish and sea life - manta rays, puffer fish, starfish, sea cucumbers, we even saw Nemo and Dory! Then we hopped back on the boat and got back in the water a short time later to snorkel around independently. We headed to a satellite island where we had a delicious meal of rice, veggies, fish and chicken with soft drinks and beer. We did a tasting of all sorts of local fruits. We saw a huge Baobab tree and did a little shopping at some of the souvenir huts. Then we got back on the boat and our final stop was a mangrove lagoon. We went back to the main island and arrived around 4pm. Our trip had about 12 other tourists from many countries and it was really cool to get to chat with them. Our guides were very knowledgeable and friendly. The trip was only $65/person and we paid for our own transport from Stone Town. I would HIGHLY recommend this trip, I will never forget it!

content:
While in Zanzibar, we took several excursions, and this one truly stood out.
A paradise of flora and fauna!
You'll discover hundreds of colorful fish while snorkeling in the open ocean. (Mask and snorkel will be provided.)
On the way to the island, you'll eat fruit, which still makes my mouth water.
You'll see a magnificent stretch of fine sand and disembark to enjoy it.
Then you'll head to Baobab Island.
You'll land on an island and discover the oldest baobab tree in Zanzibar, 600 years old.
A delicious meal will be served: rice, chicken, lobster, grilled slipper lobster, vegetables...
And a perfect atmosphere.
Return to the boat by sail.
I recommend shopping around to find different guides, as prices can vary significantly.
Remember to bring sunscreen and water shoes for walking in the water.
Enjoy every moment.

content: We booked the Blue Safari with the well-known Marbella, influenced by what we'd seen online, and our recommendation is that if possible, you book directly with local people. With Marbella, we booked three excursions, and he wasn't seen on any of them. He sent other people in his place who didn't even know what we had previously agreed upon. I would have appreciated it if he had notified us that he wouldn't be there or expected; instead, he simply called at the last minute to ask how things were going and remind us what we had to pay the guide on duty. Furthermore, he never advised us on the best times for certain activities (for example, swimming with dolphins). We could have gone in the afternoon directly from the hotel, but instead, they took us in the morning, along with everyone else, and at a time when the place was practically a flea market. Knowing we were so close, we could have gone earlier or later. And this is just one example. Finally, I must mention that the price is very high for the poor quality offered. Again, if you want to do something special, hire them directly in the area. They might not speak Spanish, but I don't think that's important, right?

One more short snorkel, close to the other place - same to see.
And that was it. No sailing in areas with a chance to see dolphins - they didn’t even mention how/where to look.
The tour seemed more concerned with food and drinks (I’m guessing that’s one reason people liked it so much...?). The food was good and plenty.
Directly back to shore after that. So, too little snorkel (approx 45 min total), too little dolphins. Short visit to laguna and an island. All in all not good enough value for the price (which is very expensive! - 90 usd per person incl transfer).
Despite what others say, this (and snorkeling) in Zanzibar is not a must. Have you tried snorkeling before you will probably be disappointed, and should maybe come for the food and the sailing instead...

We chartered Never Say Never and the team of Chantal, Ali and Pepe were a delight. They made us feel instantly welcome and we were able to relax with some drinks and nibbles. We gently cruised to our destination where we were able to snorkel and soak up the surroundings. Lunch was made on-board and was delicious and generous, with the wine also being very nice.

Ultimately a great experience, delivered by a friendly but professional team. If you’re looking for a charter whilst in Zanzibar then you will be very well looked after by Zanzibar Yacht Charters.

content:
The Hamamni Persian Baths is located in a historical building of Stone Town, Zanzibar. The name Hamamni is also used to refer to the neighbourhood where the building is located.
The Baths were built between 1870 and 1888 for sultan Barghash bin Said for use as public baths, and maintained this function until 1920. They are referred to as 'Persian'" because their construction was commissioned to Shirazi architects.[1] The word '"Hamamni'" means '"the place of the baths'".

content: The tour was interactive, educational, dynamic, and fun. It's perfect for all ages. We arrived by car with the kids. A staff member met us right at the car, introduced ourselves, discussed the price, helped us cross the road, gave us some introductory information, and then started the tour. We were very lucky with Adam; he was quick to answer our questions and the kids' comments. We sampled everything: tasted and smelled the aromas—from pepper, aloe, cinnamon, ginger, lemongrass, and more. The kids really got into it, and every time they moved to a new bush or tree, they'd ask the guide a playful question: "Yum, yum, or are we just smelling the aroma?" This question became a running joke, which Adam picked up perfectly, making things even more fun and engaging for both us and the kids. We learned a lot of useful health and educational information, for example, that vanilla is a parasitic plant, and if it attaches itself to a tree, the fruit-bearing tree stops bearing fruit, and lemongrass is a good mosquito repellent, among other things. At one point, we approached the next tree, and voila, Adam had climbed it in a matter of seconds and collected some delicious fruit for us (there were so many interesting ones that I've already forgotten which ones). We started to turn back, thinking, well, nothing can surprise us anymore. Then we stopped by a coconut palm, and a young man deftly threw some kind of string over his feet and, clasping the palm in that way, began to climb the tree at lightning speed. Our mouths dropped open and we oohed and aahed in anticipation as he plucked the coconut—and there it was. It was a complete delight to see how, seconds later, the coconut was already on the ground. Before that, this clever young man had woven palm leaf crowns for the girls and us, and Adam had completed the arrangement with palm leaf glasses. Naturally, we were delighted, sharing our impressions and getting ready to leave. But even here, the tour had come to a logical conclusion. Now we were invited to a fruit tasting – coconut milk, coconut pulp, pineapple, and local tangerine. Everything was delicious and juicy – ​​simply delicious. And at the end, we were offered oils, soap, and spices. We couldn't resist, and we didn't want to – we wanted to treat ourselves to gifts and continue the pleasant aftertaste of the tour. This review turned out to be extensive, but with such a luxurious program, it's impossible to convey its charm in just one or two sentences. Highly recommended!)))

content:
The village tour was a unique experience. You can be prepared mentaly for it from what you already know from documentaries, stories, news, etc. but the raw reality will hit you once you walk around houses and/or enter inside them.
Returing to Bilal, he is from the village, he lives there, he overcame his background, he seems a guy that truly cares about his village. I had a feeling that he wanted to immerse you in the village lifestyle, show you everything around, and, most importantly, share things with the community.
Important to mention: if you can bring something for children, it is very appreciated - it can be color books, pencils, backpacks, etc. whatever you may think that can help them.
This is not a turistic tour per se, is more a cultural ride showing you the real Zanzibar, behind the resorts and 'main-road'" activities.

content:
Bilal is a kind, ambitious, and hardworking young man who clearly cares deeply about the community he lives in. He taught himself English and now supports himself through this small guiding business he built on his own.
My husband and I went on a tour with him that included a visit to a spice farm and his home village, Kisongoni. There was no car transfer included (we didn’t need one) — we used our own car and also gave him a ride. We paid $40 per person for the experience.
Bilal guided us through the village and explained how people live there and how they build their homes. He even took us into several local houses so we could see firsthand how families live. He bought small items for the children and laundry detergent, which he distributed to the families.
The experience was moving, and at times quite emotional. Even if you try to prepare yourself by reading or watching videos online, nothing really compares to seeing the reality with your own eyes. The local people are warm and welcoming, and the children were full of joy when receiving the small gifts.
A small suggestion: if you’re able to bring anything with you — like notebooks, coloring books, crayons, small backpacks, children's clothes, detergent, or rice — these things are truly appreciated and very much needed.
Overall, I wholeheartedly recommend Bilal as a guide. This experience is not just a tour — it’s a powerful reminder of humanity, generosity, and perspective. And supporting someone like Bilal, who works hard and gives back to his community, makes it all the more meaningful.

clauses.clause_text: Even if you try to prepare yourself by reading or watching videos online, nothing really compares to seeing the reality with your own eyes.

content:
This place calls itself "ethical" because it's supposedly clean and has few turtles, undoubtedly trying to differentiate itself from the other cave already present in Kizimkazi, but the hell it is for the animals is the same.
A turtle can travel hundreds of kilometers in the ocean in a single day. Is that the case here?
The turtles were captured in the ocean (healthy) and then put in this pool to make money…
I asked in a comment on their Instagram where these turtles came from… my comment was deleted, which says it all.
These turtles don't belong here. There's no "sanctuary," no place to care for them; this place isn't ethical, it's just another prison.
Don't participate in this, don't fund this.
If you truly love turtles, don't go see them here.

The snorkeling activity was wonderful. The crystal-clear water and abundance of marine life made this experience unforgettable. We had the chance to enjoy the underwater beauty, and to top it off, we ate freshly caught octopus, which was delicious. They also offered a selection of fresh fruits that perfectly complemented the meal.
To end the day, we visited Salaam Cave. The cave itself is impressive, but what truly made this part of the tour special was the opportunity to swim with turtles. Being so close to these majestic creatures in their natural habitat was a unique and magical experience.
I highly recommend Momo Tour 100%. The organization, care, and attention to detail were exceptional. Momo is an incredibly professional and passionate guide, which is reflected in every aspect of the tour. Definitely an experience worth repeating.

clauses.clause_text: The crystal-clear water and abundance of marine life made this experience unforgettable.

content:
We had the pleasure of spending most of a day with Momo. We wanted to see the non touristy and local areas by motorcycle.
It was a great experience and we saw beautiful villages, caves we could swim in, others where we could feed the turtles and we got the best massage by a lady in Kizimkazi - all arranged by Momo. Everything was super smooth. We give him our highest recommendation.
When we come back to Zanzibar, we will for sure reach out to him again.
Thank you for showing us what we wanted to experience. It was a great day 🙏🏻

Don't expect to see lots of wildlife, but the peace and unspoiled nature of the mangroves is wonderful. The equipment is good, and the guides are fantastic; you can tell they really enjoy what they do.
Arranging everything is easy via WhatsApp, and the start time depends on the tides. Transfers can also be arranged. We were lucky last week and were able to start at a time that allowed us to even catch the sunset. In total, we were out for just under three hours.
Asante sana!

We learned a lot about the mangroves and the wildlife, and our guides were incredibly warm and attentive. To top it all off, we were treated to fresh fruit, and we were so sad that we had to rush back to the hotel and couldn't stay longer.
Highly recommended! It was so much fun and incredibly relaxing and peaceful! Fantastic! 😊

They also organized a shuttle service.
Great guides, great tour, highly recommended.

content:

We even got to see the sunset and spotted fireflies on the way back. Water was provided for everyone, and at the end, we enjoyed delicious melon and pineapple. It was absolutely perfect. This trip is 1000% worth it. Thank you to the whole team. We will never forget this amazing kayak tour. Asante Sana!!!

content:
In my opinion, one of the best activities in all of Zanzibar!
A beautiful 2-hour kayak tour through the mangroves, partly through narrow, shallow side channels, and partly in wider channels leading to the open sea.
Water is provided during the tour; fresh pineapple is served afterward.
A tuk-tuk from Bwejuu costs 10k; arrange your return trip in advance, as there are no spontaneous transport options so deep inland.
Highly recommended for anyone who can hold a paddle!

content:
Beautiful environment, verry nice to be surrounded by nature, the water and the birds.
For us it was the best activity we did in Zanzibar.
There are no pushy venders, no pushy tour guides who want to sell you a boating trip. Only your verry friendly captain and the mangrove forest.
Nice escape of the busy Zanzibarian life.
Note: you will always be kayaking against the tide (against current) but it is noting too sporty. The captain foresees enough resting spots.
In the end you get some delicious pineapple.

content: Together with my partner and our wonderful, professional guides, I joined a kayak tour through the mangrove forest at high tide and it felt like gliding into another world. The stillness of the water, the whisper of the trees, and the gentle rhythm of our paddles created a magical atmosphere. We drifted past flocks of birds, schools of fish, and tiny crabs dancing along the roots. The landscape was breathtaking, unlike anything I’ve ever seen before. It was a truly unforgettable experience, and I can’t recommend it highly enough.

clauses.clause_text: We drifted past flocks of birds, schools of fish, and tiny crabs dancing along the roots.
It was a truly unforgettable experience, and I can’t recommend it highly enough.

content: Absolutely fantastic trip around the mangroves. Didn’t see another soul the whole time we were kayaking and it really feels like you are seeing a completely new side of Zanzibar. Saw a shedload of white and black egrets, pied kingfishers and fireflies too. Highly recommend - easily one of the best things we have done since arriving. Plus Shommy gave us some mind blowing pineapple at the end.

content:
Warning - this is adventure territory!
Bwejuu Mangroves are an absolute must - the highlight of our holiday so far.
We didn't book in advance and arrived at low tide. The guys were still happy to take us out because even though low tide means having to walk through the mangrove tunnels, we then had an amazing time snorkeling and saw hundreds of vibrant, colourful fish. Our guides were very knowledgeable about the flora and fauna, and made sure we got the maximum from our trip. The experience was rounded off with a very welcome fresh fruit platter. We also took our tuktuk driver along for the whole expedition - also a first for him and definitely not the day he was expecting!
So, if you want to canoe from start to finish, go at high tide. If you want the earthy experience complete with snorkeling and pretty fish, low tide might be better. Good footwear (water shoes) is an absolute must.

clauses.clause_text: We didn't book in advance and arrived at low tide.

content: A really fun day, probably best to call and book in advance to get the best advice. If it is high tide, you can get the canoe experience through the tunnels of the mangrove.. But the water is deeper and murky. We went low tide and walked in through the canals. There are rocks under the water, so shoes are advised. Then we canoed in the main river, which was great fun and spectacular. There are lots of fish and crabs to see. We took our own snorkels and masks and were the first to snorkel there. You see lots and lots of fish, angel fish, trumpet fish and many that are unique to thee mangrove. Apparently if you do the sunset timing you are likely to see bush babies and monkeys. The guides and owner are great fun. It's a new venture so still being slowly completed, at three end of our day we finished with fresh fruits on the tree top view point. Highly recommended. You can take a tuk tuk here for not much and it's about $25pp. All in all a great experience.

clauses.clause_text: We went low tide and walked in through the canals.
You can take a tuk tuk here for not much and it's about $25pp.

The sunset was stunning, and the tree with the herons preparing for their night's rest was a lovely sight. After nightfall, we were given headlamps, which made the return trip in the dark quite an experience. Unfortunately, the speed the owner had set was a bit too fast for one of our group.
To finish off the trip, we enjoyed some fresh pineapple.

Mangrove kayaking with Bwejuu Mangrove Tunnel Kayak🛶 a few days ago was one of the best experiences during my visit to Zanzibar.😊

I’m not proficient at kayaking so I shared a kayak with Abdul, especially since some of the pathways are narrow. This gave me the opportunity to relax and take in the natural environment around me even more since I wasn’t paddling alone on my kayak. The environment is truly serene, lush and enjoyable to listen to the sounds of nature.🌊🌿
At some point I went out of the kayak for a little swim 🏊🏾‍♀️ in the more open areas and thoroughly enjoyed myself. Abdul and Saeed even joined me in the water.😄
Bwejuu Mangrove Tunnel Kayak was established recently (about 5 months ago) and they truly have a beautiful vision. I’m excited to see how everything comes together over time as they continue to build the business. I wish them every success.✨
I highly recommend doing this activity in Bwejuu, Zanzibar.💯 Make sure to contact them, at the latest the day before, as this activity is dependent on the timing of the tides.

content:
Unlike those who saw weeds, I was told, by wise and calm words, in perfect English, taking me to a place where seemingly everything could have been thrown together. In reality, I spent 45 minutes with Mohamed, until he explained that all the plants I saw around me were medicinal... and therefore the natural pharmacy of that area. I stayed for five days inside the forest and it was magical. At sunset, we emerged into the mangroves and surreal views appeared before you... flocks of birds as the sun set, to the sound of crabs snapping their claws.
I ate with them and lived among them, and it was the best experience I could have had to get to know the real Zanzibar. If you love resort life, leave it alone. It's not for everyone. If you're looking to experience nature, meet the people, visit plantations or a school, with a knowledgeable guide who will introduce you to a functioning ecosystem, contact Mohamed of Zala Park directly and ask for a program proposal, as I did... I guarantee you won't regret it.
Habari

place_name: PAYO Quad Zanzibar: Adventure and Discovery in the Heart of the Island
content:
⭐⭐⭐ 3 out of 5 stars – Great tour, but with some room for improvement
My girlfriend and I participated in the quad tour on the morning of September 6, 2026. Overall, we had a good time, but in our opinion, there are a few things that could be improved.
We were picked up directly from our hotel with a slight delay. Upon arriving at the tour operator's location, we received a good and easy-to-understand briefing on how to operate the quads. Each participant had to start the quad themselves, drive forward about 4 meters, engage reverse, drive back, and then turn the quad off. This allowed us to familiarize ourselves with the vehicle before the actual tour began.
Afterward, we were given helmets. However, these seemed somewhat unhygienic, as they had obviously been worn by many people. A disposable balaclava or hygienic cap would have been preferable.
The actual tour then began. There were about 10-12 quads in total. The entire tour lasted about 4 hours, of which approximately 2 hours were actual driving time. The route led over varied terrain and through different areas. There were three stops in total: one at a beach, one in a local village, and another at a beach or harbor. This gave us a glimpse into the surroundings and life on Zanzibar, in addition to the quad biking.
Our quad bike's low fuel warning light was already illuminated at the start. During the ride, it switched itself off several times while driving over bumpy and rocky sections. We can't say for sure whether this was actually related to the low fuel level – but given the circumstances, a connection is certainly plausible. It would be advisable to ensure that all quad bikes are adequately fueled and in perfect working order before the tour begins.
Important: Be sure to wear clothes that you don't mind getting dirty! 😄 We were literally covered from head to toe in fine brown dust and sand after the tour. We therefore strongly recommend wearing long trousers and a long-sleeved top, as well as clothing that can be easily washed afterwards.
We found the tour to be very reasonably priced. The regular price would have been €58 for two people. Thanks to a discount code (Tripadvisor), we ultimately only paid €41 for both of us and a quad bike. For this price, the experience was satisfactory, and the overall value for money was good.
In conclusion: The quad bike tour was varied and generally enjoyable. We particularly liked the different routes and stops. However, in our opinion, there is room for improvement regarding the hygiene of the helmets, as well as the technical condition and refueling of the quad bikes.
Therefore, we give it 3 out of 5 stars. With better-maintained and adequately fueled quad bikes and more hygienic helmets, a significantly higher rating would be possible, in our view.

place_name: PAYO Quad Zanzibar: Adventure and Discovery in the Heart of the Island
content:
If you love adventure, speed, and a good dose of dust on your face, then the Payo Quad Bike tour in Zanzibar is an absolute must-do! It’s one of those activities that gives you both an adrenaline rush and a genuine feel of local life.
The experience runs from 2 p.m. to about 6 p.m., and it includes visits to three key locations the first beach, a local village, and another scenic beach where the tour wraps up with fresh fruits for everyone.
Before hitting the trail, the team gives a brief 15-minute training session on how to operate the quad bikes simple, practical, and great for beginners. Each quad bike can carry two people (a driver and a passenger), and the machines are solid four-wheel, off-road beasts with good suspension and braking.
Safety is taken very seriously. Everyone is given a helmet, and the group moves in a single file to avoid accidents. There’s a lead instructor in front and a supervisor at the back, making sure no one gets lost or left behind. The pace changes along the way sometimes fast enough to get your heart racing, other times slower so everyone can catch up and enjoy the view.
The ride starts off on a smooth, open road where you feel the wind and take in the scenery. Then comes the real fun the off-road stretch. During my ride, the trail was extremely dusty, so much that visibility was low even with glasses and a helmet! But honestly, that’s part of what made it so thrilling it’s raw, messy fun.
The village stop was another highlight. Locals, especially the children, came out to welcome us with songs and dances, including the lively “Jambo Jambo” tune that instantly puts you in a good mood. We interacted with them, shared sweets and biscuits, and got a brief explanation of their culture and way of life. It was warm, genuine, and memorable.
The final stop was another beachside location where we relaxed, enjoyed fresh tropical fruits, and admired the view of the ocean. You could see boats floating nearby and even watch locals working on traditional wooden boat-making a fascinating sight.
The journey back took us through both the village and city roads, giving us one last wave of excitement and scenery.
Overall, the Paiu Quad Bike Adventure is a must-try for anyone visiting Zanzibar. It’s exciting, immersive, and incredibly well-organized. Between the thrill of the ride, the warmth of the local community, and the beauty of the stops, it’s an experience that deserves a solid 10/10.

content:
If you are traveling to Zanzibar, do not miss the Mamas of Zanzibar cooking experience. In fact, if you did nothing else in Tanzania, I would still say this experience alone would be worth traveling halfway around the world for.
From the moment we arrived, Maskat and the Mamas made us feel incredibly welcome. There is something so genuine, warm, and personal about the experience that is difficult to put into words. You aren't simply attending a cooking class; you are being welcomed into a community, sharing food, stories, laughter, and a glimpse into a culture in a way that feels incredibly authentic and special.
I've done cooking experiences all over the world, including in Vietnam and Argentina, and while I've enjoyed every one of them, this experience genuinely stands out as world-class. There was something completely different about the connection we felt with the Mamas and the care they put into making us feel at home. The food was fantastic, but what made the experience truly unforgettable was the people.
Maskat deserves a special mention as well. Herwarmth, enthusiasm, and genuine passion for the Mamas and for sharing Zanzibari culture made the entire experience even more meaningful. You can tell how much this means to her and how empowering this is for the community.
We left with full stomachs, huge smiles, and memories that will stay with us for a very long time. Of everything we did during our time in Tanzania, Mamas of Zanzibar was truly one of the standout highlights of our entire trip.
I cannot recommend this experience highly enough. If you're debating whether to book it, just do it. You will not regret it.

content:
If you want to walk all the way to the end of the reef on your own, where the waves break... forget it! I tried it, took a huge risk, and had to give up maybe 30 meters from the end.
It was like a labyrinth with increasing difficulty. At first, you walk through shallow water and sand at low tide. Then there are more and more sea urchins, and here and there you also see moray eels or fish among the coral. Finding a way through the sea urchins, where sometimes you only have about a foot's width of space to stand... difficult and risky. And you shouldn't walk on the coral. For one thing, you'll damage it, and if a piece of coral breaks, it could slice your legs down to the bone.
If you want to go there, get a guide or someone to take you by boat. Luckily, I met two local fishermen there who guided me on foot from the reef back to the hotel.

content:
I was wandering around Stone Town and came across St. Joseph's Cathedral—the one with the two towers visible from afar, walking from the market toward the sea.
I didn't go inside, but even from the outside, you can sense the power of the place. Stone walls, slightly darkened by sun and salt, and the scent of the ocean wafting from the street right to the gates.
Standing at the entrance, you can immediately imagine how it was built: the late 19th century, the heat, French missionaries laying the foundation stone, surrounded by sandy streets and the hum of a port city. And now—the same cathedral, the same towers, and seagulls above them, just like then.
I wanted to go inside, but the doors were closed that day. So I stood outside, listening to the hum of the organ and children's voices coming from within.
There's something powerful about it—as if history hasn't ended, but lives on, quietly, within these walls.

content:
St. Joseph's Cathedral, located in Stone Town, Zanzibar, is a significant historical and architectural landmark. Constructed by French missionaries between 1893 and 1898, the cathedral's design was inspired by the Marseille Cathedral in France, evident in its prominent twin spires that dominate Stone Town's skyline.
The cathedral's interior once featured paintings depicting scenes from the Old Testament. However, these artworks were unfortunately destroyed during a restoration in 2014. The building materials, including tiles and stained glass windows, were imported from France, reflecting the European influence on its construction.
Situated in the Baghani area off Kenyatta Road, the cathedral remains an active place of worship for the local Catholic community, hosting several masses each Sunday and occasionally on weekdays. Its twin spires are easily visible from various vantage points in Stone Town and from the ocean, making it a notable feature of the city's landscape.
In the narrow churchyard, there used to be a tall palm tree, which appeared in most pictures of the church; the tree was cut down sometime in the 2000s.
As one of the most important historical buildings in Stone Town, St. Joseph's Cathedral attracts numerous visitors and continues to be a testament to Zanzibar's rich cultural and religious heritage.

place_name: Taxi and Tours with Juma Zanzibar
content:
An exceptional day with Juma! We chose the dolphin tour followed by a barbecue on a beautiful island (sandbar).
Juma's highlights:
He picks you up from your hotel in his comfortable taxi.
He's incredibly reliable (he drives carefully) and punctual.
His boat has two engines, allowing us to get from one place to another faster and, most importantly, before the other boats.
We swam alone with the dolphins; he stops precisely in the open sea and follows us in the water with the boat—it was extraordinary.
His barbecue was fabulous; we even had lobster!
The boat was private for our family, and there were two of them to take care of us.

The food he prepared on the sandbank was not only fresh and delicious, but truly the best meal we had during our entire stay on the island.

place_name: Taxi and Tours with Juma Zanzibar
content:
We had an amazing time with Juma and his team! They were incredibly friendly, professional and made sure everything was perfect.
Our day started with a boat trip, and on the way to the sandy island, we were lucky to see dolphins. Once we arrived, we went snorkeling and were amazed by the vibrant marine life - colorful fish, corals, and other sea creatures.
Later, we headed to the Sand Bank, where Juma’s team prepared a delicious seafood lunch featuring tuna, shrimp, calamari, potatoes, lobster, and fresh fruits. It was absolutely mouthwatering! We spent 2-3 hours relaxing, swimming in the crystal-clear water, and enjoying the pristine white sandy beach.
On the way back, they took us to see sea stars, which were spectacular. The variety of colors and sizes was truly fascinating. To end the day, we visited the mangrove trees, adding a perfect touch to an already wonderful experience.
This was one of the best trips we’ve had in Zanzibar. We highly recommend Juma’s tours — his team is knowledgeable, professional and ensures a memorable experience.
Asante sana Juma and all the best for you and your team! 🫶🏻

content:
I'm disappointed. We contacted Mago after reading reviews on Google. The reviews couldn't be better. And that was the case at first. We used his services for a few days, went to Jozani, and a few times to Stone Town – he's responsible, communicative, and everything he said he did (his prices are average). From the very beginning, we talked about a trip to Tanzania, to Arusha for a safari. It was two days and one night.
We agreed on Tarangiri and Ngorogoro National Parks, and the price per person, including roundtrip airfare, was $520. For two, it was $1,040. He personally wrote this amount down on a piece of paper. And the price was discussed daily. He asked for $500 upfront (for airfare). He said to pay the rest to the person who would meet us in Arusha. Before departure, I reiterated that I should pay the remaining $540 to the person who would meet us. Mago confirmed this. By this point, I trusted Mago completely and it never even crossed my mind that this man could cheat.
But! When we arrived in Arusha, the man meeting us started demanding $900 ($400 more!), and he even said the safari was scheduled for Manyara National Park, not Ngorongoro. Naturally, I didn't have $400 on me. With a return ticket in two days, and my wife and I standing in the middle of Arusha, our safari had become a major bummer. We immediately called Mago, and he started accusing me of being deaf, saying he'd said $1,400 for two from the start, and that I'd misunderstood and that I should pay. We'd discussed the price of $520 per person (including airfare) with him several times. How he'd turned $520 per person for two into $1,400, I don't know. But from his words, I understood one thing: I was the fool and it was all my fault.
Later, after reading online, I realized it's common practice in Zanzibar to say less to ensure the client buys (and Mago knew our budget was 1,000, and if he'd initially said 1,400, we simply wouldn't have flown). Overall, the safari turned out completely different from what we expected—with a ton of problems to solve. Lying is not nice, Mago! I'm disappointed. I don't recommend using Mago.

content:
The Blue Lagoon was touted everywhere as a dream tour: sandbank, fruit, snorkeling, seafood BBQ. GetYourGuide was full of top ratings. Sounds like paradise – unfortunately, it was anything but.
It started with our guide simply "handing us off" to the captain on the beach. Because of the low tide, hundreds of tourists had to walk to the boats – a veritable mass migration. Our captain then spontaneously decided to just leave us standing there, because other guides told us to wait. Spoiler alert: Nobody came back.
After 1.5 hours, we were spotted by chance by another guide and promptly "added" to an Italian group.
Then we were taken in a small rowboat to a completely overcrowded dhow. Understandably, the people there didn't want to let us on. Particularly absurd: A couple had booked a private tour for two – and yet they were still stuck on this overcrowded boat with us. Organization at its finest.
So, another transfer: from the rowboat to a small motorboat that took us to a sandbank. No shade, tons of tourists, a quick bite of fruit (yes, they had some), but the mood had long since soured. We stayed for about 30 minutes. The sandbank was so crowded that we wondered how another boat could even dock there.
Afterwards, we wanted to go to the BBQ. Problem: We had no boat left.
So we waited two hours in the blazing sun (sunscreen is highly recommended; the Zanzibar sun is intense). This left us with a grand total of 10 minutes for snorkeling, since the waiting time was, of course, deducted from the actual activity.
The BBQ took place on an island geared entirely towards mass tourism: markets with cheap trinkets, crowds of people, and a food area that made you fear food poisoning rather than look forward to seafood. Not a trace of lobster, tuna, or calamari – we played it safe and got fries. At least they were hard to spoil.
When the captain later came to collect our snorkeling gear, the moment of relief arrived:
"Oh shit – these are the people I lost."
No joke. After that, there was a frantic search for someone who spoke English, half-hearted apologies, we had to leave the nice group, and were put up somewhere else again because this boat was bigger.
Finally, a quick stop in a bay for a dip – very quick – and then finally back.
Conclusion:
This tour is perfectly organized if the goal is to make tourists wait as long as possible, change boats multiple times, and shatter any illusion of a relaxing excursion. Absolute mass processing, no planning whatsoever, zero romance, zero relaxation.
If you want to experience the real Zanzibar: stay away.
If you like chaotic vacations: have fun.

At the second spot (the starfish spot) the corals were dead for sure and there were many sea urchins. Also our captain picked up a starfish to show us, which you absolutely shouldn't do! As a tourist, I'm aware that such excursions are negative for the environment. Therefore, I always try to book local guides who know the area well and take care of the reef.
Unfortunately, that wasn't the case here.

Too many boats, too many tourists makes for an unhappy visitor and an abuse of nature and an unsustainable tourist attraction.

content:
We found this spice farm on Google Maps because of its great reviews, and it turned out to be exactly what we were hoping for.
We specifically wanted a small, authentic, locally run spice farm — not a big tourist operation or a commercialized attraction. And that’s exactly what we got here.
We contacted him via WhatsApp (the number is listed on Google Maps) and the communication was super quick and friendly. We arranged a time for the next day without any complications. He also asked in advance if we would like to stay for lunch and what we preferred — fish, meat, or vegetarian — and mentioned that the meal was definitely worth it.
The price was only $12 per person including lunch, which is honestly incredible value for the experience you get.
At first glance the spice farm almost looks like a simple garden — a bit wild and very natural — but once you start walking through it, you realize how much is actually growing there. There are so many different trees, plants, fruits, vegetables and spices hidden all around the property.
The tour itself was amazing. He is an incredibly friendly and funny host with lots of jokes and even some German skills, which made it extra fun for us. The whole experience was very interactive: we smelled, tasted and tried to guess many different spices and fruits — probably 10 to 15 different things — and we received small samples of many of them as well.
After the tour we sat down traditionally on the floor and were served lunch. Everything was freshly prepared and incredibly delicious. It felt very authentic and homemade, and we were also served tea with the meal.
At the end we had the chance to buy some spices directly from the farm — and the prices were unbelievably fair. For example, I bought eight large, high-quality vanilla pods for only about 2–3€ in total, plus several other spices. It didn’t feel touristy or overpriced at all — quite the opposite.
This place is the real deal: authentic, welcoming and run with a lot of heart.
Absolutely recommended — 10/10.

content:
Beautiful spot. Locals collect starfish and leave them here. Otherwise, you'd have to be really lucky to find one while walking on the reef.
I recommend either going there with the hotel staff or trying to attract a Maasai, who will approach you anyway as soon as you start walking towards the reef at low tide. Of course, you might initially think the Maasai are trying to sell you something. Nope, they'll tell you all about the reef and are great conversationalists. They'll ask you lots of questions, so don't hesitate to ask them too. You'll learn all sorts of things about the language, culture, and the Maasai themselves.
We went with the hotel staff, and some Maasai joined us. They were very helpful, showing us exactly where to go, because depending on the location, it's like a labyrinth with the sandbanks, seagrass, sea urchins, and sharp coral. The Maasai were a great help to us, even with the hotel staff present. They also helped the elderly, supporting them, offering a hand, and so on. At the starfish spot, they posed with us for selfies and took group photos. We talked and laughed a lot. When we got back, we bought quite a few things in their shops to show our appreciation.
