content: OK, let me tell you about this place. We were staying at the Royal Mandarin hotel and I started walking towards the low tide when Masai men reached out to me and told me about this place. I saw that it’s real through the comments but let me tell you more details about it. Those men definitely come near you and help you by being very respectful and polite, but they expect money from you. To be honest, they definitely deserve it because they truly take care of you. They show you different sea creatures as you’re getting closer to the starfish spot. They clear out the sea urchins that they’re on your way and they show you the right path. One thing that it’s misleading is that they try and reach you by walking for 50 minutes towards that spot and then when you say that, you’re in a rush to get back, you can get back in 20 to 30 minutes. But I definitely recommend going there. Just make sure that you have enough time to walk to that spot. Stay there and enjoy and then go back. I would say wake up really early because the sun is unbearable at times start walking right there and they even collect all the starfish and bring them to you. I don’t think it’s ethical to touch the starfish at all, but those men definitely do show you their mouth their eyes so they touch them. They also grab them and put them on you to take a picture. They put them on my head on my shoulders and on my hands. And they do make Christmas trees with all the starfish. The starfish look healthy and some are really large so I hope that they have been used to humans touching them. Nevertheless, it’s a really great spot and a really great idea to do in the morning while you’re staying on that side of the beach. Just make sure that you definitely have money on you because reaching that spot is not possible without the Masai. We left them 10,000 in cash each person.

There are Massai men on the beaches that will walk with you, guide you through the best route and show you the sea creatures on the way. They are friendly, respectful and caring towards the sea creatures. I was shown the sea urchins, sea cucumbers and clown fish as well as the starfish. The young Massai man that walked us out even insisted I wear his shoes to avoid injury as I had gone out barefoot, which I would not recommend. Altogether we spent about 2 hours enjoying this experience. The pickup was on time, and Abdul told us a lot about the island, and we could ask him anything. The boat trip was lovely. We were lucky enough to see dolphins and were able to swim right above them. The water off the sandbar at Mnemba Island was simply stunning! There were so many fish to see. The snorkeling was fantastic. Afterwards, we had a delicious fruit platter with lots of fresh fruit. WARNING: extortionist boat ride!
i booked a private catamaran for my friends and family to celebrate my birthday november 2023. i paid US$2000 which converts to over $5 million TZ shilling for an 8hr ride!! for that price i expected a certain level of service.
The Good:
1. the boat was in good condition
2. the chef prepared an amazing lunch that was satisfying and enjoyed by all 24 passengers.
The BAD (and these's much):
1. via email the plan was to be picked up at our hotel's dock. due to the extreme tides in zanzibar this was not a true option. i was dishonest of azam to say it was possible when it wasn't. had i known in advanced, i could have made appropriate transportation plans.
2. poor communication once in zanzibar - i was not given the correct whatsapp number for the captain and VICTORIA the company liaison did not adequately help with facilitating day of communication.
3. we were forced to go to the beach that azam operates from meaning unexpected cost of transportation resulting in a 2hr delay to the start of our ride. upon arrival, NO ONE was there to greet all 24 of us ranging from age 73 to 3! after getting help from a kind employee, we were escorted to small boats that brought us to the catamaran. POOR customer service.
4. we sailed near but not up to mnemba island. i chose NOT to pay extra for snorkling in that area; however half way through our sail, we were detained by what i describe as pirates and neither our captain, nor VICTORIA (via phone) came to our defense but rather appeared to be in cahoots with the pirates to extort money from us. initially the ask was for US$5 per person for our time near mnemba island, however since we never stopped by the island, the asked dropped to US$3. still refusing to pay, the captain spoke with victoria and the pirates and the final settled price was a total of US$50. this back and forth took almost 1HR of the boat ride!! the pirate boat was called 'TOM CAT.'"

content:
Mangapwani Slave Chamber Tour
Slave Chambers: Built around 1880 from the cave and connected to the seaside 2kms away, the area is surrounded by varieties of indigenous trees such as Breadfruit, Ramboutants and scent shrubs.
It was an important transit point for the captured slaves to be sold to the outside world at the time of the abolishment of slavery in 1873. Between 1880-1905, the chamber was being used as a place of concealment of the human cargo pending their disposal.
A utilized as the hideout by the Arabs for their human cargo ready for shipment. The four hour guided tour begins and ends at your hotel. Mangapwani (“Arab Shore”) lies in a district where many Arabs used to live.
In the village there is a Police Station, also a large government “Bungalow” which was built by the Arabs who originally owned Prison Island. Newly opened Serena Restaurant is nearby the Slave Caves. Swimming, Sun bathing may be done widely.

We had the most amazing day on the Tamasha Dhow boat trip! From the moment we stepped on board, Natia, her husband, and the entire crew made us feel incredibly welcome. Their genuine hospitality, kindness, and enthusiasm made the experience truly unforgettable.
We were traveling with our own group of eight people (4 kids). Although the boat could have accommodated more guests, we were given the option to keep it private and not have strangers join us.
The trip itself was fantastic. We were lucky enough to see dolphins, and we really appreciated that the crew chooses not to chase or disturb them. Because of this respectful approach, you’re not surrounded by 20+ other boats competing for the same dolphins, which made the experience feel peaceful, authentic, and much more enjoyable.
We also stopped at a beautiful reef where we enjoyed some great snorkeling. On top of that, we were treated to a delicious homemade lunch and fresh tropical fruit later in the day – such a lovely touch!
Everything was perfectly organized, relaxed, and filled with smiles. If you’re looking for an authentic, friendly, and memorable boat trip in Zanzibar, we can wholeheartedly recommend Tamasha Dhow. Thank you for giving us such a wonderful day!

content:
Unfortunately, this tour was a huge disappointment. We chose the Nakupenda, Prison Island & Stone Town tour.
The organization was disastrous: Upon pickup, we were quickly charged, shoved onto some random bus, and then disappeared. We had no idea what was going on. There was no plan for who to contact or anything else. Only after asking around did we find out it was the right bus. After a few minutes, the bus stopped at a gas station without informing the passengers. In the end, everyone had to wait 25 minutes simply because two passengers were booked on a different tour.
The bus driver drove like a maniac, completely disregarding safety. Several times we were genuinely afraid of an accident.
Once we arrived at Prison Island, we continued our journey in extremely slow boats. The boats were truly dilapidated and in terrible condition. It was as if their motto was "as long as they don't sink." Seasickness sufferers were already at their wits' end here, as the boats crawled across the sea at a snail's pace, causing extreme rocking. The island itself is run-down, overcrowded, and not very appealing.
Afterwards, we went to the Nakupenda sandbank. Instead of a dream island with clear water, it was overcrowded, with greenish-murky water, and vendors constantly pestered the guests, even while eating. Leftovers from lunch were even lying around on the beach (e.g., shrimp heads). Shady spots consisted of makeshift blankets.
The food: Perhaps okay for seafood lovers (lobster, etc.), but not for us. As an alternative, there was chicken – unfortunately inedible: My girlfriend got a small piece with meat, I only got bones with skin and cartilage. Rice and fries were fine, but the fruit was very tasty. We weren't full.
The return trip was also chaotic: A couple who had already kept everyone waiting were late again. The boat left without them, had to turn around, and the man completely lost it – aggressive, insulting, almost violent towards the guide. Very unpleasant for all the other passengers.
The Stone Town tour essentially consisted of rushing through the streets and spending a lot of time in souvenir shops.
On the plus side: The guides (especially Rasheed and Mudi) were very friendly, and there were plenty of drinks and fruit.
In conclusion: A pure mass-market experience with no quality. We were very disappointed, were even afraid at times on the bus, and would recommend the Mnemba Island tour instead – it's beautiful and stress-free.

We even filled out a receipt showing that Ali was a member. However, on the day of the tour, they took us somewhere else.

In the end, a kind employee found Ali and we got our refund.
But when you book the tour, be sure to give the money to the tour company.
We ended up giving it to Ali, and now we're stuck here.
Reporting to the police is a waste of time, and the owner says he probably took a cut, but who knows if it's all a rigged game of Go-Stop? ㅠ We got our money back, but due to scheduling conflicts, we couldn't do the Mnemba tour.
Ali frequently appears at the supermarket in front of the Malika Hotel, so be careful!

content:

But the locals don't understand anything about starfish biology; they take them out of the water for long periods of time and let tourists take photos. The stars die if they're out of the water for more than 30 seconds, so in a few years, there won't be any left.

content: Well, to begin with, we did the 1-hour hike. As soon as we arrived, a man stopped us and told us the prices and that it was mandatory to have a guide; the price for adults was $12 per person. He also told us we had to give the guide a mandatory tip of 25,000 shillings. It was laughable. After looking into it, we told him that the tip was whatever we chose, not what he had told us. And he agreed. We were already off to a bad start. Then the walk through the forest was only 10 minutes. After that, they took us out onto the street across the road, right at the entrance, and if you continue straight ahead on the left, they took you into someone's house, into a kind of courtyard, to see the monkeys. It's true they're free-roaming, but come on... then if you continue to the end of the street, you see the mangroves. Basically, you can do it on your own. You don't really see any of the forest. A tourist trap. I don't recommend it. Especially since they tried to trick us as soon as we arrived by saying the tip was mandatory. The tour price is very high for what they offer.

content: A really nice place to visit. The entrance fee is 20.000 shilling (in cash) and the money goes to the community around the cave. We visited before the rain season started so the water level was quite low, but in rain season the water level rises incredibly high (you can see the green algae on some photos taken at the top of the cave), so it would be a completely different experience to come and swim in the rain season. The water is cold when you step in (since the temperature is so high in general), but give it a few seconds and it becomes this really cool and relaxing experience. I’m really glad we went, I’m just glad I remembered to bring cash since they don’t take credit cards (as far as I could see). The water changes from quite shallow to deep in a heart beat (I’m 177 cm and couldn’t stand on half the area), so just know how to swim (or float) or stay close to the edge of the water. Oh, also, this is a natural cave so the stones in the water are sharp, this is not a pool, just so you remember to swim and place your feet carefully 😊 They also sell drinks at the community center before you enter the cave. And there is an old style swahili house you can enter to see how they used to build them (using no metal, just wood, earth, stones, rope and palm leaves)

content:
We visited in January 2021. It's easy to find (the road is right across from the Tina House apartments). Entrance is $10 per person. It's a unique place, and the memories are unforgettable. The water is clear and cool, perfect for this heat! You probably don't need to make a special trip there, but if you live nearby, it's a great experience. We stayed there for one night; we stopped there on the way, and then went to another beach.
The incredible architectural forms created by nature itself are breathtaking. The Kuza Caves are a remarkable natural formation, ascribed mystical properties by the local population.
A freshwater pond, hidden from sunlight by a rock massif on an island amidst salty ocean waves, its very existence evokes thoughts about the origins of natural wonders.
The indigenous islanders have long considered the Kuza Caves sacred. For centuries, religious processions have come here to perform rituals and offer prayers. Ancient legends surround the stone labyrinths, which remain completely unexplored. In the deepening darkness, hidden passages and corridors can be discerned. To this day, several days a year are set aside for traditional ceremonies, when the cave is closed to prying eyes.

content:
Completely lost. We paid €90 for 3 people, and it was supposed to include:
- Boat: It's supposed to be for 10-12 people, but there were about 22 of us.
- Visit to a sandbar with a fruit lunch: We were there for 30 minutes, and the area was packed.
- Snorkeling: I don't think it was the worst snorkeling I've ever done. There were no fish, the coral was dead, and the area was full of some kind of jellyfish that, luckily, didn't sting.
- Visit to the island with the oldest baobab tree: You can see it in 5 minutes, and then they rush you to lunch without letting you explore the island.
- Seafood lunch: They pile you up on rice and fries, then serve you a mini salad, half a mini lobster (it must have been a European lobster, judging by the size), a tiny piece of tuna, 3 prawns, and 4 small pieces of octopus. Nothing like the picture they advertise.
- Visit to the Blue Lagoon with mangroves: The place is beautiful, but you only get access and they give you 15 minutes to swim, without allowing you to walk or boat around the rest of the lagoon.
- 5 beers: After we had already paid, they told us they weren't included and that some of the salespeople always do that to attract customers without actually including them. On top of all this, there were many hours in the sun, little shade, and a completely wasted amount of time.
I DO NOT RECOMMEND IT!

content:
We just finished the Blue Safari excursion, and it was undoubtedly one of the biggest disappointments of the trip.
There were about 30 of us on a traditional boat, all crammed together with very little space to sit. During the first part of the excursion, there was no shade, which made the journey especially uncomfortable. After lunch, they did provide shade for everyone, but some of us had already gotten sunburned.
One of the main attractions, the Blue Lagoon, wasn't visited because, they said, the tide wasn't right. From there, we were supposed to see the mango trees, but we couldn't see them for the same reason. As an alternative, they told us we could swim there since the boat couldn't get close, which isn't a realistic or safe option for everyone, and in practice, we didn't see anything.
Instead, they took us to a supposedly deserted sand island that was completely overcrowded, full of tourists and vendors, with no charm whatsoever and a tourist market atmosphere. A pristine island? Not at all.
The fruit picnic was clearly insufficient and poorly distributed for so many people. Only the quickest ate; some didn't even get a taste of certain fruits. The organization was nonexistent.
The snorkeling is a deception. There's no sign of the coral, colorful fish, and crystal-clear waters shown in the advertisements. It's done among boats, in murky water, surrounded by people, and you always see the same small fish. The seabed is gray, with nothing remarkable about it.
The food doesn't justify the price either. Nothing like a "great seafood feast": rice, potatoes, vegetables, and a few shrimp, octopus, and half a lobster cooked over a fire—a bit dry—with no real option for seconds except for the rice. It was adequate as a basic meal, but far from what was promised.
Finally, the "cultural" part is limited to seeing a baobab tree without any explanation, followed by free time in a shopping area clearly designed to get you to spend money. Nothing more.
Pay €150 for two people for this excursion? Never. This is a completely disproportionate price for a poorly organized, oversold tour focused solely on squeezing money out of tourists.
WE ARE TOURISTS, NOT FOOLS.

• Low-quality food: plain white rice, fries, a small piece of tuna and overcooked octopus.
• Overall, a wasted day for what should have been the main activity.
Would not recommend this experience.

For my wife and me, it was an unforgettable experience that we will never forget. If you're thinking about skydiving in Zanzibar: You're in the best hands here! 🪂🪂

content:
Negligent, Unsafe, and Completely Inhumane – Only Consider for a Single Tandem Jump
I initially signed up for this company’s skydiving certification course, but it turned out to be one of the worst decisions of my life. While they might be acceptable for a one-time tandem skydive, their training courses are shockingly unsafe and their practices outright negligent.
I was rushed into a solo skydive despite clearly not being ready for it. Their lack of proper training and assessment resulted in a devastating accident that left me hospitalized for 8 days and 7 nights. The physical and emotional toll was immense, but what made it worse was their complete lack of support afterward.
Neither the CEO nor anyone from the team contacted me during or after my hospital stay. I was left alone on the island to cope with the aftermath of their negligence, without a single call, visit, or offer of assistance. Their inhumane and unsupportive behavior made an already traumatic situation even worse.
If you’re just looking for a one-time tandem skydive, they might be okay—but do not trust them for any training or certification. This company cares nothing for your safety or well-being. There are far more reputable and responsible options out there. Avoid them at all costs.

The funny thing is that construction continues, and I can't imagine what it will be like in high season. There are endless vendors selling coconuts, sarongs, massages, jet skis, dolphin tours, banana leaves, ebony tags, bracelets, necklaces, and God knows what else, to which must be added swarms of Maasai trying to accost you in every way possible. The problem is that it all takes place on a beach a few hundred meters long, creating chaos and absolutely no tranquility. If Nungwi continues like this, Sardinia is better.

content:
Those negative reviews ⬇️ aren't recognisable.
The entrance is 10-20.00 TZ ( Fukuchani Cave, Ruins & village tour). The tour guides are very informative & friendly.
Unfortunately, due to high seawater, swimming isn't possible in the cave sometimes (therefore, it is important to ask the tour guide & negotiate the entrance fee beforehand).
The ruins are historically interesting. It was slavemarket in the beginning & later converted to a trading building. There is a school on the opposite site.
The village is nomadic & wonderfu area. Absolutely adorable children & locals. REMEMBER to bring candy for the children ( and there are many of them 😅). The Baobao tree is secret to the locals. You can taste mango & other fruits - if you're lucky😉
DO NOT take pictures without asking the individuals ( just because you paid fee entrance doesn't entitle you to take pictures of everything).

This place showed clear and disappointing racism. When we arrived as a group of 4, no one bothered to explain how things worked, even after we had paid. While we were trying to figure things out on our own, a white couple arrived and was allowed to go ahead of us and enter the water before we did.

The staff initially refused to give us the seaweed needed to feed the turtles and when they finally did, 1 of us who was barely in the water for two minutes was told to get out. The reason given was that another white couple needed “the spot” to take photos even though only one of us had entered the water and the rest were still waiting.
The treatment from the support staff was humiliating and unfair. When we raised this issue with management as we were leaving, instead of listening, the guys who were discriminating us became argumentative and made dismissive remarks toward us.
It was a very unpleasant experience and a real shame. No one deserves to be treated this way because of the color of their skin especially by people who know how it feels to be discriminated against themselves since they are also blacks.

content:
An amazing place... small, but incredibly valuable. Sick turtles are brought here and then returned to the ocean after rehabilitation. You can feed them algae, though be careful, as they can bite you while chasing a leaf. There are different sizes: smaller, larger, and even one truly enormous individual.
In the second pool, you can enter the water and swim with the turtles, but I passed on that because they poop in the water 😉 The turtles love to be petted and aren't afraid of people at all, which makes interacting with them truly special.
You can spend unlimited time there, admiring the animals at your leisure. There's also a restroom and a shower available after leaving the pool.
An incredible, moving experience... absolutely worth a visit!!! 🐢💚

content: Horrific experience. I’m not sure how this place is still open. If I could give zero stars I would. Just look at the AI overview of this place if you have any hope that this place is worth your time. I rarely write reviews but this place was so unsettling it felt morally wrong to not warn future customers. Putting aside the arrogant and careless nature of the staff, the turtles were absolutely feral. My friend stepped into the water for 30 seconds and was immediately bitten on her thigh. The way these turtles behaved was unnerving. They were climbing all over each other, clearly desperate to get out of the small sewage smelling pool they’re confined in. They claim they let them go out into the wild eventually, which is probably when they become too animalistic to expose to customers. They also admitted they take their eggs off the beach before they leave their sack. I’m not surprised these poor creatures act out, I would too if I was trapped like that. Oh, and the staff’s solution to treat my friend’s wound? Just rub some mouth wash on it. I’m ashamed I paid for something so unethical. Save yourself. Trust me.

As soon as I got into the water, I was immediately surrounded by at least 10 to 15 turtles, even though about seven other visitors were also feeding them at the same time. And what was very unpleasant was that one turtle bit me hard in the stomach. You can still see the bite marks two weeks later. Our children were then too scared to go back into the water and only fed the turtles from the side. We wouldn't visit this aquarium, or any other for that matter, again. Water turtles are definitely not pets you can cuddle! 😏

content:
A SERIOUS SAFETY WARNING: Negligent, Dangerous, and Life-Threatening Experience
I am writing this review as a formal complaint and a serious warning to any individual or family considering using Zanzibar Water Sports for an excursion. Our experience was not merely disappointing; it was life-threatening due to the company's gross negligence and complete disregard for customer safety.
Our snorkelling excursion began with several red flags. We were led to believe the trip was organised through our hotel, only to discover it was operated by this external company. The booking process was unprofessional; we received only a paper slip, with no formal documentation, no safety briefing, and no health and safety checks conducted before we left the shore. This initial lack of protocol was a clear indicator of the dangers to come.
The situation escalated dramatically when we were taken to a second location to see dolphins. The staff rushed us, telling us to hurriedly put on our gear and get in the water. Feeling pressured, I entered the water as instructed while the boat's engine was off.
To my horror, the moment I surfaced, the driver started the engine.
I was immediately swept under the boat and pulled into the current created by the moving vessel. I was fully submerged, drowning and fighting for my life as the boat drove directly over me. The propellers passed inches from my head and body before striking my ankle, cutting it down to the bone.
After screaming for the driver to stop, I managed to swim back to the boat. The complete lack of preparedness was appalling:
* No First Aid Kit: There was absolutely no first aid kit on board. My severe, bleeding wound had to be bandaged with a t-shirt.
* No Emergency Training: The staff showed no signs of first aid training or any ability to handle a medical emergency.
* A Negligent Return Journey: I was forced to endure a 40-minute boat journey back to the hotel while actively bleeding and showing clear signs of shock, with no medical assistance offered.
Upon our return, the situation did not improve, and we had to take our own private taxi to a hospital for professional medical treatment, which included stitches and an X-ray.
This was not an unfortunate accident; it was the direct and predictable result of a company operating with a shocking level of negligence. The key failures include:
* Failure to provide any safety briefing.
* Reckless and dangerous operation of the boat.
* Failure to ensure the area around the propeller was clear before starting the engine.
* Failure to carry basic, essential safety equipment like a first aid kit.
This company's conduct is a danger to the public. Engaging in their services is a significant risk. For your own safety and the safety of your loved ones, I implore you to avoid Zanzibar Water Sports at all costs.

We did the Discover Scuba Diving course in a group of 5 with 1 instructor. 4 of us had never dived before and 1 had previously done another Discover course but wasn't certified.
We were assured when booking that we would have at least 2 instructors, and only realised after we were on the boat on the way to the open water dive that we would only have 1. We had a very good instructor who helped us all feel calm about diving for the first time, but when diving he was not in sight of all of us. There were prolonged periods of time where I was alone with the instructor and we couldn't see the rest of our group above or below the water.
One of my friends also only got to dive for half the time as the rest of us, as she was left on the boat for at least an hour with no explanation while the rest of us went in - the instructor got all of us ready, told four of us to get in and then left her on the boat and asked her to wait there. She had to negotiate afterwards to have the price reduced for this and they agreed to take off $10.
I would have opted to go with another company if I knew that we would only have 1 instructor, but we were promised when we paid that we would have at least 2 and assured that it would all be very safe. Thankfully the experience was ok anyway and nothing went wrong, but in hindsight it wasn't safe that we were left alone with 1 instructor and it was of course disappointing that our friend only got to dive for half the time we'd expected.

Our boat had a group of snorkelers, and the crew never explained that there may be jellyfish. One member was stung and had to simply suffer on the boat. Would’ve been very helpful to advise or provide snorkelers a skin suit.

My recommendation to the shop is to improve safety standards with the guests. Thorough dive briefings go a long way in building trust.

content:
Overall experience was mediocre. Advice, communication, and information before the dives were poor and unprofessional, but the equipment was good.
I did two dives and two snorkeling trips with the dive center and I have to say that the communication beforehand, especially regarding trip selection and information about dive sites and conditions, was really poor to nonexistent. We were only asked what we wanted to do, as if we already knew the area. We were simply pressured to get onto one of the boats as soon as possible. They even pointed out that we were there for several more days, didn't necessarily have to leave the next day, and could therefore dedicate ourselves to the days with the best conditions. I then inquired about the weather and wind, as Mwemba Island is on the side of Zanzibar that was very windy that day. The guy at reception just looked out at the sea and said: "Look, it's calm." Well, sure, on that side of the island it is. But on the other side, it was very windy the next day (just as the weather forecast predicted). I asked if another day would be better, since it was supposed to rain tomorrow. He replied: "It's August, it rains in August." It had just rained yesterday and it was raining again the next day on the trip.
Generally, very little attention was paid to the guests' concerns. "Are there jellyfish?" "No!" And then there were lots of jellyfish that stung people. Snorkelers, some of whom were doing it for the first time, weren't given any information, not even a hand, and then they had trouble in the water with the waves, the current, or their equipment.
Then someone had an asthma attack. Oxygen was on board, but the crew wasn't trained for emergencies and they took a long time to connect the bottle to the mask and turn on the valve. The young man is doing well now, though.
Of course, there are some more professional staff members, but the overall attitude was clearly evident.

content:
Poor organization and dangerous.
Our dive was supposed to start at 10:00 AM. Since one of their clients was running late and they didn't want to do two dives, they made us wait an hour sitting down until 11:00 AM to start together.
When we started the dive,
my buoyancy compensator (BCD) started automatically releasing bubbles. I told the instructor, and he said it was fine.
I noticed something was wrong because my air level was dropping very quickly.
After 25 minutes, I was on reserve, when normally after 45 minutes I still have 70-80 bar of air.
The instructor saw it, and we started the ascent. As we began to ascend, my pressure gauge broke, and a lot of bubbles started coming out. We didn't have time to complete the safety stop, and I surfaced with 15 bar of air.
It's clear I could have ascended without the stop, but ideally, I should have used air from a buddy and completed the stop.
When I asked for an explanation on the surface, he said yes, I was right, but that it was okay, it wasn't a big deal.
If I hadn't noticed my air level dropping so rapidly when everyone else's was at 70, I would have run out of air and an accident would have happened. But since they don't seem to care about the regulations here, they haven't paid much attention.
Honestly, look for another diving school because safety comes first; don't risk it by going to this one.

content: I'm left with a bittersweet feeling from this experience. The organization and diving experience were terrible. I booked a scuba dive with them, and a snorkeling trip for my wife in Nmenba, which only this company offered if my wife and I wanted to go together. The journey to the island is a bit long, as it takes about an hour and fifteen minutes by boat, while other companies with faster boats do it in about half an hour. Once we arrived, they paired me with a guy who had insisted he needed a refresher course, as he hadn't dived in a while. At reception, they'd told him it wasn't a problem, but when the divemaster realized this, he disagreed, which was understandable. This resulted in losing about 15 minutes of the dive, as the divemaster started refreshing his basics: clearing his mask, retrieving his regulator, etc. When we finally started descending, the seabed was beautiful with a variety of fish, but the coral was in pretty bad shape. The dive lasted 45 minutes, and even with 90 bar of pressure, the divemaster ended it. On the way back, and this is what bothered me most, they asked us which hotel we were staying at. I replied, "Tanzanite Beach," and they said okay, they'd drop us off at the water's edge and we could walk there. This wouldn't be so bad, except it's impossible, since the beach in front of the hotel is rocky, not sandy. I mentioned this to the crew, and they said it was fine, they'd drop me off at the hotel next door. I don't know why I agreed, since I had to carry the backpack I'd brought, which contained some clothes, my phone, my wife's phone, and some other gear. So there I was, arms raised, trying to keep my backpack dry, while I tried to walk to the sand, which wasn't easy with the waves and the rocks at the bottom of the beach. This is not a company I would dive with again. The only nice thing has been the staff.

content:
A great experience, the idea is original BUT
On paper, Zanzibar SeaWalk sounds amazing. In reality, it's a disaster of organization and poor communication.
On the day, apart from a "hello" and the request for payment upon arrival, there was absolutely NO communication. We had an appointment at 2 pm, and we were simply told by message that the experience would last approximately 90 minutes, without any further details. Nothing. No explanation of how it would work, no actual schedule, no mention of a wait time.
We finally set off at 2:15 pm on an extremely slow boat, and it took us AN HOUR to reach the platform. An hour for a journey that should have been much shorter. Arriving at 3:15 PM (for an activity scheduled to end at 3:30 PM, remember), we discovered a huge crowd: more than 20 people already waiting on the platform, not counting our group of 14 who had just arrived. Knowing that only 5 people are allowed on at a time, for about 30 minutes per group (the time it takes to descend and ascend, plus the 20-minute experience itself), it was obvious the wait would be endless… but of course, no one explained anything to us or came to see or talk to us, yet again.
We waited. A long time. A very long time. Standing in the blazing sun, without water, without information, without instructions, without anything. At 4:45 PM, exasperated, I went to complain myself to the person who seemed to be in charge. He put pressure on his team, but it was already far too late: there were still two groups ahead of us.
The worst part? Everyone on the platform had received the safety instructions… except us. We were only given them because I insisted and asked again. In terms of professionalism and safety, it was practically nonexistent.
We finally got off around 5:30 pm, three and a half hours after our scheduled time. Yes, the experience itself is fun and the idea is original. But the sun was already setting, and since there were still three groups after us, we were rushed through: we didn't even get to experience all the planned activities, like the famous “I ❤️ Zanzibar” frame. Frustrating and unfair after such a long wait.
We left again at 6 pm with, as if by magic, a much faster boat. As a result, instead of returning around 3:30 pm as planned for an activity that was supposed to last 90 minutes, we got back at 6:30 pm. Three hours late.
No water during the wait.
No apologies upon arrival. The same old lack of communication.
In short, clearly, not the slightest consideration for customers.
In summary: a brilliant idea completely ruined by disastrous organization and a shocking lack of communication. We felt like mere numbers, abandoned on a platform, without information, respect, or professionalism.
If a problem had occurred earlier in the day, and someone had come to talk to us and explain, I would have understood; it happens. But under these conditions, no, I cannot accept it.
I absolutely do not recommend Zanzibar SeaWalk until they resolve this fundamental problem: they don't know how to manage or communicate with their customers. And in a tourism and security-related business, this is simply unacceptable.

content:
The Sea Walk experience in Zanzibar is undoubtedly one of those activities that will stay with you forever. From the very beginning, you'll notice the team's high level of professionalism: the explanations are clear, the equipment is top-notch, and the safety measures ensure you feel completely at ease at all times.
The most magical part comes when you descend underwater and begin to walk slowly along the seabed. The feeling of being surrounded by schools of colorful fish, swimming around you with complete ease, is simply indescribable. The clarity of the water, the tranquility of the surroundings, and the beauty of the marine ecosystem create a unique atmosphere, almost like being in another world.
It's an activity that combines adventure, safety, and wonder in equal measure, ideal for both those who have never dived and those who already love the sea. Walking underwater, without needing any prior experience, and experiencing such close contact with marine life makes the Sea Walk a beautiful, safe, and absolutely unforgettable experience in Zanzibar. Thank you!

Unbeknownst to our group we left one of our purchases in the market and he arranged to have it picked up and brought to us the next day. We did the Spice Tour which was delightful, we explored the rich lush forest as the guide demonstrated the islands array of spices , he demonstrated the uses for cooking and medicinal purposes. The guide made the tour a grand challenge and interactive by seeing who in our group could identify the many spices. The tour to Prison Island is a must for a nature enthusiast as we saw century old tortoises . The trip to Nekupenda was amazing it’s truly a surreal experience. Thanks to the teams advice we arrived early and could enjoy the crystal clear waters and marine life whilst our captain provided and guide made up a tent and us with a scrumptious seafood feast . content:

Swimming with and feeding the turtles in the crystal-clear cave was such a special experience!
We also booked jet skis, and Bamba arranged the most incredible drone footage, which gave us memories we’ll cherish forever.
The highlight of the trip was definitely the Mnemba Island boat tour for my 25th birthday. Swimming with the dolphins was truly a once-in-a-lifetime experience. The boat wasn’t overcrowded, which made everything feel so much more personal, and we even enjoyed fresh fruit on the island. The only thing I wish was different is that we could have spent a little longer on Mnemba—but honestly, that’s just because we didn’t want the day to end!
Bamba genuinely went above and beyond to make sure everything was perfect. His communication, organisation, and attention to detail were outstanding. I will recommend him to absolutely anyone visiting Zanzibar, and I’ll definitely be coming back—just because of the amazing experience he gave us.
Thank you, Bamba, for making my 25th birthday trip so unforgettable. See you again soon!

content:
Ngome Kongwe, also known as the Arab Fort and by other names, is a fortification located in Stone Town, the capital of Zanzibar. It is the oldest building and a major visitor attraction of Stone Town. It is located on the main seafront, adjacent to another landmark building of the city, the House of Wonders (former palace of the Sultan of Zanzibar), and facing the Forodhani Gardens.
It was built by Omani Arabs after expelling the Portuguese in 1699. It was used as a garrison and prison in the 19th century, and as a terminal of the Zanzibar railways 1905-28. A new guardhouse was built in 1947 and used as the ladies' club, and an amphitheatre was added in the 1990s. It is now the headquarters of the Zanzibar international film festival.'

content:
“Early is on time, on time is late, and late is unacceptable!”
― Eric Jerome Dickey
TL;DR: This is a quote that ZanRaha seems to live by, and if you need a reliable transport and tour service, Fabian and his team are the company you can not only count on, but will most likely go above and beyond.
Having had the privilege of and opportunity to travel over the years, we have taken many airport transfers in various countries. While most have been punctual, professional, etc., ZanRaha stands out from just about any other transfer we’ve ever hired. Unlike most companies or hotels whom are waiting with a sign and simply drive you from point A to point B, Fabian and his team immediately greet you like family; like cousins or nephews you haven’t seen in years. His smile is instantly inviting, his laugh and exuberant way about him are infectious. This is not an act or facade for his clients, rather, it stems from something deeper. ZanRaha is not merely a company, but the culmination of years of planning and the building of a dream. Spending time with Fabian and his team, you get the sense that your time with them is very personal. They not only want you to have a safe and enjoyable transfer or tour, but are also true ambassadors of their country.
From the very beginning of our time in Zanzibar, even prior to our arrival actually, Fabian started communicating via WhatsApp, several weeks before our trip. He helped to coordinate many things for our large group as we were headed to the island for a wedding. As we exited the airport, Fabian was personally waiting outside at arrival and made himself easy to find. Additionally, he helped with finding and activating sim cards, offered suggestions for things to see and do, and made a superb recommendation for a 14-person bus for our group, rather than the 2 smaller 6-person vans we had originally booked.
When it came to our tour day, we had the pleasure of having Mr. Barraka as our incredible tour guide and Mr. Ali as our adept driver. Our day started with the suggested tour of a spice farm, and was wonderful. There are certainly the “tourist” elements within the tour along the way, but that’s to be expected on an excursion like this. This is a strong source of income for the country, and we are all there to spend money and enjoy a vacation. Thankfully, the pressure to buy something is not shoved down your throat like so many other places one can travel.
After the time on the farm, we made our trek to Stone Town to begin the next tour of the day. As with almost anything pertaining to family and large groups, plans and schedules quickly fell apart in the face of travel cancellations, restrictions, and all the joys that have come with attempting to traverse the globe during these Covid times. Mr. Barraka was both amazingly helpful and patient while we attempted to sort out family logistics problems. He found us banks, post offices, Western Unions, and adapted to our changing needs as the day took unexpected turns. Even during the obstacles throughout the day, he still took time to point out interesting details, fun facts, and some city history as we moved from place to place in our efforts to get the remaining family to the Island. While time was quickly eaten up by family drama, Mr. Baraka adapted to the situation and, as pockets of time became available, ensured we saw the key items we requested during our planning; namely the lunch spot the bride wanted to go, and the museum the mother of the bride wanted to see. An additional note regarding Mr. Ali, he is absolutely one of the most expert drivers we have ever seen! Between navigating the bumpy dirt farm roads, the fast moving highways of the island, and the tiny streets of Stone Town, his precision control of the bus was quite a sight to behold, and we felt completely safe the entire time.
Full review on other sites without character limits.
If you have not yet booked an airport transfer or tour company in Zanzibar, look no further than this organization. Time and travel with ZanRaha truly ensures your trip will have Hakuna Matata.

The locals were upset about this but we couldn't understand what she was saying. She started screaming to us aswell because we were already standing in queue to get to the bridge but apparently it wasn't our time yet to stay in line. I asked one of the staff members what and why she was screaming but he didn't want to tell us because it was not so nice to translate.
Zanzibar, you have a beautiful island but your taxi drivers, luggage carriers and the people who sell merchandises/fruit should learn not to continue harassing others. One 'No'" should be enough to stop continuing be annoying."

content: Zanzibar ferry services, particularly aboard the Kilimanjaro ferries, offer a surprisingly smooth and comfortable journey across the Indian Ocean. The onboard experience is calm, well-organized, and a welcome escape from the bustle of city life. However, the contrast becomes clear upon arrival or departure at the Dar es Salaam terminal—where the scene can be quite chaotic. The entrance and exit areas are often crowded and disorganized, with aggressive porters and minimal signage adding to the confusion. Still, once you’re past the terminal frenzy, the ferry ride itself is a breath of fresh air—literally and figuratively.

content:
You should absolutely book first class tickets and be sure to pick them up in advance. My group was not aware that we needed to pick up our tickets from a special office quite a ways away from the terminal, so we were in panic mode when we arrived. A local helped us out and we got the tickets in time, but the rest of the group (me included) ended up waiting in the main outdoor terminal during that process. It was unbearably hot. There are no fans in the entry area and the air is stagnant, humid and hot. There are no lines when waiting to get your passport stamped. It comes down to who can push to the window and slap their passport on the counter first. Yeah, I had to do that. Feels rude but you will stand there forever if you don't. After that if you have a first class ticket, there is a special air-conditioned lounge for you. It is TOTALLY worth it. There are ample sofas and recliners everywhere. Free instant coffee is offered as well. On the boat first class get an air-conditioned cabin with comfy recliner chairs. The economy seating is stuck out in the heat.
One thing that kinda annoyed me is the unorganized baggage claim situation. You need to pay attention to what baggage cart your luggage is put on. Each cart has a number, and despite what they might tell you, first class luggage is picked up in the same area as economy. There is no claim check to determine that the luggage is picked up only by the owner. It is just a mass mob of people, not at all like the airport, snatching up bags. I did get a little paranoid of someone taking my bag. I keenly watched the carts being rolled out in order to ensure that I got my bag.

content: It is an experience if you are a person who flies in airplanes. We went from Dar to Zanzibar around New Year on a special ferry because it's so busy. It was pure chaos - but it works. Here's what you need to know. Get tix a few days in advance. Bring passports - Zanzibar is a whole 'nother country. Arrive earlyish. Ignore the porters unless you want to tip them. You'll be in a mass of people chugging through. People will jockey for position. Eventually everyone will get through. Do yourself a favor & don't bring too much stuff. The legroom is tiny but there is room under the seats. find your spot & if you're up to it, go out on the deck after you get underway. This is the economy model. If you want to pay $50 or more you can sit up top with way more room & a snack. Its fun & it's an experience!

But what I saw there was Disneyland, huge groups of tourists, the distances between people and animals are not respected, they for sure suffer from stress because of this, even if they are used to humans.
The most surprising for me was not only the visitors but even local guides moved the trees, pushed inside the bushes to take the best picture of the monkeys for the tourists (10cm from their face).
A lot of tourist screaming when a monkey gets too close to them, or jump over them to move to another tree.
Huge human traffic jam in the forest but also taxi traffic jam on the road crossing the forest to pick up people and drive them 500m further for the mangrove. Why not make one beautiful walking tour instead of this big shit show with taxis?
I think you should increase a bit the price of the entrance and have a limited amount of visitors per day. Also ensure visitors and guides respect the distances to avoid stressing animals.
I wish you all the best for the future, and good luck with the preservation of this beautiful eco system.

The whole setup was a bit Chaotic in my experience as European (as things go in many part of Africa I suppose).
I started my tour with a group and a guide. We walked through the forrest. My guide was friendly, but we were with a big group: he was mostly spending time on keeping the group together, but when asking questions I heard he was quite knowledgable. We saw 3 of the Colobus monkeys (2 in a tree and one up close who was sleeping). I was content with the (amount of) monkeys we saw. That being said - the walk through the forrest could have been longer - it felt a bit rushed.
After the monkey-part, you get driven by your own driver to the Mangrove part of the forrest. This was not explained, so it felt as if the tour suddently ended for it to continue again later. My original guide never came back (some people in our group didn't come with a driver, which I suppose brought some trouble to the system), so a lot of my group mates went with their driver to the Mangrove part. My driver wanted to wait for a guide for the information. Eventually (after a 30minute wait) he sent me with a new guide who unfortunatly didn't know much about the Mangrove.
I payed quite a lot for the tour (70dollars), which was not worth it --- But I find the price the park itself asks (12dollar for entrance + fee for the guides) fair & would definetly do the tour again for that amount.

place_name: Jozani Forest National Park Mangrove Walk
content:
You can easily avoid the $12 entrance fee.
The park is divided into three zones. The first, where the ticket booths are located, is dedicated to flora. You could enter without paying, but you might get caught. A guide isn't mandatory; it's a 30-minute walk to see the plants.
On the other side of the road are the monkeys and the mangroves. I think you can visit these areas without paying and without going through the first zone. In fact, there's no enforcement whatsoever, and it's a roadside path where you can easily see the monkeys. If you want, you can venture further in; we did, and it was great. A guide isn't necessary.
The mangroves are at the end of this path; it's a 20-minute walk along a wooden boardwalk over the water.
I recommend driving down, as it's a 15-minute walk, which can be tiring in the heat.

content:
The stars it's earned are because the place is beautiful and seeing the monkeys in their natural habitat is always a treat. But the way it's organized ruins everything.
You arrive and they tell you that you can only pay in cash, even though they have a card reader on the table. Okay, we'll let it slide.
They only allow you to go with a local guide, which I understand perfectly; there has to be someone monitoring the route and ensuring that the rules posted at the park entrance are followed.
BUT everything loses its meaning when the guide talks about only five plants and rushes through the forest, making it impossible to take photos because of the rush and the crowds. It's all about getting to the monkey enclosure quickly, and once you arrive, the rules seem to disappear for both the tourists and the guide. Nothing is respected, not even the three-meter social distancing or staying on the path. It suddenly becomes a free-for-all of tourists hunting for the best photo and video to upload to social media. It's not just that people lack respect; the guide was encouraging you to approach the monkey even when there were already 15 people surrounding it.
Then they have to take you by car or bus to the mangrove area, which is beautiful and peaceful, and your stress dissipates.
I wouldn't recommend this to someone who is aware of and respects animals. If you absolutely want to see the monkey up close and brag about having been right next to it, go ahead. The guides themselves will help you achieve that.

place_name: Jozani Forest National Park Mangrove Walk
content: Jozani Forrest is part of Jozani Chwaka Bay National Park, and is famous for being home to the endemic (meaning found nowhere else) Red Colobus monkey. The park covers approximately 50 m² and is a remnant of tropical primeval forest dating back several hundred years. The Zanzibar Kirk's red colobus monkeys have a reddish-brown coat with a darker back and head, and the males have a plume of white fur on their temples. The population numbers around 1,500 individuals. Blue Monkeys also live here, but they are very shy, and even if you do come across them, it's difficult to take a photo, unlike red colobos, which practically pose. After the monkeys, we looked at rain trees and ended up in a mangrove forest, where walking on wooden footbridges, you can see the plant formations up close.

place_name: Jozani Forest National Park Mangrove Walk
content:
The area is very popular with tourists who come on excursions organized by hotels for several tens of dollars. A little tip: from the east coast, take any daladala (shared taxi) and get dropped off at the forest for 1,000 shillings (less than €0.50). From Stone Town, take a daladala heading towards the east coast.
There are two types of tours: the grand tour (7 km) and the short tour (1 km for $12). They are accompanied by a guide.
We weren't lucky enough to see many colobus monkeys. It was just one of those days... The mangrove visit is included in the price. It's not very interesting at low tide.
It's still worth doing, though, as it allows you to see the interior of the island, and its appeal depends on luck and the time of day.

How can a sick person come to work among other people. The toilet in the national park smells so bad that you want to vomit as soon as you get close to it from the stench coming from it. The entire tour lasts about 1-1:30 hours, while when booking an appointment through the agency it says that the tour of the park lasts 3 hours and that you walk 8 kilometers on a path through the forest and monkeys. A very unpleasant experience… I do not recommend going to this place.

content:
This place is a disgrace! First, we arrived, paid €10 per person at the entrance, and the guy told us we'd get the receipt later. So far, so good. Then we got to the forest entrance, and there, a forest ranger told us we had to hire a guide, it was mandatory… a guide to follow us and show us monkeys… Honestly, we didn't need it! So we told him no thanks, we didn't want to pay for a guide!
To that, he replied that the guide wasn't free; we'd just have to leave him a tip (to me, it's the same thing) and that if we didn't agree, we could leave.
Which we did; we got back in the car and headed to the first office to get our money back. They categorically refused to give us our money back… after 10 minutes of negotiation, threats, and calm, they finally gave us our money and we left. In short… I'm not here to tell you not to go, but to warn you about their disrespectful practices towards tourists! I'm fed up with being ripped off every time!!!

This forest is very unique. On the one hand, there are free-spirited monkeys jumping through the trees and checking out tourists, fiddler crabs living in the mangrove forest, and the mangrove forest itself is also quite charming.
But on the other hand, there are constantly flying midges that bite you. Praetor, wear a tracksuit; it might rain, but it barely reaches the ground. And there are corals. They're a real nuisance. Watch your step, you could fall and hurt yourself.

content:
So, it's definitely an activity worth doing! But read my review first.
Positive points:
- The magnificent animals; if you're lucky, you'll see loads of them.
- The price isn't high, even though the trip is very quick.
- The mangrove forest is magnificent, but it's best visited at high tide. Seriously, don't go if it's low tide.
Negative points:
- The idiotic tourists who are ready to do anything to get a photo for their crappy Instagram feeds... we saw tourists touching monkeys, breaking branches to make them fall... show some respect for nature and animals, please!
- The speed of the trip.
Otherwise, I highly recommend this activity.

place_name: Jozani Forest National Park Mangrove Walk
content:
The entrance fee is approximately $10 per person (tip for the guide not included).
We had a private guide. He took us on a tour of the mangrove and explained the different types of trees. Then we went to see the monkeys (up close), first the colobus monkeys and then the black monkeys. We didn't see any chameleons (they're mostly around in the morning and very difficult to spot). But the guide had a video of all the animals we didn't see and explained where to find them.
The guided tour doesn't last very long. And you have to be lucky with your guide. Some are truly passionate, others less so and try to move as quickly as possible to take on more clients (they are volunteers and are apparently only paid through tips).
After the tour with your guide, you can explore the entire forest on your own until closing time. We encountered many species (centipedes, spiders, butterflies, squirrels, elephant shrews, birds, etc.), but you might see many more (chameleons, snakes, dik-diks, mongooses, etc.).
Bring: trousers, sneakers, mosquito repellent

place_name: Jozani Forest National Park Mangrove Walk
content:
A great place for a stroll. There's a nice, modern footbridge and a large gazebo with benches (oh, how wonderful it is to lie on them in the shade!).
There's also a descent down to the river. We saw lots of small fish with long noses in the water.
You can get here from Stone Town without a tour, just take a minibus. Buses 326, 310, or 309 are good options. The stop is in Jozani village, then walk about 1 km along a dusty dirt road past the turtle park.
In Stone Town, buses 309 and 310 can be found at the bus station on the eastern outskirts of town, near the stadium. It's a bit out of the center.
Bus 326 is based near the historic center, on Karume Street, near a long multi-story building and the market.
In February 2021, the fare was around 2,500-3,000 shillings. It depends on your luck. Some locals gave 1500, some 2000.

content: Kwale is the island home to the giant baobab tree, linked to Africa's magical tradition. Even today, some people, although it is frowned upon by the Islamic religion, go there to practice rituals that straddle the line between magic and polytheism. The destination of the famous Blue Safari, an excursion that is absolutely worth doing, unfortunately, is overrun with all kinds of waste. Restrooms are in terrible condition. Several years ago, I would have recommended this excursion with my eyes closed. Today, on my 4th Blue Safari, I was greatly disappointed, despite the fact that nature offers wonderful spectacles, from snorkeling to the mangrove lagoon and beyond. Seeing the island in such conditions was a shock to the memories it left me with years ago.

Like all the other caves in Zanzibar, this one is unethical. The turtles are captured in the ocean and then kept here for their entire lives.
Contrary to what you're told, this isn't a sanctuary or a place to care for them; it's just another prison where they are held captive. Turtles belong in the ocean where they are free to swim and live as they please! Not fed and touched by tourists all day long! Don't fund animal abuse!

content:
A typical beach vendor approached us on the beach. We wanted a one-day safari to the mainland, including flights, with a toddler and a pregnant woman, as a private tour.
That's exactly what he promised. We compared the price with online portals, the hotel, a tour operator, and a local contact. Everything seemed a bit cheaper, but not significantly so.
Payment by card wasn't possible with him, only at the airport. That's where the first rude awakening came: an extra $50 for card payment.
Once we arrived at the destination: no private tour, but a group tour.
That alone made it significantly more expensive than the competitors! The vehicle itself was rather old; it couldn't handle some of the roads. As a result, the other vehicles saw considerably more animals, such as lion prides. We learned this over lunch.
We ended up speeding along gravel roads with just a pregnant woman... The plane then had a flat tire on landing... apparently, that happens with older technology.
In short: we went on a trip, but it was neither good nor cheaper. Other providers would have offered a refund.
I hope my review helps others with their decision.

What a fabulous trip we had today! Alibaba was really knowledgeable, helpful and professional. He picked us up from our hotel at 6am (an early start to beat the other boats!) and quickly got us to the boat where we met the Captain and Deckhand. They were also excellent.
We headed out in choppy waters to the first snorkeling site. The Captain jumped into the water with us to show us around but the visibility was not as good as expected so they suggested we got back in the boat and tried somewhere else. (Nothing is too much trouble for these guys!)
A high-speed blast later and we’re on the other side of the island where the water was calmer and visibility much better. We snorkelled around for a while looking at some amazing fish until Ali said he’d heard where the dolphins were playing, so it was back in the boat and a blast over to the dolphin playground, (en-route we had some lovely fresh fruit for breakfast).
We quickly found a pod of maybe 20+ dolphins and watched them for ages. In time, a lot more boats arrived to the point where it was getting too crowded. I got the impression we could have stayed as long as we liked, but I think we were all feeling it was getting overcrowded so made the decision to head back.
This was an excellent trip and extremely good value. Would highly recommend seeking Alibaba out for a trip whenever you’re in Zanzibar!

If you're reading this, you've discovered the perfect guide—stop searching and book him now! We enjoyed a snorkeling, dolphin-swimming, and sandbank boat tour around Mnemba Island (Bill Gates Island). Ali aimed to be the first on the water to maximize fish sightings. Picked up promptly at 6 AM, he provided snorkeling gear (unlike others who had to rent). He works exclusively with one captain, whose boat matched the look of others but the motor was more powerful and reached the dolphins first, thanks to Ali’s choice. The captain had a deckhand (the others didn't), and wow this young man could swim!!! He spotted dolphins, guided our kids and pointed out fish, while other boats all followed Ali’s lead.
The trip was completely stress-free. Ali went out of his way to ensure we saw plenty of dolphins, exceeding expectations.

content:
I arrived at Shangani Park in the late afternoon. The sun was already setting toward the sea, the air warm and slightly humid.
The surrounding area was quiet: some were sitting on a rock, others were strolling along the water, children were running along the sand.
Nearby Stone Town bustled with life, but here it was like a small island of silence.
The park has stood by the shore for a long time. It's part of the same coastal area that developed during the Sultanate. Traders would come from the ocean, load up on spices, and then head back. From that era, Stone Town retains a unique blend of Arabic, Swahili, and Indian culture.
Shangani has also absorbed this history, although it's not much older than the buildings around it. But when you sit on a stone slab and look out to sea, it feels as if hundreds of years have truly passed.
I walked along the water's edge. There was a faint scent of seaweed, the boats moved slowly, and the fishermen chatted. The place has its own calm rhythm. You can simply sit and watch the day flow smoothly into evening.
As darkness fell, I caught myself thinking that the park isn't memorable for any particular "effects." There's no pretentiousness here. It's all about the atmosphere and the feeling of an old coastline that has seen many different eras. And for a moment, you become part of this long history.

content: We went to this turtle ‘conservation’ site because it seemed to have the best reviews of the area and heaps of websites were claiming it was ethical. But scratch the surface a little and it becomes very clear that this place knows the right words to say to tourists who just want the Insta photos and might ask simple questions to alleviate their tourist guilt about animal welfare. Staff claim the ‘conservation’ piece is around ensuring the fisherman don’t eat the turtles (something which was made illegal in 2012…) or kill them as part of the bycatch, and can then earn money from bringing the turtles to this place. There was also claims of saving injured turtles but the staff member couldn’t point out a single turtle that had an injury. So then instead of releasing the turtles into a dedicated safe water space, this place keeps them for years so they can get the tourist dollar. The staff member kept saying they release them every year on 20th February. He couldn’t tell me exactly how many are released (the video he showed was only three turtles), what the name of the volunteer organisation was from Europe that he claimed offered vet assistance, or even which turtle had been kept the longest or for how many years. He literally said they only release some in February because it’s low season and can’t get the tourist dollar anymore. So it was very clear to us that this isn’t a conservation project (and claiming so is just flat out greenwashing). It was a money making scheme. I get it - everyone has to make a buck. But don’t claim conservation when it’s more about keeping turtles in a huge pond for years and over feeding them. If the Insta girls want photos with turtles, don’t pretend it’s about conservation. Just know what you’re walking into and how exploitative it is.

content: Whilst in Zanzibar in Nov2020, we visited the Nungwi Mnarani Marine Turtle Conservation Pond which was formed by a local fisherman in the early 90's with the intention of educating the Zanzibar people to stop the exploitation of these beautiful creatures and teach people to rather be conscientious of their conservation. All turtles brought to the sanctuary are either as a result of being caught in fishing nets and/or injured, and they are fed & cared for in natural tidal ponds and tiled 'nursery' areas until the annual release date of 20th February, when those that are healthy and strong again, are set free and returned to turquoise ocean waters ... a very emotional and special day on their calendar. The sanctuary relies solely on donations and charges a minimal fee to visit, all of which goes toward the upkeep of this wonderful initiative. Although the Sanctuary is fairly rudimentary, when one considers globally how much damage is being done to our planet, their efforts really are are highly commendable; their guides are well spoken, informative and intensely passionate about their mission. For insight into the lifecycle of these gentle giants and to do your part in helping stop the vicious cycle of hunting and destroying these beautiful creatures, we highly recommend you take the time to visit this special place.

content:
An unforgettable experience – highly recommended!
I recently visited Green Tours in Zanzibar and was truly impressed. The site is beautifully set within nature and has been well-established for almost 3 years. What stood out most to me was the owner’s vision: he wants to show tourists the often not seen animals from the Jozani Forest – but always with great respect for nature. No animal is kept for more than three months, and many are released even earlier, especially when they have babies. This approach actively supports biodiversity.
I was also particularly impressed by the butterfly center. Butterflies are regularly bred and released into the wild, again with the goal of supporting local species. The owner works closely with the government and obtains official permits for all activities – which gave me a real sense of trust and responsibility behind the project.
Another highlight was the integrated spice farm. There are many clearly labeled plants and spices to discover, and I learned so much about their origin and use. Our guide was excellent – very friendly, spoke perfect English, and explained everything in an engaging and informative way.
For just €10, I experienced an incredibly educational and exciting afternoon, while also supporting a project run with true passion and care. If you love nature and want to learn more about Zanzibar, Green Tours is a real hidden gem. I can truly recommend it!

clauses.clause_text: No animal is kept for more than three months, and many are released even earlier, especially when they have babies.
For just €10, I experienced an incredibly educational and exciting afternoon, while also supporting a project run with true passion and care.

content: A unique experience, the best my girlfriend and I have had in Zanzibar! The owner is a wonderful person, infinitely kind, he welcomes you warmly and leads you into the cave. Once back up, he gives you a tour of the facility (modern, beautiful, and spotlessly clean), you feed the chicks, rabbits, and turtles, you see a stunning butterfly enclosure, banana trees, papayas, fried passion fruit, and all kinds of other fruits, and finally a free welcome drink from the fridge. And the package is very cheap too. An unforgettable experience, a fantastic place, and incredibly kind staff.

content:
A historic building in Stone Town located near The Africa House Hotel. It was the home of the famous Arab merchant B. Muhammad Al-Marjebi, also known as Tippu Tip, a major slave trader, between 1837 and 1905. It was a private residence, but during the Zanzibar Revolution of 1964 it became a block of flats, which meant its complete deterioration.
It is not formally open to visitors, and is in such a state of decay that it has been described as "the most magnificent squatter house in all of Africa". The large ornate carved wooden door still bears witness to the great wealth of its original owner.

First, research the history of this house. It's difficult to find without photographs. Locals dislike this place, as they do anything related to slavery. It's currently undergoing restoration, and there's trash nearby. You can identify it by the plaque.
Tippu Tib, or Tib (1837 – June 14, 1905), real name Hamad bin Muhammad bin Jamah bin Rajab bin Muhammad bin Said al-Mughrabi, was a Zanzibar-Swahili merchant and businessman of mixed descent, known by the nickname "Tippu Tib," which he acquired as a result of an eye disease that left him blind. A notorious slave trader, plantation owner, and governor serving the sultans of Zanzibar, he organized numerous trading expeditions to Central and East Africa seeking slaves and ivory. Tib built his own trading empire and later went into clove cultivation in Zanzibar. Tippu Tib met and assisted many European explorers of Africa, including G.M. Stanley (who scouted the area during the expedition to find David Livingstone) and Livingstone, whom he once helped with provisions when Livingstone, due to circumstances, lost a significant part of the expedition's baggage. He witnessed the historic meeting between Livingstone and Stanley. On February 24, 1887, he became governor. After his death, the house was privately owned and later used as an apartment building.

content: Still a bit in doubt whether this is okay for the turtles or not. Upon entry, for which costs 10 dollars per person, you get a container of fresh seaweed to feed them, and you could also stand in the water with them. I actually wasn't planning on doing either, but the turtles immediately came to the side all together for the seaweed. I did see a number of turtles with a missing fin or a small wound on their neck, but otherwise they seemed quite healthy. I mainly wonder how these turtles can be released back into the wild, as they claim, given how much human contact they have and how they look to humans for food. It was a large pool, and they can swim away if they don't feel like it anymore, but still... there were also a number of babies; they came from eggs that were taken from a nest because only 1 out of 100 eggs hatch in the wild, so they do part of the incubation. Beautiful in itself, but they were sitting in a transparent kayak, 15 of them, with algae. They were given food, and then they are allowed into the pool after a year. I'm not entirely sure, but ethically speaking, I would still advise against it given the feeding and touching. Zanzibar does a lot for tourism, so I get the impression that it presents a better image, as is the case with many animal-related activities on this island.

content: We chose to take a trip to Pungume with Damian based on the positive reviews we'd read... what a mistake! It was my fourth time in Zanzibar and my worst excursion experience. The sea was very rough that week, and while other operators canceled their trips (we found out later), he went ahead with the tour, demanding payment (which wasn't cheap...) in advance. That should have been a red flag. Once we arrived at the site, he realized he'd forgotten the life jackets! Needless to say, snorkeling for our 5 and 8-year-old daughters without life jackets in such rough seas was out of the question. Luckily, nothing serious happened on the way there, because without life jackets it could have become very dangerous. We were given a measly pineapple, while the few other people out at sea had platters of fruit, and he had promised us tropical fruits. Upon our return, we asked for a partial refund because we hadn't been able to go snorkeling, but he ran off without asking for anything more. Be warned, as is often the case in Zanzibar, service providers don't bother maintaining the quality of their services once they have good online reviews. In any case, for us it was a truly disastrous experience :(

clauses.clause_text: We chose to take a trip to Pungume with Damian based on the positive reviews we'd read...
what a mistake!
It was my fourth time in Zanzibar and my worst excursion experience.
The sea was very rough that week, and while other operators canceled their trips (we found out later), he went ahead with the tour, demanding payment (which wasn't cheap...)
That should have been a red flag.
Once we arrived at the site, he realized he'd forgotten the life jackets!
Needless to say, snorkeling for our 5 and 8-year-old daughters without life jackets in such rough seas was out of the question.
We were given a measly pineapple, while the few other people out at sea had platters of fruit, and he had promised us tropical fruits.
Upon our return, we asked for a partial refund because we hadn't been able to go snorkeling, but he ran off without asking for anything more.
In any case, for us it was a truly disastrous experience :(

content:
We chose Damian Dolphin Tours for a half-day snorkeling trip to Pungume Island from Kizimkazi. The boat ride, which was supposed to take 35 minutes, turned into an hour and ten minutes on rough seas. When we arrived at the snorkeling spot, we didn't get off the boat because the swell was too strong. We went to rest on the island to warm up and dry off. After an hour on the beach, we headed back, stopping 15 minutes from Kizimkazi to swim in calmer waters. Upon our return, we saw Damian to explain our dissatisfaction. The trip should have been canceled due to the weather (as other tour operators had done). He offered another trip the next day as compensation. Since this wasn't possible for us, we asked for a partial refund. He left us in the hands of someone who agreed to give us 15% of the price paid, instead of the 40% we had requested. In short, the value for money is deplorable, and the company shows little concern for safety or customer satisfaction.
There are quite a few companies that offer these excursions; if you have to choose, avoid Damian Dolphin Tour.

content: Damian did a great job, met him on the beach at bottom the Kwanza resort. It was our first day here on our honeymoon and we were a bit apprehensive at first but after a very pricy trip organised by the hotel that didn’t blow our socks off we thought we give it a go. Damian was great, very helpful and polite with a wide knowledge of the area. Comparing this to the hotel, Damian was much better as for a smaller cost we got a private boat which with hotel was shared. The food was better than the hotel ( my wife and I aren’t into shellfish and stressed this to Damian) we got fresh bbq grill swordfish and full chicken breast with salad and fruit where as with the hotel just chips and deep friend chicken wings. Damian gave us free water, soft drink and beer if you wanted it. The hotel’s venture gave us water and pop and tried to make us pay to go the loo with our meal which was bloody ridiculous. Activity wise Damien’s snorkelling masks were much better not steaming up every 2 minutes as with hotel who claimed they were diving masks- they weren’t. After a lengthy boat ride we went to mangroves, saw monkeys, went snorkelling and found starfish which Damian got photos of us with (we then retired the starfish to the sea). After which we ended up in a sandbank island and had a dreamy bbq on the beach, under shaded table and chairs. As we were pretty sunburnt we didn’t want to stay to long a Damian was more than happy to depart early and take us home. He even offered to take us for more snorkelling if we wanted as he seemed to just want to make the experience as good a possible. A great day out. Can highly recommend.

content: We took a guided tour with the knowledgeable guide Idrisa on a rainy morning. The weather lent the tour a mysterious atmosphere. The tour was incredibly thorough and informative. From ginger, turmeric, cloves, and pepper... to vanilla and the queen of spices, cinnamon, everything was covered. We also saw some fruits, such as pineapples, tangerines, papayas, and oranges. After the tour, you have the opportunity to buy your own spices on site. A refreshing coconut drink straight from the palm tree is included in the price. I highly recommend the Spice Farm in the interior of Zanzibar. Go there and experience the wonders of nature! 👋
