content:
A truly wonderful experience!
We arrived spontaneously in the evening and were given a two-hour tour. We were allowed to try many things and even take some home with us.
To top it all off, coconuts were even harvested from the palm tree right before our eyes, and we were then allowed to try it ourselves.
As a lovely souvenir, we also received handmade crowns and other small gifts. Everyone was incredibly friendly and welcoming.
A fantastic and authentic experience – highly recommended!

content:
It was a fantastic experience.
Mohammed, dressed as another employee, showed us around the farm and explained everything.
It was very interesting, and I highly recommend it to anyone interested in the culture, spices, and the people.
After the tour, someone entertained us by bringing a coconut down from a palm tree, and we each received a coconut to drink from, along with small gifts like a bag and crowns.
If you like, you can also buy spices produced on the farm. There's no pressure or pushiness to buy their products.
The price per package was $2 (and there were other, more expensive spices available, but I can't remember which ones).
The tour cost $10 per person, which I think is perfectly reasonable considering the wealth of information and the amount of time spent (much better than the Slave Museum in Stone Town).
I would gladly do it again anytime, and all the best to the people there.

content: We had an unforgettable day with Ibrahim. First, a lovely walk to discover spices, smelling them, trying to identify their aromas, and tasting them. All this at a leisurely pace. We also saw the expert climber who goes to collect coconuts: impressive! And at no point were we asked for a tip. Then we went to the village to cook. We received a very warm welcome, and there, we all prepared pilau, chili, salad, cooked bananas, spinach, and chiapati together! We also discovered jackfruit. The women were incredibly friendly; we were truly at the heart of their home. Then we ate in their house. Everything was delicious. Thank you so much for this wonderful day.

content: We had a lovely tour at the Village Green Spice Farm. Booking the tour via WhatsApp was hassle-free. Learning about the origin of the spices we use every day, smelling them, tasting them, and seeing how they grow naturally is incredibly interesting and fascinating.
But without a doubt, the highlight, and an absolute blast, was the coconut demonstration. Watching one of the guys climb to the very top of a towering palm tree while singing was a truly breathtaking spectacle that left us speechless.
If you come to Zanzibar, you can't miss this visit, and if it's with Ali, even better! Highly recommended!

content:
We came here with our 5 children in tow, ages ranging from 12 years old to 1 year old. This place is amazing for the whole family! We can’t recommend it enough.
It was very informative for us adults and the kids enjoyed themselves too. They were each given a basket made from banana leaves. Then the guide gave them a sample of all the spices we saw and learnt about. This made them very excited to collect as many plants as possible. What a huge relief it was for us!
We also got to taste many different kinds of fruits like oranges, pineapples, limes, coconuts and jackfruits. It’s like we went on a fruit hunt plus fruit buffet lol.
The farm is stroller friendly and we had no trouble pushing our little one in it the entire journey.
Entrance fee is $10 per adult and $5 per child. We didn’t mind paying because that means no hard selling and, you really get to enjoy the farm comfortably with good energy all around. Plus, you get to support a good cause! This spice farm supports the village nearby in terms of education for the local school, electricity for the town and sustainable income for the locals. Money well spent!
I highly recommend this farm and would definitely return in the future. You will not be disappointed.

content: A wonderful place with a variety of trees and herbs. English-speaking guides lead you around the vast grounds, picking fresh leaves to sample, and lovingly explaining almost every plant. But that's not all: the visit also includes sampling fresh pineapples straight from the garden, tangerines and oranges from the trees, and coconuts from the palm trees, all accompanied by lively performances and songs. At the end, they'll even weave various banana leaf crafts for $10 per person. A definitely recommended place. There's one catch: the guides are independent and not included in the official tours. This means that if you book a tour of a beach farm, you won't be taken to this place. Plus, these lousy "tour guides" are simply exploiting other farms, sharing with them the profits they make from bringing tourists. Visiting this farm supports local farmers. So, if you want to combine business with pleasure, come here. Official tours last about an hour, but we had to stop local farmers after two and a half hours because we had other plans, and they were ready to talk about themselves for another three hours.

I recently had the pleasure of visiting the Village Green Spice Farm in Mitakawani, Zanzibar, and I must say it was an extraordinary experience!
Informative Tour: The guide was incredibly knowledgeable and passionate about the spices. He shared fascinating insights into the history and cultivation of various spices, making the tour both educational and engaging.
Diverse Spice Collection: We were introduced to an impressive variety of spices, including cloves, nutmeg, cinnamon, and many more. The aromatic experience was simply delightful!
Interactive Experience: The tour was interactive, allowing us to see, smell, and even taste some of the spices directly from the plants. It was a hands-on experience that truly enhanced our understanding of the spice trade.
Highly Recommended: I wholeheartedly recommend the Village Green Spice Farm to anyone visiting Zanzibar. Whether you're a spice enthusiast or just curious about the local culture, this farm offers a unique glimpse into the rich agricultural heritage of the island.
Overall, our visit to the Village Green Spice Farm was a highlight of our trip, and we left with a deeper appreciation for the spices that play such a vital role in the local cuisine. Don't miss out on this gem during your travels! 🌿
hakuna matata
Herbert and Verena

content:
We would like to dedicate this review to our guide Ali for our visit to Village Green Spice Farm on October 6th, 2022.
Spice tour was a highlight of our visit in Zanzibar. There are numerous farms and agencies organizing it. We were referred to Village Green by our hotel; besides, the five star rating on Google is self-explanatory. Unlike many of the spice tours organized by others, Village Green focuses on the tour and the customer experience, instead of making quick money by forcing the visitors to buy species in the farm. As you may know, the species can be purchased at a lower price in the market of Stone Town.
We already contacted Village Green Spice Farm on WhatsApp. This was useful because they could help to book a reliable taxi, or to communicate with the taxi driver to go to the right place. Although our taxi arrived later than the 10am tour, Ali waited for us with patience and a big smile. Ali grew up in the village, he has good connections with everyone we saw in the village that day, he is knowledgeable and passionate about the species, and he speaks perfect English. During the tour, he first introduced us the common species of Zanzibar: he cut them freshly from the trees at the demo area, let us smelled and tasted some of them. In addition, we also tasted some local fruits. Next, he took us into the village, where he climbed up the trees of around 10 meters high to get nutmeg and Zanzibar apple for us. Finally, we went back to the demo area, where a colleague of Ali performed coconut tree climbing while singing, we also got delicious coconut juice to drink. In addition, Ali made fun gadgets for us with the plants during the tour. The tour lasted for about 2 hours. In the end we paid our ticket as earlier communicated, no surprises and no forcing to buy species or to pay other fees.
All in all, with Ali we learned a lot about the species of Zanzibar, had a great tour, and got many herbal/fruity gifts to bring back home with us. The value of the tour far exceeded the cost of the tickets. More importantly, the guys at Village Green Spice Farm have a reliable and trustworthy way of organizing the tours which is sustainable. We would definitely recommend Village Green Spice Farm to our family and friends who are planing to visit Zanzibar. Thank you again Ali for the wonderful tour! Our apologies for the delayed review: we have been busy with work and other things.

content: This was definitely one of the highlights of my recent trip to Zanzibar. These guys are really passionate about there work. The tour was highly informative and very interesting. After the tour one of the guys climbed a coconut tree and we were given fresh coconut water to drink and freshly chopped coconut to eat, it was really such a delicious treat. They went over and above all expectations by making each of us a hat out of palm leaves. Thank you so much to Aikad,Cotei, Shwar and Abilah for making memories to last a lifetime. content:
Ali and his friends at the farm represent the most authentic experience we had so far in Zanzibar. They are a group of few young people who have allocated a part of their village farming lands for developing a touristic attraction. And yet this is done in a charming and naive manner which keeps it simple and beautiful. We came with the kids who were quickly trapped by Ali’s riddles. Along the way, Ali cut different types of leaves and asked the us to guess what spice it was by their odors. Some brought quite surprising realization. He also formed all types of games and tools for the kids by cutting branches and leaves he picked from the farm. At the end of the tour, one of the boys climbed up a coconut tree to harvest few delicious coconuts. At the end of the tour we were offered to buy spices from the farm at reasonable prices.
In this way Ali and his friend are contributing to their community villagers in the most efficient and charming way. Not pushing for anything and respecting us and their owns.
Highly recommended!! Enjoy!

clauses.clause_text: At the end of the tour, one of the boys climbed up a coconut tree to harvest few delicious coconuts.

content:
We happened to drive past this spice farm (more like an open field) and decided to go in.
It turns out this cooperative farm is run by the village. A young man gave us a two-hour tour, showing us and letting us taste dozens of fruits, vegetables, and spices.
The tour ended with us tasting a freshly picked coconut and visiting the shop. I highly recommend this authentic and informative visit.

content: This was the highlight of our trip in Zanzibar. Ali works at the Village Green spice farm and gave us an amazing tour of all of the crops. The entrance fee only cost 10,000 shillings or five dollars per person. During the tour Ali walked us around the different parts of the farm showing us various spices like pepper cinnamon ginger and fruits such as watermelon avocado oranges Mandarin mango trees and passion fruit. Of course we got to try this delicious produce during the tour. We also learned about a lot of the local spices which they use for medicinal purposes. Afterwards we watched Ali’s colleague climb a coconut tree! He picked coconuts for us to enjoy. Ali is such a kind and welcoming person- his English is really spectacular and he explained everything to us. After the farm tour he invited us to visit his home village Mitakawani village also know as Green Villiage. He helped us purchase some pencils which we gave out to the local children. It was such an incredible and genuine experience and I highly recommend visiting this spice farm. They can even arrange transportation from your hotel at a fair price (that’s what we did). If you want to contact Ali please WhatsApp him +255 779 801 567 to make an appointment for a visit.

content: Superb spice farm! The visit lasted a good two hours and we were never bored. We were the only visitors, which is much better than the crowded, tourist-packed spice farm factories. This demonstration farm is a cooperative in the neighboring village. Easy to find, a discreet sign indicates the entrance via a small track. It's best to rent your own car. 10,000 shillings per person for entry plus a tip for the young man who climbs the trees. A good price compared to those charged by tour operators. Thanks to them for this fantastic visit where we learned so much, tasted lots of fruit, and finally saw what the plants from which the spices we all use come actually look like. We left with gifts woven from the spice stems right in front of us.

content:
We came on the recommendation of friends. We planned to stay for two or three hours, but it turned out to be almost six.
The guys' extraordinary attitude. You can feel that they love their life and their work. The farm is a natural environment for the community. The residents of the village grow plants and use them together.
The farm is not a tourist attraction, but a real settlement.
You can get acquainted with fruits, vegetables and spices that grow on a large territory to the right and left of the road. There are two similar marks on the map, but this is one object.
Priceless experience. Wonderful detailed stories about the plants, and about the lifestyle, diet, customs of the local community.
All the fruits that will be ripe during your stay will be kindly offered to you to taste.
They prepared a traditional lunch for us - sheli-sheli (breadfruit) and kachumbari.
I definitely recommend visiting. Don't wait for a tour. Travel on your own. Support this extraordinary place. We came to Dala Dala. From the village of Kinyasini 61 Dala Dala.

content:
This spice farm is a must-see when you fly to Zanzibar! Don't book a tour through your hotel; take a taxi or rent a car and drive there yourself. You'll be greeted immediately by friendly staff. We were met by our guide, Ali, who spoke excellent English. He gave us a tour of the farm, pointing out and explaining every single fruit, spice, and plant. We were given a "box" to pick at the entrance, and we filled it all up.
His friend walked with us, picking sweet fruits from the very tops of the trees. The stuff they sell along the road or give you in hotels isn't as sweet as what you'll try here. It was educational and surprising. The tour was dynamic; we didn't even notice how we'd walked for an hour and a half. We were introduced to the "king" and "queen" of spices and given gifts. Do you know what cinnamon root smells like? What fruit is "alcohol" in large quantities? And who are the "king" and "queen" of spices? Find out all about it here!
Thank you, staff! May you and your business attract more tourists, and may your village prosper!

content:
Absolutely an experience and well worth seeing, especially with children from about 5-6 years old. It's not very cheap, and you get a bit of a feeling of being ripped off. Nevertheless, we bought a full hour ticket, and after being told "the turtles don't bite," we went into the cave and found that after 20 wonderful minutes, we'd actually seen enough.
Unfortunately, we then discovered that the turtles do indeed bite. They don't attack viciously or aggressively, but they do snap at things that might be edible based on their color. My son and I got a few nips, but nothing too bad. Unfortunately, my little one was bitten very hard by a large turtle, resulting in a deep, bleeding cut and a huge bruise all around. That was enough, so we left after 30 minutes, mainly because of this, and showed the bite to the guide, who then informed the rest of the staff. At the ticket counter, we were given iodine to apply to the wound, which, along with bandages, was readily available under the table. So we weren't the first victims of a bite. So much for "they don't bite." There was no apology, no compensation for at least the lost half hour for the person who was bitten. Nothing at all. In short: worth seeing, expensive, unfriendly, and also somewhat dangerous! The complete lack of any attempt at accommodation or apology was the main reason for the poor rating.

content:
**HIGHLY RECOMMENDED**
This is one of the best caves out of everything I've researched. Nobody told me about this cave! I just googled caves and I got this as a suggestion!
First of all you can drive yourself (recommended) from paje, Jabiani takes about 30 minutes.
Ofcourse you can take taxi as well, once u reach the Google map designated area you just need to follow the well marked signs boards it will take directly to the cave,
And ofcourse there is very helpful locals who will help you as well.
Once you reach Sadi (not sure but I think that's his name) he helped me with all, they gave us 3 pack seaweed to feed the turtles.
I paid 64000 shillings for 2 adults and 1 kid. (Kids under 3 goes free i guess) For 30 minutes.
Once we enter the pit they made sure the pit is really nice and we'll maintained also lots of vegetation and plants, sitting areas, so once you get down it's very easy there is a shallow area and the water goes deep then it becomes shallow & steps with rocks etc and there is a wooden bed also there if u want to sit on it.
And the Turtles, there is a Huge to all sizes i think around 8-9 of them! Do they bite ? Idk coz I didn't get bitten! They were friendly coz I was feeding them all the way! I think if u feed them well they won't bite. There is a staff with in the cave to help us and guide us how to feed them, so you dont need to worry.
Make sure you take waterproof cover for your phone coz you can get nice shots underwat as well (if u don't have action cameras)
There is some goodies you care to buy, some usual stuff you see.
So far the best hidden cave in the island.

Lunch was served on the sandbank, and it made the experience even more enjoyable. Eating fresh food while surrounded by the ocean was truly unforgettable.
The only downside was that it was quite crowded, so it wasn’t as private as we expected. However, the natural beauty of the place definitely made up for it.
Overall, the Sandbank is a must-visit destination in Zanzibar. The breathtaking views, clear water, soft white sand, and relaxing atmosphere make it an experience you’ll never forget. 🌊🏝️☀️

We took the tour with a so-called fisherman who prepared a succulent barbecue meal for us. At the end of the barbecue, he dug a hole and threw the ashes in. I told him not to do that... The response: hakuna matata pole pole. In short, environmental awareness hasn't reached everywhere yet, so it's up to all of us to raise awareness during our visit.
As for snorkeling, a few reefs are accessible but not particularly interesting. It's still nice to see a few starfish and swim with clownfish.

The place, which should be a small natural paradise, is completely ruined by overcrowding: too many people and an excessive number of boats make it impossible to enjoy the scenery. There's not even room for a peaceful swim, as the sea is literally flooded.
The situation is made worse by the condition of the beach, which I found dirty and full of plastic. In some places, it looks more like an open-air landfill than a tourist destination.
It's truly a shame to see such a naturally beautiful place neglected and managed in this way. I hope that measures will be taken in the future to limit the influx of people and preserve this corner of nature.

As soon as we disembarked, they told us to sit down for lunch; we preferred to wander off to take a dip, cool off, and enjoy the sea.
Unfortunately, I saw filth everywhere, tourists' and locals' waste shamelessly left behind.
That strip of sand had been devastated by the total disorganization of tour operators and the greed of those who bring hundreds of people to a place that should be protected, not exploited to the bone. An embarrassing management, which manages to ruin one of the most beautiful places in Zanzibar.
Unfortunately, I strongly advise against it.

content:
Review of Nakupenda Beach
Our trip to Nakupenda Beach was truly unforgettable! The boat ride to the sandbank was an amazing experience, offering stunning views of the crystal-clear waters and the surrounding beauty of Zanzibar.
The sandbank itself was breathtaking—soft white sands surrounded by turquoise waters, creating a paradise-like setting. The food provided during the trip was absolutely delicious, adding to the overall enjoyment of the day.
One of the highlights of our visit was the chance to interact with a charming five-month-old monkey—such a unique and delightful experience!
Nakupenda Beach is a must-visit destination for anyone traveling to Zanzibar. We had an incredible time and hope to return in the future to relive the magic of this special place. Highly recommended!

content: We went to this sandbar in the morning (we were supposed to go in the afternoon, but we followed the tide). There are tons of other people, but the sandbar is very wide, and we had a great time. We had a tent set up by the guys from the agency that accompanied us as a base. For swimming, it's best to avoid the area with all the boats, which unfortunately, but inevitably, dirty the water. The water was generally beautiful, and we saw lots of fish and coral very close to shore thanks to our masks and snorkels. It's a shame we also found so many plastic cutlery on the seabed! Since it's a sandbar completely exposed to the sun, it's best to bring plenty of water and sunscreen, otherwise you risk sunstroke and burns. The sandbar's location is ideal for a trip to nearby Prison Island, or Turtle Island; the excursions are usually combined.

content: We booked excursions and safaris in Zanzibar with Astaztour. They offered excellent service and a Russian-speaking guide named Hassan. Our excursion included a visit to Prison Island, the disappearing island of Nakupenda (which means "I love you" in Swahili), and a walk through the Old Town. Boats depart from the beach behind the Old Fort. It's best to plan to arrive at the disappearing island in the morning to fully appreciate this snow-white strip of turquoise ocean before high tide, as there are fewer crowds in the morning. Our excursion went perfectly. We had a pleasant group of people, and everyone was happy. We first visited Prison Island, and then, with music playing on the speaker, we headed to the disappearing island. Along the way, we were treated to fruit and also tasted a delicious octopus broth (highly recommended for men) made by a funny guy named Totty. There weren't many people on the island when we arrived, so there was plenty of room to set up on the spit. Incidentally, we were the only ones with chairs and a table (our guide made sure of that); the rest of the tourists were dining on the sand. Yes, the lunch was excellent: fried shrimp, octopus, lobster, and tuna, paired with refreshing drinks (which you can buy on the island itself)—perfect. After enjoying the ocean and waiting for the tide to come in, we began packing for the return journey. Ahead of us lay a stroll through the streets and sights of the stone town.

clauses.clause_text: We first visited Prison Island, and then, with music playing on the speaker, we headed to the disappearing island.

content: Pingwe Beach boasts golden sands stretching into azure waters, fringed by swaying palm trees. The charm doesn't end at the shore. Nearby coral reefs teem with marine life, offering kaleidoscopic underwater vistas for those eager to explore. The eastern part of Zanzibar is characterized by distant ocean tides, which change daily. For a few hours, the water simply recedes, making swimming virtually impossible. Pingwe, however, is a bit different. As the tide gradually recedes, sandbanks and beautiful emerald lagoons form. During this time, you can enjoy a paradise-like view. The water is a stunning color and crystal clear. Even at low tide, you can swim in the ocean at Pingwe, as the water doesn't flow directly into the reef, unlike in other places on the east coast.

content:
Sometimes you have moments while traveling that make you feel: I'll never forget this.
For me, it was the sailing experience and sunset on Mimi the Dhow in Jambiani.
The sea was calm, the water turquoise, and the wind just right to glide us silently across the Indian Ocean. No engine noise, no crowds—just the gentle flapping of the sail and the sound of water against wood.
What made this experience so special was the intimacy. No massive boat, but a small, warm setting where you immediately feel welcome. The crew was genuinely friendly and relaxed.
Fresh mangoes and avocados…so ripe, sweet, and creamy that you almost forget what fruit tastes like at home.
Mimi the Dhow is not a standard excursion. It's an experience.
A moment of slowing down and true enjoyment.
If you're in Zanzibar and want to experience something truly beautiful, then this is highly recommended!

content:
The East Africa Slave Trade Exhibition is one of the most impactful and essential visits in Stone Town.
Located in the former slave market and next to the Anglican Cathedral, this exhibition allows visitors to understand one of the harshest periods in East African history.
The most harrowing aspect is the old underground chambers where slaves were held in inhumane conditions before being sold. Seeing these spaces and hearing the historical testimonies makes the visit deeply moving.
The exhibition is well-designed and helps visitors understand the historical context and the human impact of this trade.
It's not a "pretty" visit in the usual sense, but it is very valuable and highly recommended for understanding the true history of the place.
In short, the East Africa Slave Trade Exhibition is a must-see in Zanzibar. A harsh, emotional, and essential place that leaves you with profound reflection.

place_name: East Africa Slave Trade Exhibition (Slave Chambers - Cathedoral Church Of Christ)
content:
For centuries, Zanzibar was the center of political and economic power in East Africa, as well as the site of the region's most notorious slave market.
People captured on the mainland were brought to Zanzibar in chains to be sold, often enduring horrific hardships during the journey.
Because of its importance to the slave trade, the island played a pivotal role in the abolition of slavery in East Africa.
The market was closed by order of the Sultan in 1873, and an Anglican cathedral was built on the site in 1879.
The cathedral was considered a symbol of emancipation from a tyranny that affected all the peoples of the region.
The cathedral holds immense cultural, historical, and moral significance, not only in East Africa but also internationally. It is notable for its Saracen architecture, which created a typically Zanzibari eclecticism by fusing elements from Zanzibar and the Middle East with decorative motifs from late Victorian Gothic and Arts and Crafts styles.
The methods used to construct the cathedral were also technologically groundbreaking for the time, pushing the boundaries of local coral construction.
The nave's unique concrete roof, with its barrel vault and crushed coral stone, was designed and built before reinforced concrete technology became widespread. Today, the former slave market is one of Stone Town's most popular attractions, drawing over 100,000 visitors annually. Stone Town was declared a World Heritage Site in 2000, and the rich and diverse origins of its inhabitants have fostered the development of a unique cultural heritage in the area.

place_name: East Africa Slave Trade Exhibition (Slave Chambers - Cathedoral Church Of Christ)
content: For centuries, Zanzibar was home to the region's most notorious slave market. People captured on the mainland were brought to Zanzibar in chains to be sold. The closure of the Zanzibar slave market played a significant role in the abolition of slavery in East Africa. The slave market was closed by order of the Sultan in 1873, and in 1879, an Anglican cathedral was built on the site. The cathedral was seen as a symbol of emancipation from the tyranny that affected all inhabitants of the region. The East African Slave Trade Exhibition (EASTE) was established in the St. Monica Hostel, adjacent to the cathedral. The hostel was built as a hospital shortly after the cathedral's completion and is now a listed heritage site. The East African Slave Trade Exhibition tells the history of the slave trade in the region and the role of the former slave market in Zanzibar. It features audiovisual recordings of local residents discussing the significance of slavery's legacy in their communities and is connected to the Education Center, where classes on the same topics are offered. The exhibition officially opened on June 15, 2016.

place_name: East Africa Slave Trade Exhibition (Slave Chambers - Cathedoral Church Of Christ)
content:
Biggest scam I experienced on the island.
1) When you show up at the entrance you are approached by a random person claiming to be a guide. Guides are mandatory and they demand a tip.
2) Cash accepted only and they do not offer a refund despite requesting an odd number for cash payment. Of course, the visitor is the one that has to pay extra.
3) the guide rushed us through as fast as he could. He was an older gentleman, and was reading from his phone for all the facts. Often repeating himself up to 3 times. We asked questions, and he said wait until the end. Then disappeared at the end without answering any questions but not before collecting his demanded payment. The total tour was 20 minutes and over charged. Generally the guide was quite rude, and kept grabbing our arms to usher us through the tour faster in order to get to the next group of people.
The facility is worth seeing due to the history display and where the slaves were housed. I wish this was an entry fee only and not with the mandatory guides. I would have rather walked around alone than with the poor guide we received. If I were to do this again, I would try to get a guide that was providing a full town walking tour.

place_name: East Africa Slave Trade Exhibition (Slave Chambers - Cathedoral Church Of Christ)
content: This was a place where slaves were brought from Africa and sold in Zanzibar under European supervision and implemented by African and Arab traders. They were then transported to Europe and America. There was another similar center for selling slaves in Recife, Brazil, where male and female slaves were brought from Africa to be sold to traders and then transported to Europe, especially Spain and America, to work as servants and laborers. Arabs did not participate in this, except for traders supported by Europe out of greed. Zanzibar was a gathering point for Africans from Congo and Kenya before they were transported to Europe. This museum contains only photographs, along with pictures of the Arab and Omani rulers of Zanzibar, and a depiction of the slave prison cells.

content:
It's not worth the visit, all you'll see is an exhibition of panels with information you can find on the internet, a simple church and a morbid work of art that is the tourist attraction at $5 per entrance and some guides who assault you at the entrance and who explain things that are not true and sell a shameful past as an attraction.
Stone Town was home to one of the last open slave markets in the world, presided over by Arab traders until it was closed by the British in 1873. The slaves were sent here in dhows from the continent, so crowded that many got sick and died or were thrown overboard.
Below the Santa Monica guesthouse, dozens of slaves and women and children were imprisoned for days in cellars full of people with little air and without food or toilets. Even after two minutes down there, under the low ceiling, the atmosphere seemed poisonously oppressive.
The guide said that the slaves were led outside and lined up in order of size. They were tied to a tree and whipped with a stinging branch to test their worth. Those who did not cry or faint were given a higher price in the market. Africa has its share of cruelty and suffering, but these stories prick our conscience as if it were the first time.

place_name: East Africa Slave Trade Exhibition (Slave Chambers - Cathedoral Church Of Christ)
content: You can visit after reading the history. Admission is $5 at the ticket office. The site includes a temple, a monument, and a white museum building with slave quarters in the basement. The museum has photographs and a history in English. You can read everything without a guide. The entrance to the basement is unmarked, so you might miss it if you don't know it's there. There are two restrooms on the site. The temple stands on the site of a slave market, and services are held there. It's easy to find; it's visible and appears on maps.

content:
Excellent local museum very well set up and very well worded, being the son of a museum curator i was very happy! I took a walking tour from my hostel for $10, $5 was used as entrance for the museum. Water around this area is very cheap much cheaper than anywhere else. The slave chamber and museum are fascinating but depressing as hell! The monument to the slaves struggle is in excellent condition 20years later and the 2nd only Christian church is just marvelous. The head priest who abolished slavery was an amazing man who was british yet translated the Bible into Swahili and helped many former slaves convert.
The museum also houses much info about David Livingston and his help with regards to the slave trade.
The space museum is located very close to the border of stone town and the local market which is well worth a walk through.

content:
The cave is a bit hard to find, because only a small path goes towards the entry. But the position of the geo tag is correct. We drove to the entry by scooter, which was possible if you have a bit of skill.
When we entered the cave a local guy came and wanted money from us. We told him, we dont give money and just walked further. Then he leaves. I am very sure, that the entry is free.

content:
We were provided the bare minimum and felt the money we spent was wasted for the following reasons:
- the guide was able to speak minimal English, which caused confusion numerous times and an inability to give historic or cultural context to the sites we visited. A condition of the tour was that we would have an English speaking guide. This severely hampered the experience. We understand that we are in a fortunate position to be able to communicate with locals who speak English as a second language, but when you are paying for an English speaking guide and the guide is unable to understand most questions, this is subpar. He couldn’t communicate clear instructions which left both us and the guide frustrated.
- to get us to go somewhere, the guide would snap at us which felt disrespectful
- the guide seemed confused when taking us to Kuzma Cave and didn’t know much about it.
- when we went Jozani Forest, the guide had to rely on other guides for directions as if he didn’t know where to go to see the monkeys
- the guide fell asleep multiple times while we were driving between locations and on the boat. The driver of the boat even joked with us about the guide being asleep and inattentive
- the guide played Instagram Reels loudly on his speaker in the cave disturbing the peace of our visit and others, and was playing on his phone throughout the day
- he frequently took calls from others (both driver and guide took calls while in the car)
- the guide was almost almost 1 hour late. The guide and company had conflicting excuses as to why they were late
-We cut lunch out on our own accord, but the tour was only 5 hours instead of the advertised 10. Even with lunch, we still would’ve been cut short at least 2 hours.
We believe the local operator was utilizing a contracted guide rather than their own. The guide didn’t even know the name of the operator we booked with, which stunned us. He was wearing a polo for another tour company. I’m sure the local operator is a good broker for most trips, but they selected a guide that did not meet standards, especially considering how much money we spent.
We cannot recommend booking with Zanziplanet based on the disrespect to us and others in the area from the guide throughout the trip (falling asleep, snapping, playing zit popping videos on Instagram with EDM at full volume in the cave), the lack of English language capability, and the severe delay. We saw everything we were promised, but at a steep price and with a guide that left a sour taste in our mouth.

I recently had the pleasure of going on multiple boat tours in Matemwe, Zanzibar with Chris, and it was an unforgettable experience from start to finish. Chris was incredibly flexible with his schedule, making it easy to arrange the tour at a time that suited us best. His great cooperative nature made the entire planning process a breeze.
The tour itself was just phenomenal. We were taken to see and chase dolphins, which was nothing short of magical. Watching these beautiful creatures in their natural habitat was a once-in-a-lifetime experience. Chris then took us snorkeling, where he lured the fish with food, allowing us to literally touch and interact with them. It was surreal being so close to such vibrant marine life.
One of the highlights was when we stopped to explore starfish and sea urchins. Chris guided us as we held and touched these fascinating creatures, adding an extra layer of wonder to the day. The water was crystal clear and filled with colorful fish, making every moment so mesmerizing.
Chris also provided a platter of fresh and delicious fruits, which were a perfect, refreshing treat during the tour. He had all the necessary gear, ensuring we were well-equipped for the adventure. We even went snorkeling twice—once during the main tour and again on a special starfish exploration.
Overall, everything was amazing and so enjoyable. The best part? The price was incredibly affordable, making this tour one of the best deals for tourists. Chris knows all the best spots, ensuring that every stop was more beautiful than the last. I just can't recommend this tour enough!

content:
Paje, this large village on the east coast of Zanzibar, is extremely popular with tourists, especially thrill-seekers who enjoy kitesurfing and wing foiling.
The entire coastline is dotted with small boutique hotels, resorts, and tourist residences, all lined with restaurants and kitesurfing centers. Everything here revolves around the tides; there are two high tides and two low tides a day. The spectacle is breathtaking. When the tide is coming in, you can swim; there are a few waves, but they aren't dangerous. However, at low tide, you have to walk hundreds of meters to get waist-deep in the water. At low tide, you can see the seaweed farms where women from the cooperatives come to harvest the seaweed to make cosmetic products.
The only downside to the beach is the beach boys, or so-called Maasai, who pester you all day long to sell you souvenirs. They are very persistent, even if you ignore them. They don't seem aggressive to me. But there's nothing we can do about it; as tourists, we're visiting their territory and their country. I don't understand people who are annoyed by their presence.
Their presence, along with street vendors selling exotic fruits, women offering hair braiding services, and women selling swimsuits, gives the island a rather unique atmosphere.
If you're not happy about their presence, simply go home.
However, it's essential to haggle before buying. You can easily get something for half the asking price.
On the other hand, if you're on a restaurant terrace or relaxing on your hotel's sun loungers, you're sure not to be bothered by the Maasai, as they are forbidden from approaching tourists in these areas.

content:

The potential for kitesurfing is enormous, but the lack of designated areas sometimes makes it difficult: fishermen, jet skis, boats, swimmers, and tourists on foot or horseback all find themselves in the same space.
Be careful, at high tide, especially with the strong tidal coefficients of August, the beach is completely submerged. There's then no space left to prepare your equipment or simply stroll around. The waves even crash against the edges of the raised terraces of some beach hotels, to the point that guests can no longer stay there as a precaution.
A superb place, but one that would really benefit from better organization to allow everyone to fully and peacefully enjoy it.

content:
🌴 Zanzibar – Paje Beach, our second home ❤️
For my wife and me, Paje Beach in Zanzibar has long been more than just a vacation destination – it's our second home.
A few years ago, we bought a plot of land there, and with every visit, our connection to this unique island grows stronger. As soon as our house is finished, we'll be spending several months a year in Zanzibar.
What makes Zanzibar so special for us is, above all, the people. Their warmth, friendliness, and helpfulness are extraordinary. Added to that is their infectious zest for life, their serenity, and their ability to find happiness in even the smallest things. You can feel a genuine sense of community and heartfelt hospitality everywhere you go.
Paje Beach captivates with its stunning white sand beach, the turquoise waters of the Indian Ocean, and an atmosphere that instantly slows you down. Here, you can leave everyday life behind and enjoy life at its finest.
The island itself also has so much to offer. A trip to Stone Town with its winding alleyways, spice and fish markets, and fascinating history is just as essential as a side trip to Tanzania by small plane for an unforgettable safari.
We're certain of one thing: Zanzibar will always be a part of our lives. Anyone seeking nature, warmth, tranquility, and authentic experiences should definitely visit this wonderful island.
Asante Sana, Zanzibar – we'll be back again and again. 🌴❤️

content:
⚠️ Beware of this operator – a complete scam!
We booked a boat tour in Zanzibar with a man named Ibrahim (who calls himself "Briton Boy") – and it was unfortunately one of the worst experiences of our entire trip.
We had arranged everything in advance via WhatsApp:
– a clear route with three stops
– a fixed total price
– clear agreements to avoid exactly these kinds of discussions
What followed was simply deception and a rip-off.
Right at the beginning, they suddenly demanded $50 USD for alleged government snorkeling fees – without any receipt whatsoever. This money obviously went straight into their own pocket.
Then a guided tour was initially supposed to cost $70 USD – later it suddenly became $100 USD, and they claimed we had misunderstood everything. They deliberately ignored our point that everything was in writing.
The "tour" itself was a joke:
– instead of 6 hours, it didn't even last 1.5 hours
– we hardly saw any fish
– agreed-upon stops were simply canceled
– flimsy excuses like a completely absurd "tidal system" where high and low tide supposedly occur simultaneously at different points
When we expressed our dissatisfaction, the situation became truly unpleasant and threatening:
The operator gathered several men around us and said, literally:
"Do you really think you can just get away from here if you don't pay me?"
All this while holding a six-year-old child.
In the end, we only paid the exorbitant price to defuse the situation.
👉 We would also like to warn against Mnemba Island:
Yes, the island looks idyllic at first glance – but the underwater reality is disappointing.
– Many corals are dead
– Fish are sometimes artificially lured
– Dolphins are actively hunted
– And there are far too many boats in the area at once, which ruins the entire experience
👉 Our clear conclusion:
Stay away from this operator. They make false promises, arbitrarily inflate prices, and even exert pressure if necessary.
We strongly warn everyone:
👉 Avoid Ibrahim, aka "Briton Boy" – he is completely untrustworthy.

content:
Snorkeling next to Mnemba Island, we witnessed the sea displaying its most beautiful colors, showcasing a great variety of fish. However, the area is excessively touristic, with too many boats in one place. During our swim and snorkel, we had to navigate around boats, which was not enjoyable. Additionally, the corals are noticeably affected.
We were fortunate to witness dolphins after snorkeling, but it was disheartening to see a lot of boats cutting off the dolphins' paths so that tourists could jump into the water to 'swim with them'. This is a cruel act towards the animals, and it is not an experience of watching or swimming with them, but rather hunting them! Therefore, it's vital to ensure that guides are not chasing the dolphins. We asked our guide to maintain a distance.
After snorkeling, we had a picnic on a sandbar, which was again beautiful, with shallow, clear, and warm waters. However, it was still very touristic and crowded. We advise waiting until most of the tourists have left if possible; this way, you can enjoy the area with more peace.
The sea is lovely, but there are too many tourists, polluting the waters with garbage and hunting dolphins. Therefore, Zanzibar needs to start protecting this area more; otherwise, it will be entirely dead in no time. It is heartbreaking to witness.

content: Congoman Cave gives an insight into the world of caving that is both assured and fascinating. Whilst this is a tourist attraction, it is a guided wild cave rather than a show cave. As such, visitors can expect to see the underground world, largely unspoilt by human activity. There are a number of chambers, well decorated with stal formations and crystal clear pools. Visitors are provided with helmet and light and should expect to get a little muddy. The cave environment is warm and humid, but trousers and long sleeves are probably preferred as there is some hands and knees crawling involved, A guide is actually optional but is highly recommended for those with no previous experience of caving. The time spent undergoing is entirely up to the visitor, but half to three quarters of an hour should cover it. There are facilities on the surface to clean up and enjoy some excellent refreshments. Finally, a word on photography. Cameras and phones should be taken underground entirely at one’s own risk. Getting lighting, focus and composition right in this environment is tricky, but very rewarding when it all works. Congoman Cave is highly recommended, particularly for those looking for an experience a little bit out of the norm.

The food was the only decent thing, nothing spectacular, and considering it's the only worthwhile part of the excursion, it was incredibly expensive. I don't think their cash cow will last long if they continue with this terrible management.

content:
The full-day Safari Blue Trips on the dhow sailboats are cool overall, but don't expect too much.
Although we had booked a boat for private use for $250 USD, there were five other people on board besides our three-person crew. They were using our trip as a taxi ride out to the island. We weren't aware of this, and nothing was explained to us.
No one introduced themselves, not even a hello. The sea was rough, and the eight Tanzanians in total were crammed into the corner of the boat sheltered from the spray. We, the paying guests, were left with the wet spots. Even the mother with the baby in her arms wasn't offered a seat. It wasn't until we complained that some reluctantly gave up their places.
The trip out to the island took an hour and a half, where we were dumped on a sandbar along with an estimated 100 other tourists. Two crew members came with us and laid out a large platter of fresh fruit: pineapple, coconut, and watermelon. We also had a cooler with ice-cold water, Coke, Fanta, and beer.
Afterward, our sailboat took us over to a dead coral reef. It lies right next to the sandbar. The reef is now just a shadow of its former self: the dead coral lies scattered about like on a war zone, and the sight is truly heartbreaking.
Afterward, we landed on the main island, where a sumptuous lunch was served: rice, lobster, shrimp, octopus, and squid. Here, beverage vendors sell a variety of alcoholic drinks at exorbitant prices.
For the return trip, the boat crew hoisted the sails, and we sailed back comfortably in beautiful weather.

content:
A star because there are too many people who don't realize that touching and taking these marine creatures out of the water leads to their death. Just a few seconds out of the water are enough for an air bubble to form in the hell of its delicate system of canals, causing an embolism, or causing overheating and distraction of the skin, leading to the DEATH of this beautiful animal.
The problem is that both the tour guides and the boat captains, talking to them, made me think this wasn't true or that they were deliberately ignoring this fact, knowing that their job is to show you these beautiful creatures.
So remember that touching them or taking them out of the water means killing them.
Dive in and look at them with great enthusiasm and love for these amazing animals.
PS: The photo was taken by our guide after we decided not to see them out of the water, but their job is precisely to show and touch the starfish to unaware and ignorant tourists.

content:

Our first excursion included snorkeling equipment, refreshments, and a generous fruit platter. On the second day, all entrance fees and lunch were included in the tour.
Day 1: Excursion to Mnemba Island
In the morning, we were picked up directly from our hotel and taken to the harbor, where our boat was waiting. On Mnemba Island, we had the opportunity to swim with dolphins, snorkel extensively, and enjoy the provided fruit platter on a sandbar. This experience was simply breathtaking! Around midday, we returned to the hotel and were able to relax for the rest of the day.
Day 2: Spice Tour, Prison Island, and Stone Town
The second day began with a hotel pick-up for the spice tour. Adam led us through the plantations in a fascinating way, explaining the origin and uses of the various spices and making the tour a truly memorable experience. After a delicious lunch, we continued our tour. In Stone Town, we were met by Hassan, another guide, who led us through the historical sites of Prison Island and the charming streets of Stone Town.
In the evening, Adam brought us safely back to the hotel, filled with impressive impressions and wonderful memories.
Both excursions exceeded our expectations, and we highly recommend Adam to anyone who wants to discover Zanzibar in a unique way.

content:
Visiting this beach was truly a lifetime experience. I enjoyed three unforgettable activities—the sandbank, snorkeling, and dolphins—each offering its own magic.
Sandbank: The sandbank was absolutely breathtaking. Standing on a stretch of pristine white sand surrounded by turquoise waters felt surreal, almost like being on a private paradise. It’s the kind of view that stays etched in memory forever.
Snorkeling: The snorkeling experience was simply wow! The underwater world was vibrant, with colorful corals and schools of fish gliding gracefully. The clarity of the water made it easy to appreciate the beauty beneath the surface.
Dolphins: Watching dolphins in their natural habitat was excellent. Their playful jumps and graceful movements added pure joy to the trip. It felt like nature’s own show, performed just for us.
Additional Highlights
The boat ride itself was refreshing, with stunning views of the coastline.
The staff and guides were friendly, ensuring safety while also making the experience enjoyable.
Timing the trip in the morning made the atmosphere calmer and the water clearer, enhancing the overall adventure.
Overall Impression
This beach offers a perfect blend of relaxation and adventure. From the serenity of the sandbank to the thrill of snorkeling and the excitement of spotting dolphins, it’s an experience that combines beauty, fun, and nature at its best. Highly recommended for anyone seeking a memorable coastal escape.

content:
Muyuni beach is one of those places that truly feels like nature’s wonder. Unlike other beaches where you relax along the shoreline, here you actually take a boat ride to reach the beach itself, because during the day, the tide recedes and reveals a stunning stretch of sand right in the middle of the ocean.
This phenomenon usually happens between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., when the ocean pulls back just enough to create a natural sandbank surrounded by crystal-clear turquoise water. Boats begin to arrive one after another, bringing travelers who come to soak in the sun, swim, and simply enjoy the unreal beauty of this spot.
Once there, you can relax under the sun, get a tan, enjoy fresh fruits or drinks, and just take in the 360-degree view of the Indian Ocean. It’s peaceful, yet lively — a place where you bring your own vibe. Many come with tour guides or small groups, and it’s easy to make friends while basking in the sun and wading through the shallow waters.
From Muyuni Beach, you can also see Bill Gates Island in the distance, which adds to the fascination of the view. The water is incredibly clear, perfect for swimming, and you’ll often spot starfish scattered along the sand.
While there aren’t many structured activities — no restaurants or major setups that’s part of the charm. It’s a pure, natural experience where you can disconnect and enjoy the simplicity of being surrounded by endless ocean.
Overall, Muyuni Beach is a must-visit if you love unique natural settings. The idea of standing on a beach in the middle of the sea, with the waves gently encircling you, is something you’ll never forget.

content:
This is a stunning white sand beach, perfect for snorkeling and spotting dolphins offshore. You’re sure to have a great time, but here’s an important tip: If you plan to hire a captain and guide for snorkeling, ensure they have the proper local authorization and licenses. There’s a $3 tax per person for offshore trips, and guides must comply with local regulations.
We had a bad experience when we hired a captain who lacked these credentials. Mid-trip, we were stopped by another boat that tied a rope to ours and towed us to Mnemba Island without any explanation. The crew only spoke Swahili to our captain, and we feared they might be robbers. It wasn’t until the next day we learned it was the tourist police, enforcing rules our guide had ignored.
As long as your guide follows the regulations and provides proper equipment, you’ll have a fantastic experience. Be mindful of beach vendors as well—some may offer beautiful seashells, but keep in mind it’s illegal to export them. I can't blame them, they’re just trying to make a living, and may not know these rules, but it’s important to be aware of the rules as a tourist.

content: Muyuni Beach is very beautiful, and if you walk a little further past the hotels, it's also very quiet and empty. The Mnemba Atoll is truly wonderful for snorkeling (there are many fish and large schools, although the coral is largely dead due to mass tourism), but it gets quite crowded in the afternoon, even in the off-season, so it's worth getting there as early as possible. If you want to see the dolphins, you'll have to get up early anyway. They disappear into deeper waters as soon as there are too many boats, but if you're lucky and catch them early, you can see them very close. Unfortunately, some people, lacking respect for nature, swim too close and disturb the dolphins, causing them to retreat to deeper water. If you simply remain calm and give the animals their space, they will swim close by, but you can't force anything, and pressuring them won't achieve much. It's not necessary to book an expensive tour through your hotel. Simply take bus number 118 from Zanzibar City (Saateni bus stop, departs at 6:00 AM) to Matemwe (arrives around 7:30 AM and costs 2500 TZS) and head to the beach. There you'll find many people with boats trying to sell you tours (around €15). Afterwards, you can enjoy the beach and easily take the bus back in the afternoon; they run regularly.

We had an absolutely unforgettable 3-day safari in Mikumi National Park and are so grateful to Seif for this amazing time. He picked us up on the very first day and we drove to visit the Maasai, which was a truly wonderful introduction. We stayed overnight at the 3G Mikumi Safari Lodge right in the middle of the bush – an incredible experience! The staff were so welcoming and it was simply magical to lie in bed at night and hear all the wildlife outside.
The next morning we set off on safari in a Land Rover. We saw so much: lions, giraffes, zebras, wildebeest, and an incredible number of colorful birds. Our driver knew so much about the animals and explained everything to us in great detail; it was just so much fun.
Afterwards, we went back to Morogoro, where Seif had booked us into the Hotel Eden. It was absolutely beautiful with a large garden and animals on the grounds, and the food there was also really good. Seif took perfect care of us the entire time, always providing drinks and food, and even letting us try many different fruits we'd never seen before.
The journey by train and ferry was an experience in itself and really helped us slow down. In a huge, bustling city like Dar es Salaam, with its tight 15-minute transfer times, we were incredibly grateful to have Seif with us as a local who knew exactly where to go. content:
Absolutely fantastic experience with Seif! Seif is the kind of person you feel like a friend with. He took care of everything from the air-conditioned ferry and train tickets to the smallest details so we didn't have to worry about anything and just enjoyed the ride. Our 3 day safari from Zanzibar to Mikumi National Park exceeded all expectations and I can honestly say it was an unforgettable adventure.
The ferry and train journey was a great introduction to the Tanzanian atmosphere. Instead of a fast flight that would have robbed us of the views, we enjoyed a scenic ferry ride from Zanzibar to Dar es Salaam (it only takes about 1 hour and 20 minutes) and then a comfortable ride on the modern SGR high-speed train towards Mikumi Park. Traveling overland allowed us to see more of Tanzania's life and landscape.
On the first day, Seif took us to an authentic Maasai village. It was no "theater for tourists" but a real encounter with their culture. We saw a demonstration of their signature dance, and even got to join in! It was an incredible start that immediately put us on the African wave.
The safari in Mikumi itself was incredible. The park is home to a huge variety of animals and we were lucky enough to see literally everything we could have wished for. Lions, elephants, giraffes, zebras, buffaloes and hippos – we observed all these majestic creatures up close, often just a few meters from our jeep. It was a dream come true to see them in their natural habitat, moving and living freely.
If you are planning a safari or other attractions in Zanzibar, look for Seif. His professionalism, knowledge and friendly approach made this trip the best experience in all of Tanzania!

content:
My negative review is primarily due to the poor treatment of the tortoises. Signs warn of a $50 fine for bypassing the fences, but many guides and tourists don't care; they ignore the barriers and wake up the oldest tortoise from sleeping—allegedly 200 years old—just to take group photos for there cellphones. I had heard about older animals dying recently, which comes as no surprise given how they are treated here. The security staff—at least three or four of them—were all making themselves comfortable in the ticket booth while total chaos reigned outside, people teasing the old turtles for waking then up, largely driven by guides acting overzealously in hopes of better tips.
We found this animal cruelty appalling; what is the point of charging high conservation fees? It’s a complete farce—it’s all about the commercial exploitation of these poor animals. 😢
To top it all off, at the end of the tour—right at the exit—they actively solicit voluntary donations, despite the high conservation surcharge already paid. I don't even want to know where that money goes... perhaps some to the 'hard-working'" security team?"

content:
Very disappointing experience. Prison Island (Changuu Island) has very little to see besides the giant tortoises, and the facilities are extremely limited — almost no proper restaurants, cafés, or comfortable places to rest. The whole visit took us about one hour, yet the total cost was a bit high.
What made it worse was the confusing and non-transparent payment system. Visitors are asked to pay multiple separate charges: a “government/city tax” (around $10), the island entrance fee (about $12 per person), and additional round-trip boat fees paid separately to boat operators. Even more frustrating, some boatmen try to mislead visitors by saying that if you pay them the boat fee, you won’t need to pay the tax — which is not true, as the tax is still required. This kind of misinformation makes the experience very unpleasant.
Overall, the island feels poorly organized, overpriced for what it offers, and the entire process is unnecessarily complicated. Unless you really want to see the tortoises, this trip is not worth the cost or the hassle.

The turtles live alongside peacocks and seem to be doing quite well. Otherwise, the infrastructure is rather neglected and unkempt. At the entrance stands an abandoned building, supposedly closed for renovations; it could have been a luxury hotel. These giant tortoises are impressive: huge and calm, as if time had stood still for them. You can feed them and pet them—they're not afraid, just lazily stretching their necks for leaves.
The park itself is well-kept, with plenty of greenery and shade—a welcome relief from the heat.

content: Changu Island, also known as Prison Island, is home to a hatchery for giant Seychelles tortoises. These tortoises were gifted to Zanzibar by the Governor of the Seychelles in the early 20th century and have since proliferated here in large numbers. The oldest tortoise I've seen here is 150 years old (the age of the oldest specimens is indicated by paint on their shells, which are periodically replaced). These are very cute and not particularly agile creatures; you can feed them fallen leaves or cabbage, or scratch their necks from below. Entrance to the hatchery costs 10,000 shillings per person. You can get to the island by renting a boat from the Stone Town waterfront in Zanzibar. I really enjoyed it; it's a must-see.

content:
In 1919 the British governor of Seychelles sent a gift of four Aldabra giant tortoises to Changuu from the island of Aldabra. These tortoises bred quickly and by 1955 they numbered around 200 animals. However people began to steal the tortoises for sale abroad as pets or for food and their numbers dropped rapidly. By 1988 there were around 100 tortoises, fifty in 1990 and just seven by 1996. A further 80 hatchlings were taken to the island in 1996 to increase the numbers but 40 of them vanished. The Zanzibar government, with assistance from the World Society for the Protection of Animals (Now known as World Animal Protection) built a large compound for the protection of the animals and by 2000 numbers had recovered to 17 adults, 50 juveniles and 90 hatchlings.
The species is now considered vulnerable and has been placed on the IUCN Red List by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. More tortoises, mainly juveniles, continue to be brought to the island from other locations for conservation. There is a dedicated foundation on the island which looks after the tortoises welfare. Visitors are able to observe and feed the tortoises.

content:
Tortoises Island:-(Amazing place)
Changuu Island (also known as Kibandiko, Prison or Quarantine Island) is a small island 5.6 km north-west of Stone Town, Unguja, Zanzibar. The island is around 800m long and 230m wide at its broadest point.[1] The island saw use as a prison for rebellious slaves in 1860s and also functioned as a coral mine. The British First Minister of Zanzibar, Lloyd Mathews, purchased the island in 1893 and constructed a prison complex there. No prisoners were ever housed on the island and instead it became a quarantine station for yellow fever cases. The station was only occupied for around half of the year and the rest of the time it was a popular holiday destination. More recently, the island has become a government-owned tourist resort and houses a collection of endangered Aldabra giant tortoises which were originally a gift from the British governor of the Seychelles.

content:
Really really wish I could have given it more, and perhaps if my husband and I had left 10 minutes earlier, I would have given 4 or 5. However, while we were at the sanctuary, a woman stepped into the water and the turtles all swam to her because she had food - it seemed to be going fine at first (we were in the water too and having a great time) when all of a sudden the woman screamed so loud and for so long, begging for someone to come help her that we scrambled out of there as fast as we could. Turns out that one of the two very large turtles had swam towards her foot under the water's surface and bit it incredibly hard, and it just would not let go. Many workers jumped into the water trying to wrestle the turtle off this poor woman and struggled to do so. Eventually the turtle released her foot, she was helped out and her foot was not in a good way, it was bleeding everywhere. It was a very scary experience and we count ourselves incredibly lucky that wasn't us!
I was disappointed at the urgency of the staff members there, and how they didn't seem to take the incident very seriously once the woman was safely out of the water. We stayed with her and helped to calm her down until her taxi arrived to take her to a doctor, after which I mentioned to staff that they should not keep the large turtles in the pool where people go in. They are just too big and strong and she could have lost her toes. The man agreed but I don't know if they've changed that particular policy.
I would say that this is probably a freak accident and the turtles did seem well looked after, the facilities were good and the staff were kind and helpful while we enjoyed our time there up until that incident. This place definitely sounds better than close-by swim with turtle experiences as its quieter and the turtles have a lot of space to swim. However, if you plan to visit, please remember that these are wild animals and when you go into the water, you go in at your own risk. And word of advice, if you see there are still large turtles there, maybe stick to the boat and feeding from the side, avoid getting close to them.

content:
We discovered the museum by chance. It's very small, but it offers a fascinating glimpse into her life. As the daughter of a sultan, she had a carefree life in the palace, later inheriting a large estate and meeting the German merchant Ruete from Hamburg. Since marriage to a Christian was unthinkable, she fled with him, pregnant, to Hamburg to escape the stoning that threatened her. Later, she lived in Dresden and Weimar. She died impoverished in Jena. She wrote two volumes of "Memoirs of an Arabian Princess," and the proceeds from their sales supported her.
The museum is well worth seeing; the staff member was very friendly and told us everything. (Visited November 2022)

content:
Seven years ago, this place was truly special. It felt untouched and natural — long stretches of sandy beach, very few buildings, small locally run boutique hotels and restaurants. It had space to breathe. It felt authentic, peaceful and beautifully simple.
Coming back now was honestly heartbreaking. Many of the local businesses have been pushed inland, and the beachfront is dominated by large resort complexes that feel disconnected from the island itself. These massive hotels don’t blend into the surroundings and often create a bubble where guests rarely interact with the local culture. For that kind of experience, you don’t need to travel all the way to Zanzibar.
Because of this change, we sadly cannot recommend Michamvi the way we once did.
However, there are still local restaurants and small hotels operating and we strongly encourage visitors to actively choose and support them. If you want to experience the real Zanzibar and ensure your stay benefits the community, seek out locally owned businesses. They are the heart of this place and deserve to thrive.

content: Excellent, explained everything very well. The tour lasted 2 hours. Super thorough. We smelled and tasted the various spices. Even though it was out of season for most spice trees, we still enjoyed the experience! Highly recommended! The price was very fair.

content:
Wow, what an incredible experience! Can't recommend this highly enough! It's a small family owned farm, but the owner is very knowledgeable and he speaks English very well.
It's not just vanilla either. I think he had all the spices and fruits: cinnamon, pepper, all spice, cloves, coffee, cacao, aloe vera, star fruit, and more! He had a detailed explanation of how to harvest then and all their health benefits.
I think our tour was about 2+ hours. Call ahead to reserve a time.

clauses.clause_text: Can't recommend this highly enough!
